x: 01 Overview What ForgeQE is, and everything it can do ForgeQE is a browser agent CLI. Say what you want in plain language: a goal to carry out in a browser, test cases to run from Jira, Azure DevOps, Xray or a file, a test to write, or a CI pipeline to set up. ForgeQE's agent works out what that needs, the ForgeQE engine drives a local Chrome or Chromium by default or BrowserStack or TestMu AI/LambdaTest when configured, and a run that passes becomes a test in your repo, written by Scribe , ForgeQE's coding agent. No server, database, or Docker. You configure a model and run it from the terminal. 02 Get started Install, configure a model, and sign in to your tools
What you need to run

Required Requirement Notes npm (Node.js 18+) or pip (Python 3.9+) To install @capagents/forgeqe or forgeqe-cli ; either one gives the same forgeqe command A terminal macOS Terminal, iTerm2, VS Code or Cursor's terminal, Windows Terminal A model A profile in llms.json with a working key, or Microsoft Entra ID sign-in for Azure (Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, an OpenAI-compatible gateway, or Ollama), or a GitHub Copilot seat (see GitHub Copilot seats as the model ) Internet access on first use ForgeQE downloads Bun, the agent runtime, uv, Python, and the engine into ~/.forgeqe once

Optional Optional Why Google Chrome Used when installed; otherwise ForgeQE installs Chromium. Or set browser.provider to BrowserStack or TestMu AI/LambdaTest A repo with tests Where passed runs become tests ( --repo , or code.repo ); without one, tests go in the current folder Jira, Azure DevOps, Xray, TestRail, Zephyr Scale, qTest, Confluence Sources of test cases and requirements, and where results go back gh or az For pipelines: pushing, secrets, and triggering runs Teams webhook or SMTP Monitoring alerts
Not required Installing Python, Bun, browsers, or agent runtimes yourself: ForgeQE downloads what it needs, without admin rights and without touching PATH A server, database, or Docker

Quick start bash Copy npm install -g @capagents/forgeqe # or: pip install forgeqe-cli forgeqe init # forgeqe.yaml, llms.json, and .forgeqe/ (prompts, skills, knowledge) in this folder export WP_AZURE_API_KEY=... # the key your llms.json profile names forgeqe models # check the profiles forgeqe start # the shell With GitHub Copilot licences instead of a model key, sign in rather than exporting one. The sign-in lists your seat's models, recommends one (it takes screenshots and, where the plan has one, uses no premium requests), and writes your choice to llms.json as the copilot profile, made the default. Everything then runs on your Copilot seat: ForgeQE's agent, Scribe, and the browser, desktop and mobile engines. No other model is needed: bash Copy forgeqe setup # the engine and GitHub's Copilot SDK forgeqe auth login copilot # opens GitHub in your browser to sign in, then pick the model forgeqe doctor # checks the engine, the SDK, the agent runtime, the sign-in and each model In the shell, type a request and press Enter: text Copy Go to booking.com and search for hotels in Mumbai for next weekend Run SHOP-12 and SHOP-14 from Jira, two browsers at once Write a Playwright test for that run in ../app Without the shell: bash Copy forgeqe run "Search hotels in Mumbai on booking.com" --plain forgeqe suite cases.yaml --parallel 3 # what pipelines call forgeqe models lists the profiles ForgeQE sees and marks the active one. With no profile set up, the shell's footer reads Model none set up and any request explains how to add one. With more than one profile, llm.routing: auto gives each kind of work (agent, browser, coding, review, analysis, planning) the configured model it needs; forgeqe models --routes shows the picks. See docs/MODEL_ROUTING.md .

Install bash Copy npm install -g @capagents/forgeqe # or pip install forgeqe-cli forgeqe --help That is the only install step on Windows, macOS and Linux. npm installs Bun with ForgeQE (through your npm registry, so a company mirror works); with pip, or when npm skipped it, the first run downloads Bun into ~/.forgeqe/tools (unless a Bun 1.3+ is already installed), and forgeqe setup downloads the agent runtime and uv, which fetches Python. Nothing is added to PATH or shell profiles; deleting ~/.forgeqe removes it all. Set up the ForgeQE engine once (the first live run does it automatically if you skip this): bash Copy forgeqe setup It creates ~/.forgeqe/engine/.venv , installs the engine's Python libraries, and prints the Python, the engine version, the browser it found, and the agent runtime. Google Chrome is used when installed; otherwise Chromium is installed. forgeqe setup --force rebuilds the environment.

Updating bash Copy forgeqe update # every forgeqe on PATH to the latest release forgeqe update --check # show what would change and the commands it would run forgeqe update 0.2.7 # a given version forgeqe --version forgeqe update finds each forgeqe on PATH (a bun, npm or pip install; often more than one) and updates each with the tool that installed it, skipping that tool's cached copy of the version list. Right after a release, npm and PyPI accept the upload several minutes before installers can fetch it, and bun add or npm install in that window says No version matching ; forgeqe update waits for the registry instead (up to 20 minutes, --wait MIN to change). The first forgeqe on PATH is the one your shell runs; open a new terminal (or run hash -r ) after updating. From a checkout instead of the registries: bash Copy cd ForgeQE bun install bun src/index.ts --help

Company networks On a company laptop, ForgeQE sets itself up for the network without anyone changing settings: What the network does What ForgeQE does Inspects HTTPS (Zscaler, Netskope, a firewall), with the company's own certificate Uses the certificates this computer trusts: Windows' Trusted Root store, or the macOS System keychain. ForgeQE, the agent runtime, Playwright and Copilot's runtime get them through NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS (a copy in ~/.forgeqe/cache/system-ca.pem , refreshed weekly); the Python engines check with the system through truststore; uv with UV_SYSTEM_CERTS . Certificates are still verified. Sends traffic through a proxy set in Windows Reads Windows' proxy setting (or the one proxy its automatic configuration script names) and passes it on as HTTPS_PROXY . ForgeQE's own servers on 127.0.0.1 always bypass it. Blocks downloads from GitHub or the Playwright CDN npm brings Bun through your registry; Microsoft Edge is used when Google Chrome is not installed, so no Chromium is downloaded; mirrors can stand in for the rest (below). To see where the network stops ForgeQE, run: bash Copy forgeqe doctor It shows the proxy and certificates in use, checks each address ForgeQE needs (GitHub downloads, Python packages, the npm registry, your models, Azure DevOps or Jira), and for anything blocked prints what to ask IT for, ready to forward. For IT: mirrors and settings. Set these as environment variables (for example by Group Policy): Variable What it does FORGEQE_GITHUB_MIRROR A mirror of GitHub release downloads ( https://artifacts.example.com/github , laid out as <owner>/<repo>/releases/download/<tag>/<file> ): Bun, uv, the agent runtime, Python builds and Copilot's runtime come from it. Checksums are still checked. UV_DEFAULT_INDEX (or PIP_INDEX_URL ) A mirror of PyPI for the engine's Python packages. PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST A mirror for Chromium, needed only without Chrome or Edge. HTTPS_PROXY , NO_PROXY A proxy other than Windows' setting. A proxy that needs a sign-in takes http://user:password@host:port . NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS Your own certificate file instead of the system's roots. FORGEQE_SYSTEM_CERTS=off Leaves certificates to each tool's built-in list. FORGEQE_HOME Where ForgeQE keeps its tools (default ~/.forgeqe ), for machines where programs may run only from certain folders. What still needs IT: a proxy that signs in with your Windows account only (NTLM or Kerberos), and policies that block programs in the user folder (set FORGEQE_HOME to an allowed folder). On macOS, the company's certificate must be in the System keychain, where device management puts it.

Scaffold config bash Copy bun src/index.ts init # or bun src/index.ts init --global --profile azure-gpt4o Edit llms.json endpoints, then give ForgeQE the keys its profiles name ( WP_AZURE_API_KEY , OPENAI_API_KEY , WP_API_KEY ): forgeqe auth login <NAME> saves one in your system's credential store, or put them in a .env next to forgeqe.yaml ; the engine process inherits them.

t: Signing in to the model without a key (Microsoft Entra ID)
x: Signing in to the model without a key (Microsoft Entra ID) Where keys are turned off ( disableLocalAuth on the Azure OpenAI or Foundry resource, managed identities, zero trust), set auth: entra on an azure profile instead of api_key_env . Key profiles keep working, and both kinds can sit side by side in one llms.json : json Copy "azure-entra": { "provider": "azure", "model": "gpt-4o", "deployment": "gpt-4o", "endpoint": "https://YOUR_RESOURCE.openai.azure.com/", "auth": "entra", "managed_identity_client_id": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000" } ForgeQE asks Microsoft Entra ID for a token wherever it runs, trying in this order: Where ForgeQE runs Identity it uses An Azure VM, VM scale set, self-hosted agent, App Service, Functions, Container Apps The user-assigned managed identity named by managed_identity_client_id (or AZURE_CLIENT_ID ); without one, the system-assigned identity AKS Workload identity ( AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE , set by the webhook) Azure Pipelines An AzureCLI@2 task on a service connection with workload identity federation: ForgeQE uses that task's sign-in, with no secret GitHub Actions azure/login with OIDC, then ForgeQE in the same job Your machine az login Anything else A service principal in AZURE_TENANT_ID , AZURE_CLIENT_ID and AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET (or AZURE_CLIENT_CERTIFICATE_PATH ) Give that identity the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role on the resource. Tokens are renewed before they expire, so long suites and coding sessions keep running. The browser engine signs in itself; the coding agent's runtime only takes a key, so ForgeQE gives it a gateway on 127.0.0.1 that accepts a one-time random key and passes each request on with a current token. No key is stored anywhere. auth: entra also works on an openai_compatible profile, for a gateway such as API Management that checks Entra ID tokens: set token_scope to the scope it expects (for example api://<app id>/.default ; the default is https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/.default ). The engine needs the azure-identity package, which forgeqe setup installs (and adds to environments set up before it was needed); with FORGEQE_PYTHON , install it there yourself.

t: GitHub Copilot seats as the model
x: GitHub Copilot seats as the model With GitHub Copilot licences (Pro, Pro+, Business or Enterprise), a github_copilot profile runs the browser engine and the desktop and mobile agents on your Copilot seat, through GitHub's Copilot SDK . Copilot gives other tools no model API of its own, so ForgeQE starts a small gateway on 127.0.0.1 that runs the SDK and speaks the OpenAI chat API to the engine. It signs in with a GitHub token, so no other app is authorized on your GitHub account. json Copy "copilot": { "provider": "github_copilot", "model": "gpt-4.1" } Field What it is model The Copilot model, as the Copilot SDK names it ( gpt-4.1 , claude-sonnet-4.6 ). It must take screenshots. The sign-in lists your seat's models and which of them take images. engine_model Optional. Another Copilot model for the browser engine and the desktop agent. api_key_env Optional. A variable that must hold the GitHub token for this profile. Without it ForgeQE uses COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN , then a token forgeqe auth login copilot saved, then the browser sign-in. Sign in once per machine (Windows, macOS or Linux): bash Copy forgeqe auth login copilot It offers two ways, the ones GitHub's Copilot SDK recommends: Sign in with GitHub in the browser (recommended on your own computer). ForgeQE runs GitHub's own Copilot sign-in ( copilot login from GitHub's Copilot CLI, downloaded once into ~/.forgeqe/tools and checked against GitHub's checksums). Your browser opens GitHub; approve GitHub Copilot CLI there and you are signed in. GitHub's CLI keeps the sign-in in your system's credential store (Windows Credential Manager, the macOS Keychain); ForgeQE never sees a token. On a remote machine it shows a code to enter at github.com/login/device instead. A fine-grained token , for machines without a browser. ForgeQE opens GitHub's token page: set Resource owner to your personal account and add the Copilot Requests permission, then paste the token ( github_pat_... ). Each character shows as * , and ForgeQE confirms what it got ( github_pat_11AB…Wz9Q (93 characters) ). The token goes to your system's credential store like ForgeQE's other secrets. Classic tokens ( ghp_ ) do not work with Copilot. Either way ForgeQE checks the sign-in by asking Copilot for your seat's models, then asks which one to use (recommended first; models your seat has but has not turned on are named, with the settings page) and writes it to llms.json ; the first time, the Copilot SDK downloads Copilot's runtime from GitHub (checked against GitHub's checksums). forgeqe auth shows the sign-in on its Copilot line; forgeqe auth logout copilot makes ForgeQE stop using it (GitHub keeps a browser sign-in until you revoke GitHub Copilot CLI at github.com/settings/applications). If your organization uses SAML single sign-on, GitHub asks you to authorize the organization during the browser sign-in. A Copilot Business or Enterprise seat needs your organization to allow Copilot CLI in its Copilot policies. A token reaches only the gateway's process. The engine gets the gateway's address and a one-time key that works nowhere else; the gateway refuses requests without that key and any request a web page sends. Model-run shell commands never see the token or the key. Which part uses what: Part Model Signs in with The browser engine (every browser run: run --direct , suites, monitoring) engine_model or model , on the Copilot seat forgeqe auth login copilot The desktop and mobile agents engine_model or model , on the Copilot seat forgeqe auth login copilot ForgeQE's agent and Scribe model , on the Copilot seat forgeqe auth login copilot Copilot runs one SDK session per model request, with none of Copilot's own tools and your request's system prompt in place of Copilot's. The agent's tools are offered to the model as the session's only tools; when it calls one, the gateway ends the turn and hands the call back to ForgeQE's agent runtime, which runs it (with the same permissions as on any other model) and sends the result with the next request. The gateway itself runs nothing. With Copilot and a key-based model both in llms.json , Copilot comes first: a sign-in makes it the default, and without a "default" it is the active profile. Before a model is used, ForgeQE checks that it works (its sign-in or key, and one live call, kept for a day once it passes). If Copilot does not work (not signed in, the Copilot SDK missing, the model not on your seat), the other model is used and ForgeQE says why and how to fix Copilot; if a key-based model you made the default does not work, Copilot is tried first. A model that fails its check is never used, and when none works the error lists each one with what to do. This happens with llm.routing off too: routing picks a model for each kind of work, the fallback only replaces one that does not work. --profile turns it off for one run, and llm.fallback: false in forgeqe.yaml for good: the model you chose is used as it is, and its own error is shown. Each request is billed to the seat (GitHub AI credits or premium requests, by your plan), and GitHub may rate-limit frequent automated requests. If a model is refused, check that your organization's Copilot policies allow it. ForgeQE shows no cost for a github_copilot profile unless you give it a price . In pipelines. forgeqe suite ... --no-code uses only the browser engine. Set COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN to a fine-grained token with the Copilot Requests permission, stored as a pipeline secret. GitHub also documents the workflow's own GITHUB_TOKEN with permissions: copilot-requests: write for organization repositories whose Copilot policy allows it ( server tokens ). A Copilot seat belongs to one person: prefer an organization-billed token over signing a shared pipeline in to someone's seat. GitHub Models, which ForgeQE used for the engine before, was retired by GitHub on July 30, 2026. A profile that still has engine_model: "openai/..." or github_org needs updating: drop github_org , and use a Copilot mode

The model's context window Each agent has its own context: ForgeQE's agent, Scribe, the reviewer, and the browser agent each keep their own conversation with the model. The Context panel shows the working agent's (or the last one to call the model), named on its Agent row, as a share of what it can hold before the agent runtime compacts it. When it compacts, the runtime summarises the conversation so far to make room, Activity says so, and details from early on may be gone. The browser agent never compacts: it keeps its last steps only. ForgeQE takes each model's window from its name (GPT-5: 400K, of which a prompt may take 272K; GPT-4.1: 1M; GPT-4o: 128K; o-series and Claude: 200K; Gemini: 1M; anything else: 200K) and gives it to the agent runtime, which compacts at that window less room for the answer. Where a deployment or server allows less, say so with "context" in the profile in llms.json : json Copy "ollama-llama": { "provider": "ollama", "model": "llama3.2", "endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1", "context": 32768 } For Ollama this matters: a prompt longer than the server's context length is cut from the start without an error. Without "context" ForgeQE assumes 32K for an Ollama profile; start the server with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH set to the same number.

Signing in to your tools Instead of copying tokens into .env , sign in once and ForgeQE saves the token in your system's credential store: the macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or the Secret Service keyring on Linux. On a machine without one, such as a headless Linux box, it uses ~/.forgeqe/credentials.json , readable only by you. bash Copy forgeqe auth login # pick a system forgeqe auth login jira # or name it: azure_devops, github, copilot, jira, confluence, testrail, zephyr, qtest, xray forgeqe auth # what is signed in, and how forgeqe auth logout jira In the shell, type /auth jira (or /auth alone for the status). Tokens are typed into the prompt box unseen, shown as dots, and never sent to the agent. System How you sign in Azure DevOps Sign in with Microsoft in the browser through the Azure CLI ( az login ); ForgeQE saves nothing, and the Azure CLI renews the sign-in. Or paste a personal access token: the token page opens with the scopes to tick. Azure DevOps Server (on-premises) uses a personal access token. GitHub Sign in with GitHub in the browser through the GitHub CLI ( gh auth login ): ForgeQE shows the one-time code and opens the page. Or paste a token. Needs gh installed. forgeqe auth login copilot can use this sign-in for a github_copilot profile. GitHub Copilot forgeqe auth login copilot : Sign in with GitHub in the browser (GitHub's own Copilot sign-in), or paste a fine-grained token with the Copilot Requests permission. ForgeQE checks it with Copilot and lists the models your seat has. For a github_copilot profile; see GitHub Copilot seats as the model . Jira, Confluence Your Atlassian API tokens page opens (Cloud) or your personal access tokens page (Server/Data Center); create one and paste it. Confluence on the same Cloud site as Jira reuses the Jira sign-in. TestRail, Zephyr Scale, qTest, Xray Cloud The page with your API key opens, or ForgeQE says where to find it; paste it. Anything else forgeqe auth login OPENAI_API_KEY (any variable name) saves that one secret: a model key, a Teams webhook URL, an SMTP or saved-login password. Atlassian's OAuth sign-in needs a client secret, which a command-line tool cannot keep secret, so Jira and Confluence use API tokens: they are what Atlassian recommends for scripts and tools. Each token is checked against the system before it is saved, and the system is switched on: a saved Jira sign-in sets the site URL too, so sources.jira is not needed in forgeqe.yaml . Saved values go in under the variable names the config already reads ( JIRA_API_TOKEN , ADO_PAT , ...). A variable exported in the terminal is used before a saved sign-in, and a saved sign-in before a .env file, so pipelines keep using their secrets. The shell commands the agents run never see the saved secrets.

t: Choosing the model and the browser
x: Choosing the model and the browser forgeqe.yaml selects the active profile: yaml Copy llm: models_file: ./llms.json active: azure-gpt4o routing: auto # off | shadow | auto: each area of work gets the model it needs # routes: # limit or pin an area: browser: [gpt4o, gpt54], coding: gpt54 browser: headless: true max_steps: 40 # a checkpoint: a run still making progress carries on, up to 3x timeout_seconds: 600 vision_detail: low allowed_hosts: [] judge: false # true: a second model call checks each finished run and can fail it overlay: true window: maximized # visible browser: maximized | viewport (a window of viewport's size) video: true # video.mp4 of each run, shown in its report # start_url: https://staging.example.com judge is off by default. When it is on, one more model call reads the finished run's steps and screenshots and can fail a run the agent completed, for example when five scores were read off one results page rather than one step per item. That strictness sent runs into loops of re-checking, so turn it on only when you want that second opinion. Each step waits for the tab the agent is on to finish loading (up to 8 seconds, 3 for a tab that stays blank) before the page is read, so a result that opens in a new tab is not mistaken for a blank page. With a visible browser ( headless: false or --headed ), ForgeQE opens on its own start page, and every page it drives gets a glowing edge and a bar along the bottom showing, in plain words, what the step is for and what the agent is doing ("Step 19 · Check whether the results can be sorted by Fastest · Looking through the page's buttons"). Your mouse and keyboard are locked while the agent thinks and unlocked while it clicks and types, so a stray click can't change the test. None of this appears in the screenshots the model sees or in the report. overlay: false turns it off. forgeqe login <name> shows the same bar without the lock, since you are the one signing in. A visible browser opens maximized. window: viewport opens it at viewport 's width and height instead; a headless page is always that size (1280×800 by default). Each run is recorded to video.mp4 in its run folder, and the report plays it on the run's page; video: false turns recording off. The video needs packages that forgeqe setup adds to the engine (an engine set up before this version gets them on its next run). start_url is optional. Leave it out and the agent picks the site from the goal; ForgeQE never guesses a URL from the goal text. allowed_hosts empty allows every host. Set ["example.com"] to keep the browser on that domain and its subdomains. prompts.step_instruction is appended to the engine's system prompt; the lines of prompts.guiderails are guardrails for every agent (see Guardrails above).
03 Using ForgeQE The shell, its commands, and running without it

Shell bash Copy bun src/index.ts start Type what you want and press Enter. The prompt wraps long text and grows as you type; Ctrl+J (or Shift+Enter, Alt+Enter where the terminal reports it) starts a new line, so you can paste or write several steps at once: text Copy Go to booking.com and search for hotels in Mumbai Run SHOP-12 and SHOP-14 from Jira, two browsers at once Run test plan 12 suite 34 from Azure DevOps and don't post results Write a Playwright test for that run Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs tests/cases.yaml on every PR, and make it green ForgeQE's agent reads the message and decides what it needs: a browser run, test cases from Jira, Azure DevOps, Xray, a file, or steps you pasted, a test, or a pipeline. There is no command to pick one. When a reference is ambiguous (is 12 a work item or a test plan?), it asks, and you answer in the next message; the session remembers the conversation. Its replies appear in the transcript, and so does everything its tools do: browser steps, suite progress, and the test commands ForgeQE runs. For a browser goal, the browser starts blank and the browser agent decides where to go, then works through cookie banners, sign-in prompts, and forms on the page. The transcript shows each step's goal and the actions it took ( navigate … , click "Accept" , input "Mumbai" → "Where are you going?" ), with ✗ and the error when an action fails. Everything the other forgeqe commands do is also a tool the agent can call, so you can ask for it here instead of leaving the shell: Ask for Tool Same as "Run SHOP-12 and SHOP-14", "what's in test plan 12?" run_test_cases , find_test_cases forgeqe suite , forgeqe cases "Write a Playwright test for that run" write_test forgeqe code "The checkout tests are failing, fix them" heal_tests forgeqe heal "Run all tests related to login", "run the tests added this sprint", "which tests cover checkout?" find_tests , run_tests , list_sprints (shell and forgeqe run only) "Check the smoke cases once", "monitor them every 10 minutes", "is anything failing?", "stop monitoring", "send a test alert" monitor forgeqe monitor , --once , --test-alerts "Sign in to shop", "which logins do I have?", "forget the shop session" logins forgeqe login , forgeqe logins , forgeqe logins clear "What flows does page memory know?", "forget what you learned about shop.test" page_memory forgeqe memory "What can you do?", "can you do API testing?", "do you support DORA?" capabilities forgeqe features "Which profiles do I have?", "which MCP servers will you use?", "how do email alerts work?", "install the engine", "scaffold a config in ./demo" forgeqe_setup forgeqe models , forgeqe mcp list , forgeqe docs , forgeqe setup , forgeqe init Only browser runs of the app under test become tests. When the agent uses the browser for a task, such as checking whether a story is linked to a test case in Azure DevOps or Jira, that run is marked as a task and no test is written for it, even if write_test is called on it. write_test and heal_tests run the same loops as the commands: ForgeQE runs the test command itself and a test only counts as passing when ForgeQE saw it pass. Their results, and each monitor round, appear as a card in the transcript. When a step needs you, such as signing in by hand in the browser window, a Your turn prompt shows what to do, and ForgeQE waits until you pick Done, continue (save the session) or Cancel . The slash commands control the session and show a few things directly ( /help lists them): Command Action /stop Stop what is running (or press Esc) /rerun [last|run] Run a passed run again as recorded, without ForgeQE's agent (the last one, a run folder, or its goal) /headed on|off Show the browser window (live profiles) /details [on|off] Show everything the agents do while they work: the browser agent's reasoning, page memory, engine logs, every file the coding agent reads (off by default: step results, files written, test results, problems). --verbose or FORGEQE_VERBOSE=1 starts with it on, for start , run , suite , code , and heal too /model Pick the model from the profiles in llms.json (or click the model ▾ in the status line; 04 Browser Goals carried out in a real browser, and the logins they use

t: Run any goal in a real browser
x: Browser Run any goal in a real browser Carries out a plain-language goal in a real browser one step at a time and verifies the outcome, with screenshots, a report, and the steps it took. The browser comes from forgeqe.yaml: local Chrome or Chromium by default, or BrowserStack or TestMu AI/LambdaTest when configured. Page memory replays steps that already worked on a site, so repeat runs are faster and cheaper. Ask it Go to booking.com and search hotels in Mumbai for next weekend What does ForgeQE know about the checkout page? Add Chrome on Windows 11 and Chrome 128 on Windows 10 as TestMu devices, then run SHOP-12 on both What it needs Required A live model profile in llms.json (an API key or Microsoft Entra ID sign-in) Limits Web applications only: local Chrome or Chromium, or configured remote web grids such as BrowserStack and TestMu AI/LambdaTest; not native mobile or desktop applications. Tools browser_run run_details page_memory browser_devices In detail See 4. Without the shell .

Page memory Live runs build a memory of the pages they visit, next to forgeqe.yaml . With no config file it goes to ~/.forgeqe/memory (under FORGEQE_HOME when that is set), so runs from any folder share one memory. yaml Copy memory: enabled: true dir: ./.forgeqe/memory replay: verify # verify | trust | off text Copy .forgeqe/memory/ pages/<host>/<path>.json every interactive element on the page and its locators flows/<goal>-<hash>.json the steps of a goal that passed, for replay scribe-notes.json what the coding agent learned about each repo, and the tests it wrote there Each page file lists its elements with every locator ForgeQE can build for them: test id, id, role and name, label, placeholder, alt, title, href, text, CSS, and XPath. Each locator has a Playwright string, a confidence %, and its evidence: how many visits it matched on, how often it went missing, and how often it worked or failed when used. Elements and pages carry first_seen , last_seen , last_used , and last_updated . Paths with ids in them share one file ( /hotel/* ), and query strings are ignored. Confidence starts from the locator kind (a test id or role and name ranks above text, CSS, and XPath). It is lower when the locator matches more than one element or looks generated ( #ember123 , hashed class names). It rises as the locator keeps matching over visits and works when used, and it drops when the locator goes missing or fails. How memory saves time and tokens: Replay. Running a goal that passed before replays its recorded steps directly in the browser, with no model calls. A different goal replays nothing: the agent gets the steps of earlier runs on the site, and the controls that worked there, as hints, and decides itself which of them (a banner, a sign-in, a search form) apply to its task, so a new task does not re-explore the setup. Each step finds its element by the highest-confidence locator that still matches exactly one element, then by the element's fingerprint, so a renamed button or a changed id still resolves. The transcript marks these steps ↻ and shows the locator used ( click "Search" [role 88%] ). The site's rulebook. Page memory keeps what worked; the rulebook keeps what did not. When an action fails during a run and the agent then finds one that works, it may end its answer with a line or two starting Lesson: ("On the booking page, type the date in the Check-in field; clicking a day in the calendar does nothing"). ForgeQE keeps a lesson only when that run passed, in rules/<host>.json in page memory, and every later run that starts on that site gets the rules, so it does not spend steps on the same dead end. The lesson lines are taken out of the run's summary. The book works like Scribe's rulebook (under Keeping Scribe's cost down): at most 15 one-line rules, merged when learned again, the least confirmed and oldest dropped first, expired after 180 days unconfirmed, and a rule with a link, a token, a destructive command, or wording that drops instructions is refused. ForgeQE says each new rule ( Learned for this site: … ). browser.rulebook: false turns it off; with page memory off there is none. Hand-off. With replay: verify (the default) the agent then looks at the page once and confirms the result. replay: trust finishes without the model when every step of this same task replayed. When a step cannot be found, the agent continues from that point instead of starting over. replay: off records memory but never replays. Failed runs. A run that fails keeps the steps that worked before it went wrong ( resume.json in its run folder, and in the task's flow). Running the same task again replays them and the agent picks up at the point of failure, told what went wrong last time. When ForgeQE's agent retries a failed goal with different wording, it passes the failed run ( resume_from ), so the retry starts from the same point instead of step 1. Cut-off runs. After every step, a run saves the steps that worked so far and the page memory it has learned, so nothing is lost if ForgeQE is closed, the machine restarts, or the run is stopped. Running the same task again replays those steps and the agent carries on from there; the folder of the cut-off run also has resume.json , so resume_from works with it too. When the model can't be reached (the connection dropped), the run ends as failed and keeps its steps the same way. A run that finishes removes the saved point. Hints. The agent's prompt includes the steps that worked last time on the same site and the controls those runs used, and tells the agent to do them in one turn instead of exploring the page. Tests. The coding agent gets each element's best locator from memory in handoff.md . A run that fails keeps the last good flow and counts the failure. A stopped run changes nothing. Password fields are never stored, and a value typed from FORGEQE_ENGINE_DEFAULT_LOGIN_USERNAME or FORGEQE_ENGINE_DEFAULT_LOGIN_PASSWORD is stored as the variable name and read from the environment on replay. Replay also stops before a step whose value cannot be restored, and the agent does it. bash Copy forgeqe memory # hosts with page, element, and flow counts forgeqe memory show booking.com # the host's pages forgeqe memory show https://app.test/login # elements, confidence, best locator forgeqe memory show https://app.test/login --locators --all forgeqe memory flows --steps forgeqe memory clear booking.com # prints what it would delete forgeqe memory clear booking.com --yes forgeqe memory clear courier --yes # a mobile or desktop app's memory forgeqe memory stats # how often memory stood in for the model, per area In the shell, ask ("what does page memory know about booking.com?") and the agent looks it up. For one run, --replay verify|trust|off overrides the config and --no-memory turns memory off. Commit .forgeqe/memory to share it with a team or CI, or add .forgeqe/ to .gitignore to keep it local.

t: Saved logins for the application under test
x: Browser Saved logins for the application under test Signs the browser agent in with saved credentials (including TOTP) and reuses the session; a user can also sign in by hand once in a browser. Ask it Sign in to the admin site and keep the session Forget the saved session for shop.example.com What it needs Nothing beyond ForgeQE itself. Tools logins In detail

Signing in yaml Copy logins: shop: url: https://staging.shop.test/login # or domains: [https://staging.shop.test, https://*.shop.test] username_env: SHOP_USER password_env: SHOP_PASSWORD totp_env: SHOP_TOTP_SECRET # optional: the authenticator secret (base32), for 2FA codes # save_session: false # sign in on every run The browser agent is told which placeholders exist ( shop_username , shop_password , shop_bu_2fa_code ) and types them; the engine swaps in the real values only on the matching domains and masks them in everything the model sees. For TOTP, a fresh code is computed at the moment it is typed. After each step ForgeQE saves the site's cookies and local storage to .forgeqe/sessions/<name>.json (private to your user, with its own .gitignore ), and the next run starts signed in. Page memory records the variable names, not the values, so replays type the current values and fresh codes, and tests the coding agent writes read SHOP_PASSWORD from the environment. Credentials in a message or test case. Paste a test case that says "log in as svc@corp.test with password …" and you do not need logins: at all. Before the first browser run, ForgeQE's agent remembers the credentials as a login for that site and its sign-in hosts (for Dynamics, the CRM host and login.microsoftonline.com ). From then on: goals say "sign in with the saved login dynamics" and never contain the password, so it is not in run.json , trace.md , report.html , or workflow.yaml ; the browser agent types the exact value from a placeholder, so quotes or a full stop around the password in the test case cannot end up in the password field; the signed-in session is saved in .forgeqe/sessions/ , so follow-up runs ("now open the latest case") start signed in; tests Scribe writes read FORGEQE_<NAME>_USERNAME and FORGEQE_<NAME>_PASSWORD , and ForgeQE sets them when it runs those tests in this session. ForgeQE keeps the values in memory for the session only: it does not write them to disk or put them in the agent runtime's environment. Your message itself is still part of the conversation, which the agent runtime keeps locally like any chat, and which the model provider receives. Close ForgeQE and the remembered values are gone (the saved session stays until it expires or you clear it). Ask "which logins do I have?" to see them, or "forget the dynamics login" to drop them. For pipelines and later sessions, use logins: with environment variables. Single sign-on, captchas, and security keys need a person: forgeqe login shop opens a browser on the login page, you sign in, press Enter in the terminal, and the session is saved. forgeqe logins lists logins, which variables are missing, and when each session was saved; forgeqe logins clear shop (or --all ) forgets sessions. In the shell, "sign in to shop" does the same: the browser opens, a Your turn prompt waits while you sign in, and Done, continue saves the session. forgeqe run asks you to press Enter instead, and forgeqe mcp cannot wait for a person, so it tells the calling agent to have you run forgeqe login shop . In a pipeline, set the login variables as secrets.

t: Recording a web test by hand
x: Recording a web test by hand When you would rather show the steps than describe them, record them. ForgeQE opens Chrome on the app's page with the Recorder panel docked in a corner of the page, in the same window: you click, type and choose as usual, and each action is listed in the panel as a numbered step, in order. Drag the panel by its title to another corner, or make it small (a pill that shows the step count); it comes back where you left it on every page. bash Copy forgeqe record shop --name "Apply a coupon at checkout" # a web app from env.yaml forgeqe record --url https://staging.shop.test/cart # or any page In the shell, say "I'll show you the checkout, record it" (or /record shop ). What you can add while recording: In the panel In the page: Ctrl+Shift+Space, then What it adds Check, then click an element A A check: its text, or its value for a field, or checked for a checkbox. Change the kind (text, visible, hidden, value) and mark live data (check the pattern, not this value) in the panel Variable, then click an element V Keeps the element's text for later steps: typing the same text later is written as {{name}} Wait for, then click an element W The test waits for the element to show Test data D The last value you typed becomes test data the test reads from its data note: … in the box N A note on the last step: "this is the cart page object" Pause / Undo / Stop, ✕ on a step P / Z / S Pause records nothing until you resume; ✕ removes that step Type a check in words in the panel's box, or in the terminal: the total shows "$40.00" . Quoted text the page shows becomes a check on the element showing it; without quotes, one model call finds the text that shows it on the page. A check the page cannot show yet is kept in your words, and the coding agent writes it. In the terminal, undo , pause , delete 4 and stop work too. What is recorded: clicks (a double click as one step), the final text of each field you typed in (not each key), choices in drop-downs, Enter and Escape, key chords, pages you open from the address bar, and Back. A click on a menu item that opened when the pointer went over its trigger gets a hover on the trigger first. Password fields are written as an environment variable (the saved login's password_env , or <SITE>_PASSWORD ), and text equal to a saved login's value as its variable: what you type in them is never stored. A file you choose for an upload is recorded by its path in the working folder; one outside it, a hidden file ( .env , anything under .git ), or one named like credentials or keys is listed as not recorded. Drag and drop is listed as not recorded. --signed-in starts with the saved sessions of logins: ; without it, record the sign-in too. Data that changes from run to run. A test that spells out this recording's price, date, or order number fails on the next run, so ForgeQE keeps what holds and makes the rest a pattern, a variable, or a value made fresh: In the recording In the test A check of a price, date, time, order number, or count ("$14.15", "2,463 found") A check of its pattern: /^\$\d[\d,]*\.\d{2}$/ The same value checked again later (the product's price, then the cart total) The first check keeps it as {{price}} ; the later one checks {{price}} A link or button named with such data ("Combination Pliers $14.15") Found by the part that holds: getByRole("link", { name: /Combination Pliers/ }) A date you typed The date the same number of days from today: {{$date:+3:%Y-%m-%d}} A value the app refuses twice (a new account's email) A part new on each run: alice+{{$unique}}@example.com Prices, dates, times, ids, and long numbers are found by their form; a small number on its own ("1" in the cart) stays exact, as it is usually what the check is about. When you stop, one model call sorts the values the forms cannot tell (a new account's email, "today's deal"); without a model, those stay as recorded. Each change shows in the panel with a tick box: untick it to keep the value as recorded. Recording a test case. forgeqe record --case SHOP-12 (any source ForgeQE reads cases from: Jira, Azure DevOps, Xray, TestRail, a file) starts on the case's page and shows its steps as a checklist in the panel. Click the step you are on (or Next case step ): what you record belongs to it, and a check you add there takes its expected result. Each expected result shows ✓ checked or no check yet ; Stop warns once about the ones with no check, and a second Stop stops. The test is named and tagged for the case, and mapped to it once it passes. When you stop, the run folder holds workflow.yaml and trace.md as for any run. With a repository ( --repo , or code.repo ), ForgeQE asks whether to turn it into a test. First a planner reads the repository and shows the plan: text Copy Test tests/add-to-cart.spec.ts › adds pliers to the cart Steps 2. search: HomePage.searchFor() 4. open the product: new HomePage.product(name) 6. add to the cart: new ProductPage.addToCart() New code ProductPage in pages/ProductPage.ts Checks after step 5: expect(product.price).toHaveText(/^\$\d+\.\d{2}$/) after step 6: expect(product.cartQuantity).toHaveText("1") It asks at most three questions where the repository allows two good answers (a new file, or the existing spec?), then Write it , Change the plan (say what to change, in your words), or Cancel . The coding agent replays the recording in Playwright, writes the test to the plan you agreed in the repository's framework, and asserts each check at the step where you added it. In the shell, "change the plan" comes back to ForgeQE's agent, which asks you what to change. --no-plan (or --yes ) skips the plan. Later: forgeqe code <run folder> . The recorder runs in an isolated world in each page, so the page's own scripts can neither see it nor add steps, and it records only real input: clicks and keys a script fakes are ignored. The panel's own clicks and keys never reach the page and are never recorded, and it stays above the page's dialogs. Record

t: Run manual test cases in browsers

Ask it Run SHOP-12 and SHOP-14 from Jira, two browsers at once Run test plan 12 suite 34 from Azure DevOps and don't post results What it needs Required A live model profile in llms.json (an API key or Microsoft Entra ID sign-in) Optional Azure DevOps or Jira or Xray or TestRail or Zephyr Scale or qTest, to read cases from a test management system and post results back (files and pasted text work without one): set up under sources: in forgeqe.yaml, or sign in with /auth Optional Bug filing: sources.bugs in forgeqe.yaml (Jira or Azure DevOps) Tools find_test_cases run_test_cases In detail

Test cases and suites Test cases you already have can be run two ways. In the shell or with forgeqe run , ask in plain words ("run SHOP-12 and SHOP-14", "run test plan 12 suite 34", "run the cases in smoke.yaml") or paste the cases, and the agent works out the source. forgeqe suite takes explicit references and runs the same way every time, with no agent involved, which is what pipelines call. Each case is one goal: ForgeQE tells the agent to do the steps in order and to check every expected result, and the agent's verdict decides whether the case passed. A case with no steps (plain text, a Jira story) is run from its description.

t: API steps in a test case
x: API steps in a test case A test case can mix API and UI steps ("add three products with POST /add_to_cart/{id}, then remove the first one in the cart, then pay"). The browser agent makes each API step with its api_request action, from the page, in the browser's own session: the logged-in user's cookies go with the call, and the CSRF token comes from the cookie or the page's form when the site needs one. So what an API step changes (a cart, an order) is what the next UI step sees. The verdict of an API step rests on the status the server answered, not on the agent's account of it. The run records it as an api step in workflow.yaml : method, URL, body, CSRF source, and the status and final URL the server gave. ForgeQE's replay repeats it the same way, and fails that step when the server answers differently (403 where the run got 200), so the replay and the test get past it instead of stalling on an empty cart. Scribe's handoff lists each API step with what was sent and answered, and tells Scribe to make it through the framework's API request context that shares the browser's cookies (Playwright's page.request ), asserting the status. Kept for reuse : the calls are saved as an API scenario, one per test case ( out/api/case-ado-2287/ , updated by each run), which forgeqe api and the API tools run again without a browser. The run's card says where ( API 2 calls saved as a reusable API scenario ). URLs the case gives are opened exactly as given: when the model adds a trailing slash ( /login/ , a 404 on many sites), ForgeQE opens and records the URL from the case. When a run finds a test case does not fit the application, the agent drafts the steps as they should be, from what the run found, and offers to save them. update_test_case shows the current and the new steps and asks before it changes the Azure DevOps Test Case; the reason goes into the work item's history, where the old steps stay.

When a case fails The browser run of a test case is the test, so when a case does not pass, ForgeQE works out what kind of failure it was and acts on it. The browser agent reports a cause for each failed step (it saw the page); clear evidence in the run, such as an unreachable site or a 503 page, overrides "I could not operate it". Failure What it means Bug Automation script Functional defect Every step was done and the application behaves wrong (a wrong total, no confirmation) Filed straight away Written for the correct behaviour (the test case's expected results) and marked as an expected failure naming the bug: Playwright test.fail() , pytest xfail(strict=True) . It passes while the defect is there and fails once it is fixed, telling you to remove the marker Test case needs updating The test case does not fit the application (a field or page it names is not there) No No: update the test case. The report and the comment on the test case say what the application shows instead Environment problem The application or something it needs was unavailable (an error page, a 5xx, a network failure, sign-in or test data missing, a bot check) No No. The case runs once more straight away; if it still fails, check the environment first Automation problem A control that is there could not be operated, or the run ran out of steps No Not yet: page memory keeps the steps that worked and the next run resumes from them In Azure DevOps a test plan point is recorded as Blocked, not Failed, for the last three, so the plan's failures are product defects, and the comment on the test case names the kind of failure. Tests that need attention. A coding job that ends without a passing, approved test does not leave a failing test among your tests. The files it created move to a needs-attention/<case id>/ folder beside the test, with their relative imports fixed, and a README says which test case it is for, why it stopped (the last failure, the reviewer's issues), and how to pick it up; needs-attention/README.md lists them all. The job's edits to files that were committed before it are saved as changes.patch in that folder and taken out of the files; files you had already changed are left as they are. The folder is kept out of test runs and builds: Playwright's config gets testIgnore: ['**/needs-attention/**'] , TypeScript files a // @ts-nocheck line, a Python folder a conftest.py that collects nothing, and C#, Java, or Kotlin files a .txt suffix. code.needs_attention: false leaves unfinished tests where they are. Running a case again. A case that already has a test (in .forgeqe/test-cases.json ) does not get a new one: after its browser run, ForgeQE runs the existing test first. When it passes, there is no coding job at all. When it fails, the coding agent updates that test (with the failure and the new verified run) instead of writing one from scratch. A known-defect test whose defect is fixed (the case now passes) is updated to drop its expected-failure marker; a test that passes although the run found a defect gets the defect's assertion and the marker. Mapping tests to test cases. Each test written for a test case is named <case id> <title> and tagged with the case id and link in the framework's own way (Playwright tags and annotations, a pytest marker, an NUnit property). .forgeqe/test-cases.json in the repository maps every test case to its test, with its status ( automated , known_defect with the bug, or needs_attention with the folder); commit it with the tests. For Azure DevOps test cases, a passing test is also set as the work item's Associated Automation (test name, file, type, and a stable id, with Automation status Automated), so the test plan shows the case as automated.

In the shell Ask for the cases in plain words, for example "run SHOP-12 and SHOP-14, two at a time" or "show me what's in test plan 12 without running it". The transcript shows each case's steps as it runs, and a suite card at the end: text Copy ┃ ✗ Suite failed 1/2 passed · 1m 12s · 48.2K tokens ┃ ┃ ✓ SF-1 Search Mumbai 38s ┃ ✗ SF-2 Open a hotel 34s ┃ No hotel link on the results page ┃ ┃ Report .forgeqe/reports/suites/20260928-215438/report.html ┃ JUnit .forgeqe/reports/suites/20260928-215438/junit.xml

Where cases come from bash Copy forgeqe cases cases.yaml # list them forgeqe cases cases.yaml --goal # and the exact goal each one runs Plain text. A quoted string is one case: forgeqe suite "Log in as the demo user and open Invoices" . Text or Markdown file. Each block between --- lines is a case, its first line the title: text Copy Search for hotels in Mumbai and check at least one result is shown --- Open the Deals page Check every deal has a price YAML or JSON. Header row, then a row per case. A row with an empty id (or the id above) adds a step to that case: csv Copy id,title,url,action,expected SHOP-12,Valid login,https://staging.shop.test/login,Sign in as demo,Dashboard shows ,,,Open Orders,Orders list shows Columns: id (or key ), title (or name , summary ), url , description , preconditions , tags , group (or suite , area ), requirements (or refs ), action (or step ), data , expected (or expected_result , result ). Lists in a cell are separated by ; . Gherkin. Each Scenario in a .feature file is a case, and each Examples row of a Scenario Outline is its own case. Background steps come first, and Then steps are the expected results of the step before them. Azure DevOps. Set the organization, and a PAT with Test Management and Work Items (read and write) in ADO_PAT . The MCP server is the whole organization. Leave project unset (or set it to * or all ) and ForgeQE's own calls cover every project; set project only to limit those calls to one. yaml Copy sources: azure_devops: org_url: https://dev.azure.com/acme # project: Shop # optional ado:123,456 reads test case work items: their steps and expected results (HTML turned into text), shared steps inlined, and one case per parameter row with @param values filled in. Work item ids are unique in the organization, so they do not need a project. ado:plan=12 reads every suite in a test plan and ado:plan=12/suite=34 one suite, with each test point's configuration. With no project configured, the plan is looked up in every project. ado:project=Shop/plan=12 names one. Jira. jira:SHOP-1,SHOP-2 or jira:jql=project = SHOP AND labels = e2e . The summary is the title and the description holds the steps. Jira Cloud ( *.atlassian.net ) needs JIRA_EMAIL and an API token in JIRA_API_TOKEN ; Server and Data Center use a personal access token in JIRA_API_TOKEN . yaml Copy sources: jira: url: https://acme.atlassian.net Xray. xray:SHOP-1 , xray:jql=<query> , or xray:plan=SHOP-100 for a test plan's tests, with Xray's own steps, data, and expected results. Xray Cloud needs an API key pair in XRAY_CLIENT_ID and XRAY_CLIENT_SECRET . Xray Server and Data Center go through the Jira settings above. TestRail. testrail:C12,C13 reads cases by id, testrail:run=45 the tests of a run (results go back to that run), testrail:plan=7 every run in a plan, and testrail:suite=3 a suite (needs project_id ). Separated steps ( custom_steps_separated ) become steps with expected results; the text template's steps become one step. It needs the user's email in TESTRAIL_EMAIL and an API key in TESTRAIL_API_KEY . yaml Copy sources: testrail: url: https://acme.testrail.io project_id: 1 # needed for suites, and to create a run for cases read by id Zephyr Scale (Cloud). zephyr:SHOP-T1,SHOP-T2 , zephyr:cycle=SHOP-R5 (results go back to that cycle), or zephyr:folder=12 (needs project_key ). It needs an API access token in ZEPHYR_API_TOKEN ; setting the variable is enough to turn it on. qTest. qtest:1234 reads test cases by the id in their URL, qtest:cycle=88 and qtest:suite=9 the test runs under a cycle or suite (results go back to those runs). It needs url , project_id , and an API token in QTEST_TOKEN . Result statuses are the automation status names your qTest uses; the defaults are PASS, FAIL, and BLOCKED: yaml Copy sources: qtest: url: https://acme.qtestnet.com project_id: 12345 statuses: { passed: PASS, failed: FAIL, error: BLOCKED } Several sources can be mixed: forgeqe suite smoke.yaml jira:SHOP-7 testrail:C12 . From requirements. Ask the agent to test a Confluence page, a story, or a spec file ("write and run test cases for the refund rules page in Confluence"). It reads the requirements, writes one case per rule or acceptance criterion with the main negative paths, shows them, and runs them as text cases. It saves them into a test system only when you ask. Confluence needs sources.confluence : yaml Copy sources: confluence: true # the wiki on the Jira Cloud site above, same account # or confluence: url: https://confluence.acme.com # Cloud: https://acme.atlassian.net/wiki token_env: CONFLUENCE_TOKEN # Server/DC personal access token; Cloud also email_env space: QA # optional: keep searches in one space

Running bash Copy forgeqe suite cases.yaml # one case at a time forgeqe suite ado:plan=12 --parallel 3 # three browsers at once forgeqe suite cases.yaml --repo ../app # passed cases get a test in ../app forgeqe suite cases.yaml --no-code --no-write-back --out .forgeqe/reports/smoke yaml Copy suite: parallel: 1 # browsers at once code: true # with a repo set, passed cases go to Scribe out_dir: ./.forgeqe/reports/suites Browser runs happen parallel at a time and share page memory safely. Each passed case goes to the coding agent as soon as its own browser run ends, and its test is written and run before that browser slot starts the next case: explore, hand off, code, next case. Coding jobs run one after another, so two never edit the repo at once. A case with no test says why in the report (it failed, or no model is set up). With --parallel above 1, each line of output starts with the case id. Ctrl-C stops the suite: cases already running finish closing their browsers, and cases that never started are reported as not run. At the end, ForgeQE prints the result of every case and writes to .forgeqe/reports/suites/<time>/ : report.html : a single file with every screenshot embedded; open it from disk, no server needed. Its menu has three groups. This run : Overview : the verdict, totals, step checks, browser steps, tokens, cost, what page memory saved, browser errors, accessibility issues, tests written and bugs filed; what changed since the last run; results over the earlier runs in .forgeqe/reports/suites/ ; the cases that need attention and why; results by source and by tag; the slowest cases; and what was posted where. Test results : search and filter the cases. For each case: its step table (action, expected, the agent's verdict, what it actually saw), why it failed (the failed step, the agent's last evaluation, failed actions, the screenshot), last good vs now (the same page from the case's last passing run beside this run's, and where their browser steps start to differ), the browser errors per step (console errors, uncaught exceptions, failed and slow requests), page memory (steps replayed, tokens and time saved against the last run where the agent took every step, locators that healed, flows repaired), the browser agent's steps (goal, actions, errors, time and model time, a screenshot each with the element it acted on outlined), a timing waterfall (waiting for the model, acting in the browser, replayed from memory), the accessibility issues of each page, a screenshot gallery, and its trace, workflow and handoff to read in place. Run history links to earlier reports. Failures : each failed case with what the agent reported, the evidence (including browser errors), its last passing screenshot, its bug, and text to copy into a bug report. Defects : failures grouped by what caused them, so one fix clears every case it breaks, most cases broken first, with each defect's root-cause hypothesis when there is one; it downloads as Markdown. Since last run : new failures, fixes, cases still failing, cases at least 5 s and 25% slower or faster, and new or dropped cases, against the previous run in the folder. Analysis : Trends and Flaky tests : pass rate, outcomes, duration, tokens and cost per run; cases whose result keeps changing, and cases that started failing. Both need earlier suite runs in the same folder. Time and cost : where the time went (model, browser, page memory), a timeline of the cases on each parallel worker, page memory savings per case, and tokens and cost per case. Coverage : results by requirement (a requirement fails when any case covering it fails), by group, by tag and by source. Groups and requirements come from the source: the area path in Azure DevOps, the section and refs in TestRail, the folder in Zephyr Scale, components (or the parent issue) and "tests" links in Jira, and group / requirements in case files. Accessibility : the WCAG rules of the standard you chose, checked by axe-core on every page the agent visited: the rules that passed, each rule that failed with its success criterion, level, impact, the elements and a link to how to fix it, and any accessibility budget exceeded. Automated checks are a pre-check, not conformance. Visual : every page against its approved baseline: baseline, this run, and the difference side by side, changed pages first, with the share of pixels changed and the visual budget. Performance : each page's Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP, FCP, TTFB) and load time, coloured good / needs improvement / poor by Google's thresholds, with the budgets each page went over. Tokenomics (reports with token usage): Usage : a usage summary, tokens by case, tokens over the run, and the calls that used the most tokens. Breakdown : what the tokens paid for, by agent, job, task, purpose, model, user and machine. Model calls : every request the agents sent to a model. Models : the models behind the calls, and what the listed alternatives would cost. Trends and forecast : model spend on this machine so far, and the next days at the recent pace, against the budget. Calculator : estimate what a suite will cost before you run it, starting from this run's real numbers. Optimise : where the report could have spent less on models, by how much, and what to change. Environment opens from the model card at the foot of the menu: model, browser, the model's price, start URL, ForgeQE version, machine, CI build, branch, commit, and the sites visited. It exports Markdown and JSON and prints cleanly. Up to 40 MB of screenshots are embedded, failed cases first; beyond that they load from the run folders next to the report. junit.xml : for CI test reporting; a failed case is a <failure> , a crash an <error> , a case not run <skipped> ; step verdicts are in system-out suite.json : everything above as data 01-SHOP-12/ , 02-… : each case's normal run folder (with its own report.html , steps.json , and steps/NN.jpg screenshots), plus testcase.json yaml Copy report: screenshots

Results back in the source Test cases the agent writes from an Azure DevOps or Jira story are saved there with save_test_cases , linked to the story, and the reply lists them as links; set sources.save_cases: false to keep them in the reply only. Replies in the shell render as markdown (headings, lists, tables, links). With sources.write_back: true (the default), results go back after the suite: Azure DevOps plan: a completed test run for the plan with each test point's outcome and the agent's summary as the comment. Cases read by id get a comment on the work item instead. Jira: a comment on each issue with the result, the summary, where the run ended, and the test file if one was written. Xray: one Test Execution per test plan (linked to the plan), with each test's status, step statuses and actual results, the summary, and the failure screenshot as evidence. TestRail: results in the run the cases came from, or a new run per suite for cases read by id, with step results and the failure screenshot attached. Zephyr Scale: a test execution per case with step results, in the cycle the cases came from or a new cycle per project. qTest: an automation test log per case with step logs, on the test run it came from, or on new test runs in a new test cycle. Every comment and result includes the step verdicts. If a system rejects the step details (a TestRail project without separated steps, say), ForgeQE posts the result again without them rather than losing it. Stopped cases are never posted. --no-write-back skips it for one suite.

Bugs for failures yaml Copy sources: bugs: system: jira # or azure_devops project: SHOP # Jira project key; Azure DevOps uses azure_devops.project type: Bug # issue type or work item type labels: [forgeqe] # Jira labels or Azure DevOps tags # area_path: Shop\Web # Azure DevOps # on_error: true # also for cases that could not run # group_by: defect # defect (default): cases failing the same way share a bug; case: a bug per case When results are posted, each case that failed with a functional defect (below) gets a bug: the title is [ForgeQE] <case id>: <title> , the description has the result, the steps with verdicts, the preconditions, where the run ended, the build link, and the run folder, and the last screenshot is attached. In Jira the bug is linked to the Jira or Xray test ("relates to"); in Azure DevOps it is "tested by" the test case work item. Each bug carries a label or tag that fingerprints the case ( forgeqe- and ten hex digits), so the next failure comments "Still failing" on the open bug instead of filing a new one, and a pass adds a note that it passes again. A closed bug is not reopened: a new failure after that files a new bug, titled [ForgeQE] Regression: … , that says when the old one was closed and links to it (Jira "relates to", Azure DevOps "Related", a mention on GitHub; a GitHub issue closed as not planned does not count). One bug per defect. Cases that fail the same way share one bug ( group_by: defect , the default). ForgeQE gives each failing case a signature from the strongest evidence its run recorded: a failed request (a 5xx before a 4xx) by its route and status, then an uncaught page error, then a console error, with ids, numbers and times taken out, so POST /api/cart/123 → 500 and /api/cart/456 → 500 match. Errors that the suite's passing runs show too (an analytics call, a missing favicon) are noise and do not count. The first case of a defect files the bug, titled after the defect ( [ForgeQE] shop.example.com/api/cart/:id returns 500 ) and labelled with the defect's fingerprint ( forgeqe-d- and ten hex digits) as well as the case's; every other case failing the same way is added as a comment and gets its own case label on that bug. The next run finds the open bug by either label. A failure with no browser evidence is matched by its page and what the agent saw, within one run only, and its bug is titled after the case as before. group_by: case files one bug per failing case. The report's Defects page, the terminal summary and the CI job summary list every defect with the cases it breaks. Defect history. Each suite adds its defects to defect-history.json next to the suite folders (keep it between CI runs as a cache, like the suite folders, to track a pipeline's defects). A defect is new the first time, then known ("seen in 3 earlier runs since 2 Oct"). It went away when a run did not see it while a case it broke passed; seen again after that, or matching a closed bug in the tracker, it is a regression . A defect whose cases keep changing between passing and failing across the last 20 suites (pass, fail, pass) is marked intermittent : it still gets a bug, which says so. When a new bug is filed, ForgeQE also searches the tracker once for open bugs people filed about the same route or error ( /api/cart , price is undefined ) and lists them on the bug as possibly related; it never merges them. Only defects found by browser evidence are kept in the history: a defect matched by the agent's words gets new words every run. The Defects page shows the history and filters new defects and regressions; the summaries say it next to each defect. Reproducing and root cause. Each defect gets a repro file, defects/<defect id>.md in the suite folder, and the same steps go in its bug: how reproducible it is, the case's steps with the agent's verdicts, what the browser did, where it ended, the environment (browser, device, build, commit), the failing request as a curl command with its response (the engine takes credentials out of the requests it records), and the run's files (screenshot, replay flow, every step, every API call). The first case of a new product defect runs once more into its reproduce/ folder: failing the same way makes it always reproducible, not failing again makes it intermittent ; a defect seen in earlier runs is not run again. Then the root cause, always as a hypothesis: From the evidence, at no cost: the layer (the server, the front end, access, a route that is not there, the environment) and the component (the route or the script). With defects.product_repo set: suspect commits , made since the defect's cases last passed, whose changes mention its route or error ( git log -G ), or whose files are named after it. For new defects and regressions, a read-only agent (prompt defect-rca ) reads the evidence, the suspect commits and the product's code, and writes a hypothesis with its confidence (high only when it read the code that fails and the change that broke it), what it rests on, and checks to confirm it. The hypothesis is added to the bug as a comment and shown on the Defects page. It runs for at most max_analyses defects per suite; each is one agent session (about 90K–120K tokens with gpt-5.4 in our runs), shown on its own line under Usage. yaml Copy defects: product_repo: ../shop # the application's repository: suspect commits, and the code the analysis reads # reproduce: true # run the first case of each new defect once more # analyze: true # a model writes a root-cause hypothesis for new defects and regressions # max_analyses: 3 # most analyses per suite

t: Checking test cases before they run
x: Checking test cases before they run run_test_cases checks the cases before it runs them, and check_test_cases checks them without running anything ("are these test cases ready?", "check test plan 12 against its stories"). A check uses everything ForgeQE can know about a case: Source What it finds Cost Rules on the case's text No steps or expected results; vague expected results ("works correctly", "submitted successfully"); steps that need values the case does not give ("enter valid user details"); placeholders ( TBD , <username> ); passwords in the case; several actions in one step; no start page; duplicate cases None Page memory Steps that name a field or control earlier runs never saw on that page ("email" on a form that has no email field), with what the page does have None The requirements it tests Azure DevOps: the story or PBI the case tests ("Tests" link), then its feature and epic, with descriptions and acceptance criteria. Jira: the issues the test is linked to, then their parents A few API calls, each requirement read once per check Linked documents Confluence pages linked from the case or its requirements A few API calls A RAG service (optional) Passages your own search finds for the case Your service Each case is ready , to review , or not runnable , shown as a card with what it tests ( tests PBI 2211 "Contact Us form" ← Feature 300 ← Epic 12 ) and the acceptance criteria no step seems to cover. ForgeQE's agent then judges each case against its requirements: criteria no step covers, steps no requirement asks for, expected results that contradict the requirement, controls the application does not have. The check before a run uses the rules and page memory only (no reads); check_test_cases with depth: quick does the same. RAG, plug and play. Point forgeqe.yaml at any search service over your requirements (Confluence, a wiki, specs) and the check adds its passages: yaml Copy rag: url: http://localhost:8080/search # POST {"query": "...", "top_k": 5}; answers a list of {text, source, score} token_env: RAG_TOKEN # optional, sent as a bearer token top_k: 5 # or a local command: gets {"query", "top_k"} on stdin, prints the list on stdout # rag: # command: ["python", "rag/search.py"] The answer can also be an object with results , passages , documents , or hits , and a passage's text can be text , content , or page_content (LangChain's shape). A RAG server with an MCP interface works through mcp: instead: ForgeQE's agent calls its tools. suite.case_check decides what happens before a run: warn (the default) shows the findings and runs every case, block leaves out the cases that cannot run as written, off skips the check. Ask to run a case and it runs, whatever the check found; ForgeQE's agent reports the findings with the result instead of refusing. A case whose steps have no expected results runs too: it passes when every step can be done, and the check lists it to review , since it checks no result the page should show.
