Test cases Domain and regulatory test design Every agent works as an expert in the product's industry would, automatically: the risks the industry is known for and the obligations of its regulations and standards (for example DORA, PSD2, GDPR, ISO 27001), declared in forgeqe.yaml or worked out from the story and the application. It applies to analysing requirements, writing and checking test cases, exploration, writing, reviewing, and healing test code, API tests, finding tests, and pull request reviews, labelled so coverage can be traced and citing only the control ids in the team's compliance file. forgeqe eval domain measures how well the agent does it. Ask it Write test cases for story 1234, covering our DORA and PSD2 obligations Which GDPR obligations do these cases miss? What it needs Optional The product's industry and regulations: domain: in forgeqe.yaml, with your applicable controls in .forgeqe/knowledge/compliance.md Limits Designs and checks tests for regulatory obligations; it does not certify compliance or replace an audit. Cites control or article ids only from the team's compliance file, never from memory. Tools In detail

Domain and regulations ForgeQE's agents already know the common industries and regulations: banking, insurance, lending, retail; DORA, PSD2, GDPR, ISO 27001, SOX, IDD, and more. Every agent applies that knowledge to its own job, automatically: analysing requirements, writing and checking test cases, planning exploration, writing test code (Scribe), reviewing it, healing it, writing and planning API tests, finding tests, and reviewing pull requests. Without a declaration, each works out the industry and regulations from the story, the product knowledge, and the application, and says what it assumed. Declaring yours removes the guesswork: yaml Copy domain: industry: retail banking regulations: [DORA, PSD2, GDPR, ISO 27001] notes: Payments to UK and EU accounts; customers are consumers and small businesses. The agents add the risks the industry is known for (duplicate submissions, limits, cut-off times, effective dates, recalculated premiums) and the obligations of each regulation a feature touches (audit trail, segregation of duties, data protection, incident logging, resilience), and label each test case, charter, test, or finding with what it covers, for example Domain: duplicate payment or GDPR: right to erasure . What that means for each job: Agent What it does with the domain ForgeQE's agent Adds domain and regulatory cases when it writes test cases or tests from requirements, and judges cases and release readiness against them Exploratory charters Plans charters for the domain's risks and obligations Scribe (writing tests) Asserts a covered risk or obligation explicitly (the amount, the approval, the audit entry), and carries its label into the test's name or tag Test reviewer Treats a test that drops or weakens such an assertion as a correctness issue Healing Never makes a test pass by loosening such an assertion: if the app no longer meets it, it is an app bug API tests and scenarios Idempotent money-moving calls, access per role, no excess personal data in responses, no leaked internals, audited changes Finding tests "The DORA tests" matches tests by their labels and what they assert Pull request review A change that weakens a domain safeguard or an obligation is at least a major finding Every agent session gets the domain in its instructions from one place, and the rule is domain-rule.md in .forgeqe/prompts/ , included in every agent that analyses requirements or designs, writes, reviews, or heals tests. Which requirements apply to your product, and the ids your auditors use, are your organisation's decision: list them in .forgeqe/knowledge/compliance.md ( forgeqe init adds a template), with what is out of scope. Agents cite a control, article, or clause id only when it is listed there, and name the obligation in words otherwise, so nothing in a test traces to an id recalled from memory. ForgeQE designs and checks tests for these obligations; it does not certify compliance or replace an audit.

Evaluating the agent's domain knowledge forgeqe eval domain measures whether the agent applies all this, with your model. Each evaluation case is a realistic story whose acceptance criteria leave the industry's risks and the regulations' obligations unstated, with what a domain expert expects its test cases to check. ForgeQE's own agent writes test cases for each story twice, with the domain declared (and a compliance file) and without, and a separate read-only judge decides, expectation by expectation, whether a test case actually checks it, and lists every id the cases cite. bash Copy forgeqe eval domain # the bundled cases: banking, insurance, access control, data protection, lending forgeqe eval domain --only banking-payment-transfer --repeat 3 forgeqe eval domain --cases ./evals/our-domain # your own cases forgeqe eval domain --judge-profile judge # judge with another llms.json profile forgeqe eval domain --variant declared --min 0.8 # exit 1 under 80% coverage, or on any invented id: a CI gate The report ( .forgeqe/reports/evals/domain/<time>/report.md and report.json ) shows coverage of the story's own expectations, the industry's, and the regulations', for each variant, the expectations each run missed with the judge's reason, and any invented ids (cited, but not in the compliance file). The gap between the two variants is what declaring the domain adds; the declared coverage is what you can rely on. Model answers vary, so use --repeat before drawing conclusions from one case. A case is a YAML file: yaml Copy id: banking-payment-transfer title: Send money to a saved beneficiary domain: { industry: retail banking, regulations: [PSD2, DORA, GDPR] } compliance: | # the team's compliance file for this product (optional) - CTL-AUD-01 (DORA): every payment is written to the audit log with who, when, and the values. story: title: Pay a saved beneficiary description: As a customer I want to send money to a beneficiary I saved earlier. acceptance: | - The customer picks a saved beneficiary, enters an amount and a reference, and confirms. expect: # source: story, domain, or regulation - { id: duplicate, source: domain, covers: Submitting twice does not create a second payment. } - { id: sca, source: regulation, covers: Confirming the payment requires strong customer authentication. }

Test cases Exploratory testing of a story Explores a story in real browsers beyond its scripted cases (edge cases, invalid input, boundaries, roles, state), confirms each defect by reproducing it, proposes test cases, and files bugs once the user agrees. Ask it Explore story 1234 and find bugs Test this feature beyond the test cases What it needs Required A live model profile in llms.json (an API key or Microsoft Entra ID sign-in) Optional Azure DevOps or Jira, to read the story and file bugs: set up under sources: in forgeqe.yaml, or sign in with /auth Tools explore_story In detail

Exploratory testing from a story "Explore story 1234" (or forgeqe explore ado:1234 ) tests a story's feature beyond its scripted test cases, in real browsers: Reads the story: description and acceptance criteria, the feature and epic above it, the test cases that already script it (Azure DevOps "Tested By", Jira test links), and passages from the requirements search when one is set up. A Jira key, a link, or the story's text with its acceptance criteria works too. Plans charters (6 by default, --charters N , at most 12), each with a mission, concrete steps and data, and an expected result per step: other paths and valid data, edge cases (empty, long, special characters, duplicates), invalid input, the boundaries the story states, role differences , state (refresh, back, double submit, a second tab, an expired session), and what must not happen. Expected results come from the acceptance criteria; where the story says nothing, from what a well-behaved application does, and the charter says so. Nothing irreversible beyond test data is planned, and charters that create or change data are marked. You see the charters and choose to run them all, only those that change no data, or none. Explores: each charter is a browser run, and the browser agent judges each expected result on the page and lists anything else that looks wrong. Roles are your saved logins ( logins: in forgeqe.yaml ; by default every one when there are two or more, or --roles admin,viewer ): a role's charter signs in with only that role's login on the site. Confirms: a charter that finds a functional defect runs a second time. It counts as a confirmed defect only when it fails the same way again. The failure classification decides what is a defect: an environment problem (run once more), a test that could not be done, or a charter that does not fit the application are reported as "could not explore", not as defects. Reports in .forgeqe/reports/explore/<id>/exploration.md (and .json ): each charter's result, the confirmed defects with both runs' evidence, and observations : defects that did not reproduce, browser errors (failed requests, console errors), and what the agent noticed beyond the steps. Observations are never filed as bugs. Bugs for confirmed defects only , through the bug tracker set up under bugs: (Jira or Azure DevOps), after you agree ( --file-bugs where nobody can be asked). A bug filed before for the same charter gets a comment instead of a duplicate. Proposed test cases: the charters that ran clean become regression cases, and each confirmed defect becomes a case that checks the correct behaviour (it fails until the defect is fixed). The agent offers to save the ones you pick to the story ( save_test_cases ). bash Copy forgeqe explore ado:1234 --url https://staging.shop.example/orders forgeqe explore SHOP-12 --charters 8 --roles shop_admin,shop_viewer --focus "the address form" forgeqe explore "Change the delivery address Customers can change the address of an open order. Acceptance criteria: - Postcode is required and validated" --url https://staging.shop.example Each charter is a browser run (two for a possible defect), so a session takes several minutes and costs about as much as running that many test cases. forgeqe explore exits 1 when a defect is confirmed.
06 Setup Configuration, skills, and help

Setup Test environments and their apps Knows the test environments in env.yaml (QA, UAT, …) and each one's apps: web apps and APIs by URL, Windows desktop apps, and mobile apps, with what each is for. Every agent works from the active one; switches environment on request, picks the apps a scenario needs, and carries values such as an order number from one app to the next. Ask it Place an order in the shop, then check its invoice in Billing, in UAT Which apps can you test in QA? From now on, use the UAT environment What it needs You give env.yaml with the environments and apps (forgeqe init writes one) Tools test_apps use_environment In detail

Environments and apps env.yaml (written by forgeqe init , named in forgeqe.yaml environments.file ) lists your test environments and the apps in each: web apps by URL, APIs by base URL, Windows desktop apps by .exe , and mobile apps by package id, each with a short description of what it is for. Plain values go under variables ; secrets never do, only the names of the environment variables that hold them, under secrets . yaml Copy default: qa environments: qa: start_app: shop apps: shop: { kind: web, url: "https://qa.shop.example.com", description: Customer web shop where orders are placed } orders: { kind: api, url: "https://qa.api.example.com/v1", description: Orders REST API } billing: { kind: desktop, path: 'C:\Program Files\Contoso\Billing\Billing.exe', args: ["--server", "qa-db01"], description: Back-office invoicing } variables: { company: Contoso QA } secrets: [BILLING_PASSWORD_QA] uat: apps: { ... } Your test cases stay the same in every environment; only where they run changes. The environment supplies the URLs, executables, accounts and values, and the same test, workflow or scenario runs against QA or UAT. Any layout works. The layout above is ForgeQE's own, but an env.yaml your team already keeps is read as it is: environments under environments: / envs: , as a list with a name each, or as top-level keys ( qa: , uat: ); or one file per environment with environments.dir in forgeqe.yaml a common: / defaults: / shared: block merged into each environment any http(s) URL becomes a web app (an API when its key or path says api); an absolute .exe becomes a desktop app (with a sibling args ); other values become variables secrets: keys like password , token or api_key are never shown to a model. A reference ( ${BILLING_PW} , env:BILLING_PW , %BILLING_PW% ) is recorded as a secret name; a literal value is replaced with <redacted> yaml Copy common: { company: Contoso } qa: url: https://qa.shop.example.com orders_api: https://qa.api.example.com/v1 billing_exe: 'C:\Program Files\Contoso\Billing\Billing.exe' db_password: ${BILLING_DB_PW_QA} uat: url: https://uat.shop.example.com ForgeQE's agent also sees the environment as written (secrets replaced), so a request can name anything in it ("log in as the admin_user of UAT"). Pick the environment with --env uat on any command ( forgeqe start , run , suite , monitor , mcp , …) or FORGEQE_ENV=uat ; otherwise default is used. In the shell, /env lists them and /env uat switches; asked in plain language ("from now on, use UAT"), ForgeQE's agent switches with use_environment , and any single request can name an environment ("run the checkout tests in UAT"): each test tool takes an env for that call only. forgeqe apps lists the environments and the active one's apps. What each agent gets from the active environment: Agent What it uses ForgeQE's agent The environment, its apps (with descriptions) and values in its session notes; plans scenarios across apps from them and carries values (an order number) between them Browser agent Starts at start_app when no URL is given; knows the environment's web apps by name and stays on their hosts; its values API tests Call api_app 's URL Desktop agent Starts the environment's desktop apps; types only its secrets Scribe, the healer, the reviewer Write tests that read FORGEQE_APP_<APP>_URL (or the repository's own settings), never a fixed environment URL; the reviewer flags one Tests ForgeQE runs, pack pipelines FORGEQE_ACTIVE_ENV , FORGEQE_APP_<APP>_URL / _PATH / _ID , FORGEQE_VAR_<NAME> (pipelines written by forgeqe pack pipeline init take them as the env_vars input) Reports Every run's report names the test environment There is no scenario file to write: ask in plain language ("place an order in the shop, then check its invoice in Billing, in UAT") and ForgeQE's agent picks the apps from their descriptions, shows the plan, runs each step with the right engine, and carries values from one app to the next.

Setup What ForgeQE wrote Says how much of the code ForgeQE wrote is still in the repository, and gives the trailer and footer that mark a commit message or pull request description covering code it wrote. Works with any repository, whatever system the team uses. Ask it How much of the code ForgeQE wrote is still there? Write the commit message for these tests What it needs Nothing beyond ForgeQE itself. Tools generated_attribution In detail

Generated code Generated code. What ForgeQE writes is marked, so the team can see it and measure it. A file ForgeQE created starts with one line in that language's comment, such as // Generated with ForgeQE · fq:k3x7m2qa4bdi · run 20261019-162847 ; the fq: id is a hash of the file's contents without that line, so it shows whether the file was changed since ( code.header: false leaves the line out; a JSON file never gets one). Files it only edited get no header. Every file it created or edited is recorded per run in .forgeqe/generated.jsonl (commit it with the code): the lines it added, as short hashes, never their text. forgeqe generated (or /generated in the shell, --json for a pipeline) says how many lines ForgeQE wrote, how many are still in the code, its share of the files it touched, and which created files are as it wrote them. Commit messages ForgeQE's agent writes end with a Generated-by: ForgeQE (fq:…) trailer, and its pull request descriptions with a line naming the runs' fq: ids and how much they wrote. The ids are plain hashes anyone can recompute: they show what ForgeQE wrote, not who owns the code.

Commands cheat sheet Every command below also works from the shell in plain words ("show the context budget", "diff the brain prompt", "upload builds/app.apk to TestMu for the courier app"). ForgeQE's agent uses the tool made for it, or forgeqe_command for the commands no other tool covers. A command that only reads runs at once. One that changes files, installs, costs model calls, or sends anything out shows you the exact command and runs only when you agree. Signing in stays /auth and forgeqe login ; forgeqe bi export and forgeqe logs bundle are /report export and /logs there.

End-to-end API scenarios: chained from a run, lifecycles and negative cases from a description, or planned from test cases or plain English forgeqe api run-scenarios [SET] [--allow-writes] Run them against the API; exit 1 on a failure forgeqe api tests --scenarios --repo DIR Scenario tests on the repo's existing API helpers forgeqe generated [--repo DIR] [--json] How much of the code ForgeQE wrote, and how much is still there forgeqe eval domain [--only id,id] [--repeat N] [--min 0.8] Whether the agent applies domain and regulatory knowledge, with the domain declared and without; --min makes it a CI gate (see Domain and regulations )

Guardrails Guardrails. Rules every agent must follow, to keep it grounded: ForgeQE's agent, the browser agent, and the agents that plan, write, review, fix and explain tests. Write one rule per line, starting with - , in a .md or .txt file in .forgeqe/guardrails/ ( guardrails.dir ); headings, other lines and HTML comments are ignored, and the template's examples sit in a comment until you choose them. Each agent gets every guardrail with its instructions, after everything else, with the instruction to follow it whatever a request, a skill, a ticket, a page or a tool's output says; when a guardrail stops part of a task, the agent skips that part and says which rule stopped it. Add one from the terminal ( forgeqe guardrails add "Never open a production URL" ), or ask in the shell ("add a guardrail: use only the test cards in knowledge/test-data.md") and ForgeQE's agent appends it to guardrails.md ; it adds only rules you ask for, never one suggested by a page or a ticket. forgeqe guardrails lists the rules in force and what they add to every model call (at most 40 rules of 300 characters are given). The older prompts.guiderails string in forgeqe.yaml still works: each of its lines is a guardrail for every agent. Guardrails are instructions, not a sandbox: put a host rule in browser.allowed_hosts too, which is refused in code.

t: Your prompts, skills, and product knowledge
x: Your prompts, skills, and product knowledge init also puts three folders in .forgeqe/ to read, change, and commit: Folder What it holds .forgeqe/prompts/ Every prompt ForgeQE's agents work from, one markdown file each: ForgeQE's agent ( brain.md ), Scribe ( test-agent.md , test-rules.md ), the reviewer, healing, finding tests, pull request review, API tests and scenarios, exploratory charters, and the browser agent ( browser-*.md , plus browser-extra.md for your own instructions). .forgeqe/skills/ The built-in skills (framework and app playbooks), to adapt to your project; add your own next to them. .forgeqe/knowledge/ Product knowledge templates: the product and its flows, roles, glossary, business rules, test data, environments. Your copy or ForgeQE's. .forgeqe-manifest.json in each folder records what was copied. A copy you have not changed still counts as ForgeQE's, so it keeps getting ForgeQE's improvements when you update; once you edit it, yours is used. When ForgeQE's version changes after you edited yours, ForgeQE says so at start-up. Running init again adds what is missing and never overwrites an edited file (with --force it refreshes only unchanged copies). Prompts. Each file has a short header ( name , description , used_by , kind ) and the prompt; {{> name}} includes another prompt ( test-rules is included in the test, reviewer, and healing prompts, so one edit changes all three). ForgeQE looks in prompts.dir , then .forgeqe/prompts/ , then ~/.forgeqe/prompts/ (for every project), then its own. Changes take effect on the next run or session. bash Copy forgeqe prompts # every prompt, what it is for, and where it comes from forgeqe prompts show test-agent # the prompt as the agent gets it (includes expanded; --raw for the file) forgeqe prompts diff test-rules # how your copy differs from ForgeQE's forgeqe prompts reset test-rules # back to ForgeQE's (yours is kept as test-rules.md.bak) forgeqe prompts check # each prompt against the prompting standard for its kind (exits 1 when one falls short) forgeqe prompts check brain # what to fix in one prompt: sections, rules, examples, contract, sentences forgeqe prompts eval # run the evaluation cases with the live model; pass rates against the last run forgeqe prompts eval refine --runs 3 # one prompt, three runs of each case The prompting standard. Every prompt follows one standard, and each technique is used where it fits the kind of prompt ( kind: in its header): Kind Prompts Structure Few-shot examples Execution contract agent: works with tools over many steps brain, test-agent, heal, api-tests, pr-review, find-tests Role, Objective, Execution contract, Rules, Output where routing or reply format varies Preconditions, Tools, Procedure, Stop when, On failure, Evidence structured: one answer in a fixed shape refine, api-scenarios, explore-charters, eval-judge, test-reviewer, browser-skill-select Role, Objective, Inputs, Rules, Output, Examples two or more worked examples – fragment: rules included in other prompts test-rules, domain-rule, skill-rule, conventions, the browser agent's rules rules only – – ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English everywhere, so each agent reads one clear instruction at a time: an instruction has 20 words or fewer and a description 25 or fewer, one instruction per sentence, the active voice, and approved words ("make sure", not "ensure"). At least 80% of sentences. The check covers the rules that can be measured in text and a list of common words the standard does not approve; the standard's full dictionary is licensed and not included. RFC 2119 key words state the strength of every rule: MUST / MUST NOT are absolute, SHOULD / SHOULD NOT are strong defaults the agent may break only for a reason it states, MAY is a free choice, and a numbered procedure step is a MUST. A lower-case "must" or "should" is flagged as ambiguous. conventions.md says this at the top of every agent and structured prompt, and the browser engine adds it to the browser agent's instructions. Structured prompting and few-shot examples make the output predictable: the same sections in the same order, and worked examples where the shape of the answer matters. Execution contracts tell a tool-using agent what must be true before it starts, which tools it uses and in what order (for systems: MCP tools, then query_api , then the browser), its procedure, when it stops, what it does when something fails, and what evidence its answer gives. Evaluation-driven prompting measures reliability: forgeqe prompts eval runs cases (an input and checks decided by code: a field matches or is empty, a tool was or was not used, the text keeps ASD-STE100) and compares each pass rate with the last run. ForgeQE's cases cover brain, refine, and explore-charters; add your own as .forgeqe/evals/prompts/<prompt>/<case>.yaml (the same id replaces ForgeQE's). Results are kept in <reports>/evals/prompts/ . forgeqe prompts check applies the standard to each prompt in use, ForgeQE's or your edited copy; ForgeQE's own meet it in its tests. Write your edits the same way, and run forgeqe prompts eval before and after a change. Product knowledge. Fill in the templates (or add your own .md and .txt files, in folders if you like), one topic per ## heading. ForgeQE's agent sees the list and reads what a request needs; the exploratory and API scenario planners get the sections that match their story or scenario; the browser agent gets the few sections that clearly match its goal, at most knowledge.browser_max_chars (1500 by default; 0 turns it off). Untouched templates are left out, so their examples never reach an agent. Never put passwords or tokens there: use logins and environment variables.

Setup Setup, skills, and documentation Shows the model profiles and MCP servers, installs or repairs the browser engine, creates a forgeqe.yaml, manages skills, and answers any question about ForgeQE from its documentation, this list, and its own code (the prompts, skills, and source it runs). Ask it What can you do? Which model am I using? How do I set up email alerts? Show me the icons of all agents Which version of ForgeQE is this? What it needs Nothing beyond ForgeQE itself. Tools forgeqe_setup capabilities playbook use_capabilities In detail See 2. Scaffold config .

Skills A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md : instructions that teach ForgeQE's agents something a prompt can't know, like your repo's test conventions, a framework, or how to drive an app such as Dynamics 365. The format is the Agent Skills one (Claude Code and others use it), with one ForgeQE field, agents : markdown Copy --- name: contoso-erp description: "Use when the site is the Contoso ERP (erp.contoso.com): the order grid, the customer lookup, and saving orders." agents: [browser] --- - The customer lookup opens a list after three letters; click the row whose name matches exactly. - Save with the floppy icon in the toolbar; wait until "Saved" shows in the status bar. name is lowercase words joined by hyphens, the same as the folder. Agents choose skills by description alone, so name the concrete signs it applies (a framework, a config file, a host, a product). Quote it when it contains : . Who uses it. agents lists forgeqe (ForgeQE's agent: how to handle a kind of request), scribe (writing, healing, finding and reviewing tests), and browser (the browser agent). Without agents , a skill is for forgeqe and scribe ; a browser skill must ask for browser . How skills are used. ForgeQE's agent and Scribe see the name and description of each skill meant for them, and load the ones that fit the job through the agent runtime's skill tool. A skill adds to their instructions and never overrides them. Scribe can also read files next to SKILL.md (for example references/locators.md ) when the skill points to them. Browser runs: ForgeQE's agent passes the browser skills a goal needs to browser_run and run_test_cases . For forgeqe suite , forgeqe monitor and forgeqe run --direct , the engine picks them from the goal with one short model call (at most three), and remembers the choice for that goal, so a monitor's later rounds and repeated cases skip it. --skill NAME (repeatable) fixes the list; --skill none runs without any. The chosen skills' text is added to the browser agent's prompt, at most skills.browser_max_chars (6,000) characters in total; the browser agent reads only SKILL.md . run.json , the run.done log line and the report list the skills a run used. Where skills come from , lowest to highest precedence; a later source replaces a skill of the same name: Source Folder Built-in the skills/ folder ForgeQE ships: playwright-typescript and dotnet-nunit-playwright (Scribe), dynamics-365 (browser), writing-skills (ForgeQE's agent) Global, only with skills.external: true ~/.claude/skills , ~/.agents/skills , and the repo's .claude/skills and .agents/skills User ~/.forgeqe/skills (or $FORGEQE_HOME/skills ) Project .forgeqe/skills next to forgeqe.yaml , and the repo's own .forgeqe/skills Extra each folder in skills.dirs Commit .forgeqe/skills so the team and CI share it. ForgeQE only ignores .forgeqe/reports/ ; if your .gitignore has .forgeqe/ , replace it with .forgeqe/* and !.forgeqe/skills/ ( forgeqe skills new warns when git would ignore the new skill). To change a built-in skill, make a project skill with the same name. Skills from anywhere else stay out: the agent runtime's own discovery ( ~/.claude/skills , a repo's .opencode/skills , its built-in skills) is off, and each agent may load only the skills ForgeQE's registry gives it. Skill text is trusted like the repo's own files, so global skills are opt-in. yaml Copy skills: enabled: true # false (or skills: false) turns skills off dirs: [../shared-skills] # more folders, read last disable: [dynamics-365] # leave these out external: false # true: also the global folders above browser_max_chars: 6000 # most skill text added to one browser run Commands. Command What it does forgeqe skills The skills each agent can use, where each comes from (and what it replaces), disabled skills, problems, and the folders read forgeqe skills show <name> One skill's instructions forgeqe skills new <name> --description "Use when …" [--agent browser] [--user] Start a skill in .forgeqe/skills ( --user : ~/.forgeqe/skills ) forgeqe skills check Validate every skill; exit 1 when one has a problem forgeqe skills enable|disable <name> Edit skills.disable in forgeqe.yaml , keeping its comments /skills [name] The same list, or one skill, in the shell In the shell you can also ask: "make a skill for our Dynamics date picker" or "teach Scribe our test conventions". ForgeQE's agent gathers the facts, writes the skill into .forgeqe/skills with forgeqe_setup , and it applies from the next session. It writes skills only when you ask.

Model routing llm.routing is off by default for existing projects ( forgeqe init writes auto ); shadow logs each pick in the session log but changes nothing. --profile and code.model always win, and llm.routes limits or pins the profiles an area may use. ForgeQE checks and rates the models once and keeps the result in .forgeqe/model-profile.json (you can edit the ratings). Details: docs/MODEL_ROUTING.md . List profiles, and the model each area gets: bash Copy bun src/index.ts models bun src/index.ts models --routes # the pick per area, and why bun src/index.ts models --routes --profile-models # check and rate the models again

Privacy ForgeQE sends no telemetry and turns it off in everything it starts: The engine: PostHog telemetry, cloud sync, and the price-list download are off, and the blank-tab logo its library loads from a CDN is replaced by ForgeQE's start page, which loads nothing. The agent runtime: auto-update, session sharing, OpenTelemetry spans, and the model catalogue download are off; it uses its bundled model list. The repo's test command: DO_NOT_TRACK=1 , plus the opt-outs for Next.js, Nuxt, Astro, Gatsby, Storybook, Turborepo, Angular, .NET, and Cypress. OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_* variables are removed from those processes, and your environment cannot turn any of this back on. The traffic is to your model endpoint and the sites the agent visits. Besides that, ForgeQE downloads only public files: the model price lists from models.dev and LiteLLM, once a day ( FORGEQE_PRICES=off stops them); the agent runtime from its GitHub releases, when it is not installed; and the engine's ad-block and cookie-banner extensions from the Chrome Web Store, once. Nothing about your runs is sent.

t: Model routing: the right configured model for each task
x: Model routing: the right configured model for each task With more than one model in llms.json , ForgeQE can give each kind of work the model it needs. A small, fast, cheap model can plan and review. A strong model can write code and find root causes. A model that takes screenshots drives the browser, and a model with a large window reads a large pull request. You do not need to know what each model can do: ForgeQE finds out.

Turn it on In forgeqe.yaml : yaml Copy llm: models_file: ./llms.json routing: auto # off (the default for existing projects) | shadow | auto forgeqe init writes routing: auto for new projects. With no routing line it is off. shadow decides and logs each pick in the session log ( model.route ) but changes nothing, so you can see what the router would do before you let it. Shadow still runs the live checks and the rating call described below. Whatever routing says, the model an area gets must work: its key or sign-in is set and it passed a live call (one per model, kept for a day in .forgeqe/model-checks.json once it passes; a failed one is never kept, and a failed check in model-profile.json is checked again). When it does not, the next model that works is used, a GitHub Copilot profile first, and ForgeQE says why and how to fix the first. When none works, the error lists each model with the fix. Only --profile skips this. With auto , a GitHub Copilot seat counts as costing nothing more per call, so it is picked whenever it is rated good enough. See the picks, and every model's check with its fix: text Copy forgeqe models --routes

The areas of work Area What runs in it Needs agent ForgeQE's agent: the shell, forgeqe run , forgeqe mcp tool calls; rated 4+ browser Browser, desktop and mobile runs, from screenshots images; rated 4+ coding Scribe writing and healing tests, API tests tool calls; rated 5 review Test reviewer, pull-request review, evaluation judge tool calls; rated 3+ analysis Root cause of defects tool calls; rated 5 planning Refine, finding tests, API scenarios, exploratory charters tool calls; rated 3+

How a model is picked Your choices win. --profile (or WP_LLM_PROFILE ) and code.model keep the router out. A profile pinned in llm.routes is used for its area. code.review_profile still sets the reviewer. Facts rule models out. The router never picks a model that: has no key, or failed its live check; takes no images, for browser work; takes no tool calls, for agent work; has a window too small for the prompt (a large pull-request diff, for example). The facts come from llms.json , a live check, and the public model lists (models.dev and LiteLLM) that ForgeQE already downloads for prices. A fact that nobody knows never rules a model out. Ratings pick among the rest. The cheapest model rated at the area's bar is picked. Writing code and finding root causes ask for 5, because a weaker model there costs more in failed attempts than it saves. If no model reaches the bar, the best-rated one is picked. With no ratings yet, the active profile is kept unless a fact rules it out. A failed answer escalates once. When a root-cause analysis finds nothing, or finds a cause with low confidence although it could read the product's code, it runs again on a stronger model: one rated higher for the area, or rated the same and priced higher. Both runs are counted in its cost. The same configuration and task always give the same model. A pick changes only when the models, the ratings or the size of the prompt change. Each pick is shown once ("Model for planning: mini (…)") and is written to the session log.

How ForgeQE learns the models The first routed call in a project with two or more usable profiles does this once: A live check of each model ( python -m forgeqe_engine probe ): one short structured answer and one image. This finds a deployment that does not exist, a wrong key, and whether the model really takes images. It also measures how fast the model answers. One rating call. The active profile's model receives the facts of every model, never a key, an endpoint or an account. It rates each model 1–5 for each area and gives it a tier (fast, balanced or strong). The result is kept in .forgeqe/model-profile.json next to forgeqe.yaml . ForgeQE uses it until the profiles in llms.json change (provider, model, deployment or endpoint). You can edit the ratings. ForgeQE keeps your edits while the profiles stay the same. It checks the file every time it reads it: names that are not profiles and unknown areas are dropped, and ratings are rounded to whole numbers from 1 to 5. The live checks reach every profile in llms.json that has a key, whatever llm.routes pins. A pin keeps your runs' data on one deployment; the checks carry nothing from your runs. To send nothing to the other profiles at all, use routing: off , keep one profile with a key, or pass --profile . To check and rate again (for example, after a deployment changed its model): text Copy forgeqe models --routes --profile-models

t: Limit what an area may use
x: Limit what an area may use yaml Copy llm: routing: auto routes: browser: [gpt4o, gpt54] # only these two, the router picks between them coding: gpt54 # pinned planning: auto # any configured model (the default) A name in routes must be a profile in llms.json , and an area must be one of the six above. Anything else stops ForgeQE at start with a message that names it.

What it does not do ForgeQE's agent picks its model when its session starts and keeps it for the whole conversation. Changing the model mid-conversation would drop the prompt cache and make every later turn cost more. The agent hands heavy work to the other agents, and those are routed. A rating is one model's judgement. It is kept in a file that you can read and correct.
07 Desktop Windows thick-client apps: explore a goal, record by hand, replay the saved workflow

Desktop Automate Windows desktop apps Carries out a plain-language goal in a Windows thick-client app with UFO² and saves it as a workflow with checks of the outcome, or records the steps a tester does by hand, with no model; replays saved workflows with no model, healing a step whose control moved, and fixes a workflow from chat (a timeout, a wait, a dialog to dismiss) after showing the change. Apps and the secrets they may type come from env.yaml or forgeqe.yaml desktop:. Ask it Create an invoice for Contoso in the Billing app and save it as a test I'll show you the steps in Billing: record them Replay the billing workflow with customer Fabrikam Step 4 timed out while the list loaded: fix the workflow What it needs Optional A live model profile in llms.json (an API key or Microsoft Entra ID sign-in) Required Windows desktop apps: env.yaml (kind: desktop) or desktop.apps in forgeqe.yaml You give a Windows machine, and the app in forgeqe.yaml desktop.apps Limits Windows only, one run at a time per desktop Apps whose controls UI Automation cannot see (Citrix, some Java and custom-drawn apps) are not supported yet Tools desktop_explore desktop_record desktop_replay desktop_edit_workflow In detail

Desktop apps (Windows) ForgeQE also automates Windows thick-client apps (Win32, WinForms, WPF). In the shell, ask for a goal in the app ("create an invoice for Contoso in Billing") and ForgeQE's agent uses UFO² to do it, saves the run as a workflow with checks of the outcome, and can replay it with no model. The same from the command line: bash Copy forgeqe desktop setup --ufo forgeqe desktop explore "Create an invoice for Contoso, net 30" --app billing forgeqe desktop record --app billing # or do the steps yourself; no model forgeqe desktop replay <run folder>/workflow.yaml customer=Fabrikam forgeqe desktop replay workflow.yaml --data customers.csv # once per row; columns are variable names forgeqe desktop replay desktop-tests/ --junit results.xml # every workflow in a folder, results for CI forgeqe desktop doctor # can this machine replay unattended? Workflows wait for slow apps without fixed sleeps: a timeout and retries for the workflow or a step, wait_for a control to appear, show a text or go away (a splash screen), and a dismiss list of dialog buttons to click whenever they are in the way. expect_image compares a control or window with a baseline image (saved on the first run, kept next to the workflow), with a tolerance and regions to ignore. When you know the steps, forgeqe desktop record (or "I'll show you, record it" in the shell) saves what you do by hand: Ctrl+Shift+F11 over a control adds a check of its text, Ctrl+Shift+F12 finishes. After a failed replay, ForgeQE's agent can fix the workflow (a longer timeout, a wait_for , a dialog to dismiss): it shows the diff and writes it only when you agree. For nightly runs on a machine of your own, see docs/DESKTOP-CI.md . Apps come from desktop.apps in forgeqe.yaml (an absolute .exe and an argument list), and {{secret:NAME}} reads only the variables listed in desktop.secrets . Explore and replay take over the desktop's mouse and keyboard and ask first; use a test machine and a test account. Details: docs/DESKTOP.md .

ForgeQE desktop: thick-client automation Status: runs on Windows. The CI job .github/workflows/forgeqe-desktop-windows.yml (GitHub's windows-2022 ) installs the engine and the pinned UFO², replays Notepad live with the pywinauto driver and through forgeqe desktop replay , heals a moved control from the live window, and runs a whole explore: UFO² drives Notepad with a scripted model behind an OpenAI-compatible server, the action is recorded with the control's AutomationId, and the recording replays. Not yet run: explore with a real model (the job has no key), and your own apps. See Before first use on Windows . ForgeQE drives web apps through Chrome. The desktop engine does the same for Windows thick clients (Win32, WinForms, WPF, and the native parts of Electron and WebView2 apps): say what you want in plain language, UFO² does it on the live app, and the run is saved as a YAML workflow that replays later without a model.

Use bash Copy forgeqe desktop setup --ufo # once, on Windows: the engine, pywinauto, and the pinned UFO² forgeqe desktop apps # what forgeqe.yaml allows forgeqe desktop explore "Create an invoice for Contoso, net 30" --app billing forgeqe desktop record --app billing # or do the steps yourself: no model, no UFO forgeqe desktop replay .forgeqe/reports/desktop-explore-…/workflow.yaml customer=Fabrikam forgeqe desktop replay workflow.yaml --data customers.csv # once per row; the header names the variables forgeqe desktop replay desktop-tests/ --junit results.xml # every workflow in a folder, results for CI forgeqe desktop replay workflow.yaml --update-baselines # save new baselines for its expect_image steps forgeqe desktop doctor # can this machine run replay unattended? forgeqe desktop validate workflow.yaml # any OS Or ask ForgeQE's agent in the shell or forgeqe run : "create an invoice for Contoso in Billing and save it as a test", or "I'll show you the steps in Billing, record them". Its tools are test_apps , desktop_explore , desktop_record , desktop_replay and desktop_edit_workflow . It asks before it starts the app or takes over the desktop, and before it changes a workflow. Where it cannot ask (an MCP client), the call answers needs_confirmation until the user agrees. Desktop apps come from the active environment in env.yaml (see HOW_TO_USE.md, "Environments and apps"), or from desktop.apps in forgeqe.yaml , which works without environments: yaml Copy desktop: apps: billing: path: C:\Program Files\Contoso\Billing\Billing.exe args: ["--profile", "test"] # window: "Billing.*" # for a launcher that starts the real app and exits: connect by title secrets: [BILLING_PASSWORD] # the only environment variables {{secret:…}} may read heal: true # replay asks the model to re-find a control that moved (default on) screenshots: true # one screenshot per replayed step (default on) Each run writes a folder under the reports folder ( desktop-explore-… or desktop-replay-… ): run.json , report.html , steps/NNN.png , and for explore workflow.yaml , trace.json and UFO's own logs in ufo/ . A replay whose steps were healed also writes heals.json and asks whether to write the new locators into the workflow ( --accept-heals writes them without asking; with no terminal they are never written).

How a run flows text Copy forgeqe desktop explore ──► src/desktop/bridge.ts ──JSON lines──► python -m forgeqe_desktop serve │ start the app from desktop.apps (no shell) │ UFO² in-process: model = llms.json profile, │ UI tools only, every action traced with its ▼ control's UIA properties record.py ──► workflow.yaml forgeqe desktop replay ───► bridge ──► serve (replay.py on pywinauto, no model) │ a control is not found ▼ heal.py: the model picks one of the window's real controls, by number ▼ proposed locator → heals.json, written into the workflow only when accepted

One model config: llms.json → UFO UFO picks its model client by API_TYPE through ufo.llm.base.BaseService.get_service , which every model call goes through ( ufo/llm/llm_call.py ). The adapter adds the type forgeqe : write_ufo_config writes UFO's config/ufo/agents.yaml from its template, with API_TYPE: forgeqe , the model's name, and no endpoint and no key, for HOST_AGENT , APP_AGENT , BACKUP_AGENT and EVALUATION_AGENT . ufo_bridge.install makes get_service("forgeqe", …) return ForgeQEService , which calls the profile through the openai SDK ( models.py ): azure (key or auth: entra ), openai , openai_compatible (key or Entra), and ollama through its OpenAI-compatible /v1 . Keys, Azure endpoints and Entra use the browser engine's own helpers ( forgeqe_engine.llm ), so a profile means the same thing in both. Keys stay in environment variables. Each call's time and tokens go to ForgeQE's usage ledger as the "desktop agent" (counts only, never the prompt). Explore sends screenshots, so its profile must take images: "vision": true or false on the profile says so; without it, ollama profiles are refused and others accepted. Healing sends a screenshot only to a profile that takes images. The request parameters suit the model by themselves: a reasoning model (o1, o3, o4, gpt-5, by the profile's model or deployment name, or "reasoning": true on the profile) gets max_completion_tokens and no temperature from the first call, and when the API refuses a parameter ( max_tokens , temperature , frequency_penalty , response_format , …) the call is sent again without it, and later calls to that model leave it out ( py/forgeqe_engine/model_params.py ). The browser agent does the same.

Workflow YAML ( forgeqe-desktop-v1 ) yaml Copy format: forgeqe-desktop-v1 name: Create an invoice app: billing # a name from forgeqe.yaml desktop.apps, never a path or a command variables: customer: Contoso steps: - op: launch - op: click target: {automation_id: btnNewInvoice, control_type: Button, name: New invoice} - op: type target: {automation_id: txtCustomer, control_type: Edit} text: "{{customer}}" - op: type target: {automation_id: txtPassword, control_type: Edit} text: "{{secret:BILLING_PASSWORD}}" - op: select target: {automation_id: cmbTerms, control_type: ComboBox} value: Net 30 - op: keys keys: ctrl+s - op: expect target: {automation_id: lblStatus} text: Saved - op: close Ops: launch , click , double_click , type , select , keys , expect , expect_image , wait (at most 60 s), wait_for , close . Locators use UIA properties, never screen coordinates: automation_id , name , control_type , class_name , index (when several match), and path (the ancestors' control_type and name ). A target needs an automation_id or a name . Replay looks in the launched app's own windows only. Variables: {{name}} from the workflow's variables or name=value on the command line; {{secret:NAME}} from the environment, only for names in desktop.secrets . A secret ForgeQE itself uses (a model key, a tracker token) is refused there. Values are substituted once and never expanded again. Targets take {{name}} too (a CSV row's {{customer}} as the control to click), never a secret. Keys: ctrl , shift and alt with one named key or character ( ctrl+s , alt+f4 , enter , f5 ). The Windows and context-menu keys are refused: Win+R followed by typing runs any command. Typing is literal: pywinauto's key syntax ( ^ , % , + , ~ , {ENTER} ) in the text is escaped.

Recording by hand When you know the steps, do them yourself instead of describing a goal: no model and no UFO are involved, so it costs nothing and does exactly what you did. bash Copy forgeqe desktop record --app billing --name "Create an invoice" ForgeQE starts the app and watches the mouse and keyboard (low-level Windows hooks), asking UI Automation which control each click and key went to. Do the steps, then: Ctrl+Shift+F11 with the mouse over a control adds a check: an expect step with the text it shows now (a status message, a saved total). Add one at the end, so the replay tests the outcome, not only the steps. Ctrl+Shift+F12 , or closing the app, finishes. The console shows each step as it is recorded. What becomes a step: You do Step Click a control (two quick clicks: double_click ) click with its AutomationId, name and control type Pick an item in a drop-down select on the drop-down, with the item's name Type into a field (corrections and pastes included) one type with the field's text when you move on, read from the field A key chord outside a text field ( ctrl+s , enter , f5 ) keys Ctrl+Shift+F11 over a control expect with its text Passwords: a password field is never read; its step types {{secret:NAME}} (the one name in desktop.secrets , or <APP>_PASSWORD , which the result tells you to set). Text equal to a desktop.secrets value is written as its placeholder. The typed characters themselves are never kept, only the field's text when you move on. Only the app: clicks and keys outside the app's own process are not recorded; nor are the Windows and menu keys, or controls with neither an AutomationId nor a name. The result lists what was left out. The run folder has workflow.yaml , run.json and report.html , like explore. Replay it with forgeqe desktop replay .

Fixing a workflow from chat When a replayed step fails because the app was slow or a dialog was in the way, ForgeQE's agent fixes the workflow with desktop_edit_workflow : it proposes the change (a longer timeout or retries on the step, a wait_for before it, a dialog button in dismiss , a healed locator, a corrected text), shows you the diff, and writes the file only when you agree. For example, after "step 4 timed out while the invoice list loaded": text Copy Change invoice.yaml? • new wait_for step before step 4 • step 4: retries 2 - op: click + target: {automation_id: btnPost} + retries: 2 Each change has a fixed shape ( set , unset , set_step , add_dismiss , insert_step , remove_step , set_variable ); step numbers are the replay report's. Anything else is refused. The changed workflow is checked by the engine's own validator before it is shown; one that would not run is not offered. Comments and layout are kept. The old text is kept in the reports folder ( desktop-edits/ ), and a file that changed since the edit was proposed is not overwritten. The workflow must be a .yaml inside the working folder or the reports folder.

Waits, retries and dialogs Real apps are slow in places: a splash screen, a form that loads its data, a "Tip of the day" or "Save changes?" dialog. A workflow says how to wait for them, without fixed wait steps: yaml Copy timeout: 20 # seconds a step waits for its control (default 10, at most 300) retries: 1 # tries a failed action again, after a short pause (default 0, at most 5) dismiss: # clicked whenever one of them is in the way - {name: OK, control_type: Button, automation_id: btnTipClose} - {name: "Don't Save", control_type: Button} steps: - op: launch timeout: 90 # a slow start: how long to wait for the app's window - op: wait_for # the splash screen goes away target: {automation_id: splashForm} gone: true timeout: 120 - op: wait_for # the form has loaded its data target: {automation_id: lblStatus} text: Ready - op: click target: {automation_id: btnPost} timeout: 60 # per step, over the workflow's timeout retries: 3 Each step waits for its control up to its timeout . click , type and select also wait until the control is enabled and visible (a form that is still loading greys its buttons out). wait_for waits until a control is there, shows a text , or with gone: true has gone. retries applies to click , double_click , type , select , keys , expect and expect_image . Between tries, replay pauses (1 s, 2 s, … up to 5 s) and closes any dismiss dialog. An error in the workflow itself (a missing variable) is not retried. dismiss lists at most 10 targets, checked like any target. When a control is not found, or something waits to go away, replay clicks the dismiss controls that are on screen and looks again, up to 3 times per lookup. The report and the console name every dialog closed, and how many tries a step took.

Visual checks ( expect_image ) expect compares text. When what matters is drawn (a chart, a signature, a colour, a layout), expect_image compares pixels with a baseline image: yaml Copy - op: expect_image target: {automation_id: chartRevenue} # without a target: the app's top window image: revenue-chart.png # a file name in <workflow name>.baselines/ next to the workflow tolerance: 0.01 # share of pixels that may differ (default 0.01, i.e. 1%) ignore: [[0, 0, 120, 24]] # regions [x, y, width, height] that change every run (a date, a clock) The first run with no baseline saves what it captured and passes; the report says so. Commit the baselines folder with the workflow. --update-baselines replaces them after an intended change. A pixel counts as different when a colour channel differs by more than 32 of 255, so anti-aliasing and ClearType do not fail a check. A different size (another screen scale or window size) fails with both sizes named. The report shows the baseline, what was captured, and the differences in red, with the share of pixels that differ ( images/NNN-baseline|actual|diff.png in the run folder). Image names are file names only (letters, digits, _ , - , ending .png ). A path, .. , or a link that leads out of the baselines folder is refused. Run visual checks on one machine with a fixed resolution and scale (see DESKTOP-CI.md ).

Unattended runs Replay needs a signed-in, unlocked Windows session. Before it starts the app, it checks the session and fails at once with the reason if it is a Windows service (session 0), a locked screen, or a disconnected Remote Desktop session. forgeqe desktop doctor runs the same check. To run the suite every night on a machine of your own, see DESKTOP-CI.md : a runner set up in the user's session ( ci/desktop-runner/prepare-runner.ps1 ), a nightly workflow ( ci/desktop-runner/desktop-nightly.example.yml ), and --junit results.

Updating UFO² UFO² is pinned to one commit. Moving it is checked before it is pinned: .github/workflows/forgeqe-desktop-ufo-update.yml runs weekly, or by hand with a commit. It sets up that UFO on Windows ( FORGEQE_UFO_COMMIT , which takes a full 40-character commit id only), runs the adapter tests against its real code and a scripted explore of Notepad, and says in the job summary whether it passed. When it passed: bun scripts/ufo-bump.ts <commit> writes the new pin into src/desktop/setup.ts , py/forgeqe_desktop/ufo_runner.py and this page. Run the tests and push; the Windows CI job tests the pin again. When it fails, the failing step names what changed in UFO (usually the action executor or the config layout that the adapter wraps). Keep the pin until the adapter is updated for it.

Checks of the outcome A recording of actions only proves the steps run. When UFO has finished, and before the app closes, explore shows the model the goal and the app's controls with the text each shows now, and the model picks up to three whose text proves the goal (a status message, a saved value), by number, with the part of the text to expect. A check is kept only when that text really is in that control, so the model can choose among what is on screen but never invent it; text holding a desktop.secrets value is never offered. The checks are saved as expect steps at the end of the workflow, and the report says how many there are. With none, the report and the agent say so: add expect steps by hand.

Recording UFO's own step log names the control and a per-step id, not its AutomationId, so the adapter wraps UFO's ActionExecutor.execute and records each action with the UIA properties of the control it acted on. record.py turns that trace into steps: click_input → click / double_click , set_edit_text → type , keyboard_input → keys (one allowed chord) or type , select → select . Coordinate clicks, scrolls and anything else are listed as not recorded in the report. A typed value equal to a desktop.secrets value is written as its placeholder; typed text that only looks like {{…}} is kept literal, so a model told to type {{secret:X}} cannot make replay type the secret.

Security The YAML, the trace, the app's screen text and the model's replies can all be written by someone else. The rules in the repository's CLAUDE.md apply; for this engine: No command in the workflow. app: names a desktop.apps entry: an absolute .exe (a .bat or .cmd would run through cmd.exe , which reparses its arguments) and an argument list, started with subprocess.Popen([path, *args]) . UFO gets UI tools only. Each explore writes UFO's mcp.yaml with UICollector , HostUIExecutor and AppUIExecutor . UFO's default CommandLineExecutor , which runs shell commands, and its Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF executors are left out. The adapter starts the app, so UFO never launches a program. Keys: during explore the adapter refuses UFO's Windows and menu keys too, and the report lists what it refused. No one at the console: UFO's safe guard asks before sensitive actions; explore answers no, since nobody is there. Environment: the engine process gets system settings, the profile's key variable (or Entra's) and desktop.secrets , nothing else ( desktopEnvNames ). Explore controls the real mouse and keyboard. It asks before starting ( --yes to skip; required with no terminal). Use a test machine or VM and a test account. Agent tools: a workflow path the agent gives must be a .yaml inside the working folder or the reports folder (real path, so a link out is refused); variables are names and text only; heals are reported, never written. Healing: the model picks one of the window's real controls by number; control text is passed as data, and any other answer heals nothing. Heals are written into the workflow only when accepted. Report: every value is escaped; images are only the engine's own steps/NNN.png and images/NNN-baseline|actual|diff.png . Baselines: expect_image names are file names, and their real path must be inside the workflow's baselines folder, so a workflow cannot read or overwrite another file. Unattended machines: prepare-runner.ps1 never handles a password; automatic sign-in uses Sysinternals Autologon, which stores it encrypted. Install: UFO is cloned and checked out at the pinned commit (or FORGEQE_UFO_COMMIT , a full commit id only), and the checkout's HEAD is verified; replay's packages are pinned to exact versions.

Before first use on Windows Verified in CI: setup with and without --ufo , replay, healing, the CLI, and UFO's own code with the adapter (its config, its model calls routed to the profile, the action trace, UI tools only). Still to check, on a Windows test machine with your apps: UIA coverage: Inspect.exe shows the controls that matter with stable AutomationId s. Custom grids, Java (needs Java Access Bridge), Delphi, SAP GUI and Citrix (vision only) are where UIA falls short. Explore with your model: one goal with an Azure profile and one with auth: entra ; trace.json has the controls' AutomationIds, and ufo/ has UFO's logs. Replay: the recorded workflow passes 10 runs out of 10; a renamed control is healed. Cost and time of one explore, from forgeqe usage. Found by the Windows runs and fixed: UFO's pins need Python 3.10 (pandas 1.4.3); UFO prints emoji panels to stdout, which is the engine's event stream and crashed on the cp1252 console (now sent to stderr, characters replaced); an error in UFO's own evaluation lost the recorded actions (the trace is now kept and saved).

A pipeline template for a self-hosted Windows runner signed in to a desktop session.

Running desktop workflows unattended (nightly CI) Desktop replay clicks and types into real windows. It needs what a person at the machine would have: a signed-in Windows session, unlocked, with a screen. GitHub's hosted windows-2022 runners have that, and ForgeQE's own CI runs Notepad there. Your own apps usually need a machine of your own, with the app installed, its test database, and a network route to its servers. This page sets one up as a GitHub Actions self-hosted runner. The same rules apply to Azure DevOps agents and Jenkins nodes.

t: What breaks a desktop run, and how ForgeQE tells you
x: What breaks a desktop run, and how ForgeQE tells you Situation Effect Fix The runner is a Windows service Session 0 has no desktop; every control lookup times out Run the runner in the user's session (below) The screen is locked Windows sends no input to apps No inactivity lock, no screen-saver lock A Remote Desktop session was disconnected The session is locked Leave Remote Desktop with tscon (below), or don't use it on the test machine The machine slept or the screen turned off Input and screenshots stop Power plan: never sleep, never turn off the screen After a restart nobody signs in No session at all Sysinternals Autologon Before each replay or explore, the engine checks the session ( py/forgeqe_desktop/session.py ). On a session it cannot drive, the run fails at once with the reason, instead of timing out step by step. forgeqe desktop doctor runs the same check from a shell or a job: text Copy engine ready (C:\Users\qa\.forgeqe\desktop\.venv\Scripts\python.exe) explore not set up (forgeqe desktop setup --ufo) session 1, screen 1920x1080 desktop logged in and unlocked It exits with 1 when the desktop cannot be driven, so a job stops before the suite runs.

Set up the test machine Use a test machine or VM, and a test account: the runner's jobs control its mouse and keyboard. Sign in as the account the tests will run as. Install the runner (GitHub: Settings → Actions → Runners → New self-hosted runner). Give it the label forgeqe-desktop . When config.cmd asks whether to run as a service, answer no . Run ci/desktop-runner/prepare-runner.ps1 in an elevated PowerShell ( -WhatIf first to see the changes): powershell Copy .\prepare-runner.ps1 -RunnerDir C:\actions-runner -WhatIf .\prepare-runner.ps1 -RunnerDir C:\actions-runner It stops sleep, screen-off and the screen-saver lock. It turns the inactivity lock off and registers a logon task that starts run.cmd in this account's session. It warns you if the runner is also installed as a service. It never handles a password. Sign in automatically after a restart with Sysinternals Autologon , run as the test account. It stores the password encrypted by Windows. Never put the password in a script, a registry value you write yourself, or the repository. Fix the screen size. A visual check ( expect_image ) compares pixels, so the resolution and scale (100%, 125%) must match the machine where its baselines were saved. Set them once and leave them. Restart and check that the runner shows as idle on GitHub. Then run forgeqe desktop doctor from a job.

t: Leaving Remote Desktop without locking the session
x: Leaving Remote Desktop without locking the session Closing a Remote Desktop window disconnects the session, and Windows locks it. To leave it running instead, hand the session back to the machine's console. In an elevated prompt inside the Remote Desktop session: bat Copy for /f "skip=1 tokens=3" %s in ('query user %USERNAME%') do tscon %s /dest:console On a VM, the hypervisor's console (Hyper-V, VMware, VirtualBox) needs no such step.

The nightly job ci/desktop-runner/desktop-nightly.example.yml is a ready workflow. Copy it into .github/workflows/ in the repository that holds your desktop workflows. It: runs at night on [self-hosted, windows, forgeqe-desktop] , one run at a time; installs a pinned ForgeQE and runs forgeqe desktop setup and forgeqe desktop doctor ; replays every workflow in a folder: forgeqe desktop replay desktop-tests/ --junit results/desktop.xml ; keeps the reports, screenshots and image diffs as an artifact. --junit writes one test case per workflow (and per CSV row with --data ), which CI servers show as test results. runs.json in the output folder has the same, with the path of each report. Secrets the workflows type ( {{secret:NAME}} ) come from the CI's secret store as environment variables, and must be listed in desktop.secrets or the environment's secrets in env.yaml . Pick the environment with FORGEQE_ENV or --env . Healing calls the model. In a nightly run, either give the job the model's key so moved controls are healed and reported in heals.json (never written into the workflow without --accept-heals ), or pass --no-heal so a moved control fails the run.
08 Mobile Android and iOS apps through Appium or Maestro: explore a goal, replay, run the team's flows

Mobile Automate Android and iOS apps Carries out a plain-language goal in an Android or iOS app through Appium and saves it as a mobile workflow with checks of the outcome; replays workflows with no model on Appium (healing a moved control) or Maestro; runs the team's own Maestro flows after checking them against an allowlist; uploads an app build to TestMu AI and saves its lt:// id as the app's build. Apps come from env.yaml (kind: mobile) or forgeqe.yaml mobile:. Ask it Sign in to the courier app and accept the first delivery, and save it as a test Replay the courier login on Maestro Run our Maestro flows in .maestro/ Upload builds/courier.apk to TestMu for the courier app What it needs Optional A live model profile in llms.json (an API key or Microsoft Entra ID sign-in) Required Mobile apps: env.yaml (kind: mobile) or mobile.apps in forgeqe.yaml You give an Appium server with a device or emulator (or a device cloud), or Maestro installed; the app in env.yaml or forgeqe.yaml mobile.apps Limits Explore runs on Appium only Maestro replays do not heal moved controls or compare images (expect_image) On TestMu AI, Maestro (through HyperExecute) refuses workflows that type secrets; replay those there with --driver appium Tools mobile_explore mobile_replay mobile_maestro mobile_upload In detail

Mobile apps (Android, iOS) ForgeQE drives Android and iOS apps two ways: through Appium , step by step (it can explore a goal with the model, and heals a control that moved), and through Maestro (fast replays, and your team's own Maestro flows). In the shell, ask for a goal in the app ("sign in to the courier app and accept the first delivery") and ForgeQE's agent explores it on your device or emulator and saves a workflow with checks of the outcome. The same from the command line: bash Copy forgeqe mobile doctor # does the Appium server answer, is maestro installed? forgeqe mobile explore "Sign in and accept the first delivery" --app courier forgeqe mobile replay <run folder>/workflow.yaml # on Appium (mobile.driver), healing moved controls forgeqe mobile replay workflow.yaml --driver maestro # the same workflow as a Maestro flow forgeqe mobile replay mobile-tests/ --junit results.xml # every workflow in a folder, results for CI forgeqe mobile maestro .maestro/ # your team's Maestro flows, checked first forgeqe mobile flow workflow.yaml > login.flow.yaml # a workflow as a Maestro flow, to keep Apps come from env.yaml ( kind: mobile , platform: android or ios , app_id , and optionally activity and an app build to install) or mobile.apps in forgeqe.yaml. mobile.appium names the Appium server (default http://127.0.0.1:4723 , or a device cloud's hub with its user and key in environment variables), and {{secret:NAME}} reads only mobile.secrets (and the environment's secrets). A flow kept with forgeqe mobile flow reads each secret as ${MAESTRO_<NAME>} , never its value, so set MAESTRO_<NAME> when you run it outside ForgeQE; a workflow that types a secret not listed there is refused. Team Maestro flows run only with UI commands: scripts, JavaScript in ${…} , Maestro's AI commands and file writes are refused. Details: docs/MOBILE.md . On TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest) Both drivers run on TestMu AI's devices. Upload the app build once, then use the lt:// id it prints as the app's app (in env.yaml or mobile.apps ; ForgeQE adds it to Appium's LT:Options itself): bash Copy forgeqe mobile upload courier.apk # prints lt://APP…, for TestMu's real devices forgeqe mobile upload courier.apk --virtual # for TestMu's emulators and simulators instead forgeqe mobile upload courier.apk --name courier-nightly # the name TestMu shows for the build The user name and access key come from LT_USERNAME and LT_ACCESS_KEY (or the variables username_env and access_key_env name), for example in a .env file in the project folder. They go only to the mobile engine, never to a flow or a model, and a user or key in the hub URL is refused. yaml Copy mobile: apps: courier: { platform: android, app_id: com.contoso.courier, app: "lt://APP1016…" } appium: # Appium on TestMu's mobile hub url: https://mobile-hub.lambdatest.com/wd/hub username_env: LT_USERNAME access_key_env: LT_ACCESS_KEY capabilities: "LT:Options": { w3c: true, isRealMobile: true, deviceName: "Pixel 6", platformVersion: "14" } maestro: testmu: # Maestro on TestMu, through HyperExecute cli: ./hyperexecute # TestMu's hyperexecute CLI devices: ["Pixel 6-14"] # name-version, or a pattern such as ".*-.*" real_device: true # false: TestMu's emulators Appium needs nothing else: it talks to the hub with the user and key from the two variables. Maestro runs through HyperExecute. mobile.maestro.testmu names TestMu's hyperexecute CLI ( cli ), the devices to run on ( devices ), and real devices or emulators ( real_device ). ForgeQE writes a HyperExecute project in the run folder (the flows in their folder layout, so runFlow still works, the app, fixed setup and run scripts, and hyperexecute.yaml ) and starts the CLI. Team flows are checked against the allowlist first, as always. The access key is removed from the CLI's output and from every file in the run folder; the run prints the HyperExecute job link. Secrets: a workflow that types a secret is refused on Maestro on TestMu (HyperExecute would need the value in its own vault). Replay it on TestMu with --driver appium instead. Maestro on TestMu runs Android apps; run iOS apps there through Appium. In the shell, ask in words: "upload builds/courier.apk to TestMu for the courier app". After you agree, ForgeQE uploads it and writes the lt:// id into that app's app: in forgeqe.yaml (an app from env.yaml gets the id to set there). The build must be inside the working folder; hidden folders and files named like credentials are refused. samples/mobile-testmu is a ready project with TestMu's Wikipedia sample app: copy .env.example to .env , upload the app with forgeqe mobile upload sample.apk , put the id in its forgeqe.yaml , download the hyperexecute CLI into the folder, then run forgeqe mobile replay wiki.yaml --driver appium , --driver maestro , and forgeqe mobile maestro .maestro . Details: docs/MOBILE.md .
