Use bash Copy forgeqe mobile doctor # does the Appium server answer, is maestro installed? forgeqe mobile apps # the mobile apps of the active environment forgeqe mobile explore "Sign in as the courier and accept the first delivery" --app courier forgeqe mobile replay .forgeqe/reports/mobile-explore-…/workflow.yaml forgeqe mobile replay workflow.yaml --driver maestro forgeqe mobile replay mobile-tests/ --data couriers.csv --junit results.xml forgeqe mobile maestro .maestro/ # the team's flows forgeqe mobile flow workflow.yaml # print a workflow as a Maestro flow forgeqe mobile validate workflow.yaml Or ask ForgeQE's agent in the shell or forgeqe run : "sign in to the courier app and save it as a test", "replay the courier login on Maestro", "run our Maestro flows". Its tools are mobile_explore , mobile_replay and mobile_maestro . It asks before each one starts, and desktop_edit_workflow fixes a mobile workflow after a failed replay, the same way as a desktop one.

Apps and settings Mobile apps come from the active environment in env.yaml, or from mobile.apps in forgeqe.yaml: yaml Copy # env.yaml environments: qa: apps: courier: kind: mobile platform: android # or ios app_id: com.contoso.courier # Android package or iOS bundle id activity: .MainActivity # Android only, optional app: /builds/courier-qa.apk # optional: install this build (.apk/.aab/.ipa/.app/.zip, https URL, bs://…) description: Driver app that confirms delivery secrets: [COURIER_PASSWORD_QA] yaml Copy # forgeqe.yaml mobile: driver: appium # appium | maestro: the default for replays appium: url: http://127.0.0.1:4723 capabilities: # added to every session appium:udid: emulator-5554 # username_env: BROWSERSTACK_USERNAME # access_key_env: BROWSERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY maestro: command: [maestro] # device: emulator-5554 secrets: [COURIER_PASSWORD] heal: true screenshots: true Each run writes a folder under the reports folder ( mobile-explore-… , mobile-replay-… , mobile-maestro-… ) with run.json , report.html , step screenshots, and for Maestro runs the flow, maestro.log and Maestro's JUnit report.

Workflow YAML ( forgeqe-mobile-v1 ) yaml Copy format: forgeqe-mobile-v1 name: Courier signs in app: courier timeout: 20 dismiss: - {name: Allow, control_type: android.widget.Button} # permission dialogs, when they are in the way steps: - op: launch - op: type target: {automation_id: username} text: "{{courier}}" - op: type target: {automation_id: password} text: "{{secret:COURIER_PASSWORD}}" - op: tap target: {name: Sign in} - op: wait_for target: {automation_id: progress} gone: true - op: scroll_to target: {name: Deliveries} - op: expect target: {automation_id: status} text: Welcome Ops: launch , tap , double_tap , long_press , type , expect , expect_image , swipe ( direction up, down, left or right, optionally on a target ), scroll_to (scrolls until the target is on screen), back , hide_keyboard , keys ( enter , back , tab , delete , search ), wait , wait_for , close . Timeouts, retries and dismiss work as in desktop workflows. Explore saves a tap on a system dialog (another package's control, such as Android's notification prompt) under dismiss , not as a step, so the workflow still runs where the dialog never shows; on Maestro, each dismiss target is tapped after a launch if it is there. Targets use the desktop keys, mapped per platform: automation_id is the Android resource-id (with or without the package:id/ prefix) or the iOS accessibility identifier; name is the Android text or content-desc, or the iOS label; control_type is the Android class ( android.widget.Button ) or the iOS type ( XCUIElementTypeButton ); index picks one of several matches.

Explore The model sees the goal, its steps so far, the numbered controls on screen with the text each shows, and a screenshot when the profile takes images. It answers with one action on a control by its number (tap, long press, type), a swipe or scroll, back, or done. So it can only act on a control that is on screen. When it says done, it picks checks of the outcome from the controls' current text, kept only when that text is really there, as on the desktop. The app's text is passed as data.

Maestro ForgeQE workflows on Maestro. --driver maestro writes the workflow as a Maestro flow ( flow.yaml in the run folder) and runs maestro test . Maestro's debug output gives each workflow step its result. Variables are filled in first. Values are matched literally, so Maestro's regular expressions never see them as patterns. A secret becomes ${MAESTRO_NAME} , which Maestro reads from the environment ForgeQE gives it, so a secret's value never lands in the flow file or on a command line. A value holding ${…} is refused, because Maestro would run it as JavaScript. Your team's flows. forgeqe mobile maestro <files or folders> checks each flow, and every flow it runs, before Maestro gets it: Only UI commands pass: launchApp , tapOn , inputText , assertVisible , scrollUntilVisible , swipe , extendedWaitUntil , runFlow , repeat , retry and the like. These are refused: runScript , evalScript and assertTrue , which run JavaScript. Maestro's AI commands, which send screenshots to a service. takeScreenshot , recordings and addMedia , which read or write files. ${…} may only name a variable ( ${USERNAME} ), never an expression. when: {true: …} is refused, because it is JavaScript. openLink takes http(s) or the app's own deep links, never javascript: , file: or intent: . runFlow files must be .yaml inside the working folder; links out of it are refused too. Nesting stops at 5 levels. A refused flow does not run, and the error names the command.

TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest) Both drivers run on TestMu's devices. Upload the app once, then use the lt:// id it returns as the app's app : bash Copy forgeqe mobile upload courier.apk # → lt://APP… (--virtual for TestMu's emulators) From the shell, ask in words ("upload builds/courier.apk to TestMu for courier"): mobile_upload asks first, uploads the build (it must be inside the working folder), and saves the lt:// id as that app's app: in forgeqe.yaml. The user and key come from LT_USERNAME and LT_ACCESS_KEY (or the variables the config names), for example in a .env file in the project folder. samples/mobile-testmu/ is a ready project with TestMu's Wikipedia sample app. yaml Copy mobile: apps: courier: { platform: android, app_id: com.contoso.courier, app: "lt://APP1016…" } appium: # Appium on TestMu's mobile hub url: https://mobile-hub.lambdatest.com/wd/hub username_env: LT_USERNAME access_key_env: LT_ACCESS_KEY capabilities: "LT:Options": { w3c: true, isRealMobile: true, deviceName: "Pixel 6", platformVersion: "14", build: nightly } # app: added from the app's own maestro: testmu: # Maestro on TestMu, through HyperExecute cli: /opt/hyperexecute # TestMu's hyperexecute CLI devices: ["Pixel 6-14"] # name-version, or a pattern such as ".*-.*" real_device: true # false: TestMu's emulators # username_env: LT_USERNAME # the defaults # access_key_env: LT_ACCESS_KEY Appium needs nothing else: the Appium driver talks to the hub with the user and key from the two variables. Maestro runs through HyperExecute. ForgeQE writes a HyperExecute project in the run folder and starts the CLI. The project holds the flows in their folder layout (so runFlow still works), the app (an lt:// id is passed as the device's appId ; a build file is uploaded with the project), a fixed setup script (Android platform tools 35.0.2 and Maestro 2.6.1 from its release, both checked against their SHA-256) and a fixed run script, and hyperexecute.yaml . Team flows are checked against the allowlist first, as always. Flow file names may only use letters, digits and _ . - / (and one leading dot, for .maestro/ ), because HyperExecute's shell reads them. After the job, ForgeQE downloads its artifacts (Maestro's command results and JUnit reports), so each step gets its own result in the report. Secrets on Maestro on TestMu: a workflow that types a secret is refused there for now (HyperExecute would need the value in its own vault). Replay it on TestMu with --driver appium . The access key is passed to the CLI as an argument. It is removed from the CLI's output and from every file in the run folder. Neither the user name nor the key is passed to the flows' environment. .github/workflows/forgeqe-mobile-testmu.yml runs all three on TestMu (Appium, Maestro with a workflow, a team flow) with TestMu's Wikipedia sample app, once the repository has the secrets LT_USERNAME and LT_ACCESS_KEY .

Security No commands from the workflow or the model. app: names a configured app (a platform and an id). Appium is spoken to over HTTP, and maestro is started with an argument list, never a shell. Locators go into XPath as quoted literals, so a target cannot change the query. Secrets: {{secret:NAME}} reads only mobile.secrets and the environment's secrets, and ForgeQE's own keys are refused there. Explore types a secret from its placeholder, so the model never sees the value. The engine's environment holds system settings, the profile's key, the listed secrets, the cloud's user and key, and JAVA_HOME / ANDROID_HOME , nothing else. Cloud credentials come from the variables mobile.appium.username_env and access_key_env name; a user or key in the URL is refused. TLS is verified as usual. App builds are absolute paths to an app file, https URLs, or a device cloud's own upload ids ( bs:// , lt:// , storage:filename= ); file:// and other schemes are refused.

Containers and mock services When Docker or Podman is installed, ForgeQE can start the services a test run needs, and mock an API the tests should not call. Ask in the shell: "start the database and the queue", "mock the payments API from the last run", "make a mock from openapi.yaml and point order-api at it", "show the db logs". Full reference: docs/CONTAINERS.md . The project declares its services in forgeqe.yaml. ForgeQE starts only these, and builds each command itself: yaml Copy containers: # runtime: podman # default: docker, else podman, on PATH services: db: image: postgres:16.4 # an exact version or a digest; never latest ports: [5432] # or "15432:5432" (this machine:container); always 127.0.0.1 env: { POSTGRES_DB: shop, POSTGRES_USER: shop } secrets: [POSTGRES_PASSWORD] # names of environment variables (.env works), passed by name volumes: ["./db/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d"] # read-only, inside the project ready: { tcp: 5432 } # or { http: /health, port: 8080 } timeout: 90 bash Copy forgeqe services # declared services, what runs, whether Docker answers forgeqe services up db # start and wait until ready; keeps running after the command forgeqe services logs db --lines 50 forgeqe services down # stop this project's containers, mocks included Mocks: mock_service builds WireMock stubs. From a run, they answer what the app really got. From an OpenAPI or Swagger description, or a contract set, they answer with its examples, or values made from its schemas. The mock runs on a free port of 127.0.0.1 ( wiremock/wiremock:3.9.1 , or containers.mock.image ), and its stubs are in .forgeqe/mocks/<name>/mappings . With for_app , an API app of the active environment points at the mock for the rest of the session, so API tests and the tests ForgeQE runs ( FORGEQE_APP_<APP>_URL ) use it. Session: what the agent starts (services or mocks) stops when the shell, forgeqe run , or forgeqe mcp ends. forgeqe services up keeps its services running until forgeqe services down . Asked first: services up and mock_service ask before they start anything. Guard rails: Fixed run settings: every container gets no new privileges, a process limit, ports on 127.0.0.1, read-only mounts, and labels with the project, so ForgeQE stops only its own containers. Refused service settings: privileged , network , cap_add , devices , user , and anything else that is not a service setting. Also refused: a port bound to another address, an image without an exact version, and a secret that is one of ForgeQE's own keys. Mounts: inside the project only. A mount that is or holds a hidden file ( .env , .git ), a file named like a key, or a link is refused, because a container can send what it reads anywhere. The docker, podman and compose programs only see the variables they need to find their daemon, plus the service's listed secrets. Not in the agents' shell: docker , podman , nerdctl and compose commands are refused for ForgeQE's agent and Scribe. Containers start only through these tools. Compose files. containers.compose: docker-compose.yml reads the file's services into the same list, checked by the same rules (forgeqe.yaml's own declaration of a service wins): Translated: image , ports , environment , bind mounts, command and depends_on . A ${NAME} value becomes a secret passed by name. Left out: named volumes. Mounts made read-only are listed in the notes. Ignored: container_name , restart , healthcheck and networks . Refused: build , privileged , network_mode , cap_add , devices , pid and env_file . x-forgeqe: { ready: … } sets the ready check. Without it, a service is ready when its first port takes connections. The project's containers share their own network, so services reach each other by name ( db:5432 ). Docker as the workspace and the browser. Two settings move the rest of the work into containers: yaml Copy browser: provider: docker # the browser agent, the replay and Scribe's live browser use Chromium in a container containers: workspace: # Scribe's shell commands and every test ForgeQE runs use this image image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright/dotnet:v1.63.0-noble env: { NEXUS_ENVIRONMENT: CI } browser: # optional headless: false # visible on a virtual display inside the container (some sites refuse headless) Workspace: Scribe builds, restores, runs and fixes tests in a Linux container of the project's image, with the repository at the same path. Each test run gets its own container from that image, and HOME is a volume of the project's, so package caches outlive the session. The agents and the model key stay on this machine, and ForgeQE's own agent keeps this machine's shell. .env , keys and other credential files in the repository are covered inside the containers. Browser: each browser run gets a fresh container, reached through a gateway that wants a random token. A declared service is reached by its name; an app on this machine is host.docker.internal , not localhost . --browser-provider docker picks it for one run. FORGEQE_HOST_RUN=1 runs Scribe's commands and the tests on this machine for a session. Tests in a container. With containers.tests , run_tests runs the repository's tests in that image instead of on this machine, after starting the services it lists: yaml Copy containers: tests: image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.48.2-jammy services: [db] secrets: [TEST_DB_PASSWORD] What runs: the command you confirmed, inside the container, in the repository (mounted at its own path, so the result files land where ForgeQE reads them). User: your user. Variables: only the environment's FORGEQE_* variables, the saved logins' variables, and the listed env and secrets. To run on this machine instead: ask to run the tests on this machine ( in_container: false ). Machines: Linux and macOS. Testcontainers. When a test needs a real database or queue, or the repository already uses Testcontainers, Scribe's testcontainers skill writes the test to start it from code. t: ForgeQE containers: services and mocks in Docker or Podman
x: ForgeQE containers: services and mocks in Docker or Podman Status: the tests run against a fake runtime on any OS. They check the commands ForgeQE builds, the checks on config, compose files, mounts and secrets, the mock stubs, and tests in a container. tests/containers.live.test.ts runs on real Docker (and is skipped without it): Postgres from forgeqe.yaml and from a compose file. A WireMock mock that answers a recorded run's calls. A tests container that reaches the database by name and writes its results into the repository as this machine's user. .github/workflows/forgeqe-containers.yml runs both on GitHub's Docker. There, a skipped live test fails the job. ForgeQE uses Docker or Podman, when one is installed, for five jobs: Services a test run needs: a database, a queue, a cache, or the API under test. The project declares them in forgeqe.yaml, or in a docker-compose file that forgeqe.yaml names. Mocks of an API: WireMock stubs made from the calls a browser run recorded, or from an OpenAPI description, so the tests can run without the real service. The repository's tests in a container: run_tests runs the command the user confirmed in an image, instead of on this machine, after starting the services the tests need. A workspace for the coding agents: with containers.workspace , Scribe's shell commands (build, restore, run, git) and every test ForgeQE runs for it go to a container of the project's image. The agents stay on this machine. A browser in a container: with browser.provider: docker , the browser agent, the replay and Scribe's live browser drive Chromium in a container of Microsoft's Playwright image. Scribe also has a testcontainers skill, for tests that start their own services from code (below). ForgeQE's agent uses them through two tools, services and mock_service . The CLI has forgeqe services . When neither Docker nor Podman is on PATH, the agent isn't offered these tools.

Use bash Copy forgeqe services # the declared services, what runs, whether the runtime answers forgeqe services up # start every declared service and wait until each is ready forgeqe services up db queue # just these forgeqe services logs db --lines 50 # last lines, secrets removed forgeqe services down # stop and remove this project's containers (mocks included) In the shell or forgeqe run , you can ask, for example: "start the database" "is the queue up?" "mock the payments API from the last run" "make a mock service from openapi.yaml and point order-api at it" "stop the services" The agent asks before it starts anything.

Declaring services yaml Copy # forgeqe.yaml containers: runtime: docker # docker | podman; default: docker, else podman, on PATH services: db: description: Orders database for the API tests image: postgres:16.4 # an exact version, or name@sha256:<digest> ports: [5432] # 127.0.0.1:5432 -> 5432; "15432:5432" maps another port of this machine env: # plain values only POSTGRES_DB: shop POSTGRES_USER: shop secrets: [POSTGRES_PASSWORD] # environment variable names; their values come from the environment or .env volumes: - ./db/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d # read-only; a folder or file inside the project command: ["-c", "log_statement=all"] # arguments for the image's entrypoint ready: { tcp: 5432 } # or { http: /health, port: 8080 }; without it: the container runs timeout: 90 # seconds to wait until ready (default 60) queue: image: rabbitmq:3.13.7-management ports: [5672, 15672] ready: { http: /, port: 15672 } mock: image: wiremock/wiremock:3.9.1 # the default Setting Rule Service name Lower-case letters, digits and - , starting with a letter. Names starting with mock- are kept for mocks. image Must have an exact tag or a digest. An untagged image or latest is refused, because it changes under the same name. ports Always bound to 127.0.0.1. An address such as 0.0.0.0:5432:5432 is refused. env Plain values on one line. Secrets go under secrets . secrets Variable names. They are passed to the runtime by name ( --env NAME ), so the value is never on a command line. One of ForgeQE's own keys (a model key, a tracker token) is refused. volumes Always read-only. Must be inside the folder of forgeqe.yaml, and can't be the whole folder. command A list of arguments, never one command string. depends_on Services to start first. Anything else Refused with an error, not ignored. That includes privileged , network , cap_add , devices , user , pid and the socket. Every service, whether from forgeqe.yaml or a compose file, can list depends_on . up starts a service after the ones it depends on; a circle is refused.

Compose files yaml Copy containers: compose: docker-compose.yml # or a list; inside the project ForgeQE reads each service of the file and translates it into a forgeqe.yaml service. The same rules then check it, and a service declared in forgeqe.yaml wins over the compose file's service of the same name. Compose itself never runs. Compose ForgeQE image Required; an exact version or a digest. build is refused: build and tag the image first. ports "5432" , "15432:5432" , "127.0.0.1:15432:5432" , or the long form; always bound to 127.0.0.1. Any other address, and UDP, are refused. environment Plain values are passed as they are. KEY: ${KEY} , KEY alone in the list form, and KEY: ${KEY:-default} pass the variable by name as a secret. ${OTHER} under another name, and values that mix text and ${…} , are refused. volumes Bind mounts ( ./db/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d ) are mounted read-only, and :rw is noted. Named and anonymous volumes are left out, so the container keeps no data between runs. A path outside the project is refused when the service starts. command A list, or a string split into arguments (compose uses no shell, and neither does ForgeQE). depends_on List or map form: the start order. condition is not used; ForgeQE waits until each service is ready. x-forgeqe ready , timeout , description , as in forgeqe.yaml. Without ready , a service with ports is ready when its first port takes connections. container_name , restart , labels , healthcheck , networks , expose , deploy , profiles , … Ignored: ForgeQE names, labels and networks the containers itself. privileged , network_mode , cap_add , devices , pid , ipc , user , security_opt , volumes_from , env_file , entrypoint , extends , … Refused, and the error names the setting. What was left out (a named volume, a mount made read-only) is listed in notes .

The project network Each project's containers join their own network, forgeqe-<project> , under their service name. So the API container reaches the database as db:5432 , and the tests container reaches both. No other container joins the network, and no container is on the host's network. forgeqe services down with no names also removes the network.

Tests in a container yaml Copy containers: tests: image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.48.2-jammy # an exact version; the tests' toolchain services: [db, order-api] # started first (when not running yet); the tests reach them by name env: { DB_HOST: db } secrets: [TEST_DB_PASSWORD] With containers.tests set, run_tests runs the tests in that image unless it is called with in_container: false . Its confirmation says where the tests will run. The container: Runs the command the user confirmed with the image's own shell, sh -c "<command>" , inside the container, never on this machine. Mounts the repository read-write at its own path and works in it, so results land where ForgeQE reads them. On this machine, the tests already have the whole disk. A folder outside the repository that the results go to is mounted the same way. Runs as this machine's user ( --user uid:gid ), so files it writes are yours. It also gets --security-opt no-new-privileges , --pids-limit 4096 and --rm , and it is removed by name when the run ends or is stopped. Gets only these variables: CI=1 , NO_COLOR , HOME=/tmp , the environment's FORGEQE_ACTIVE_ENV , FORGEQE_APP_* and FORGEQE_VAR_* , the saved logins' variables, and containers.tests env and secrets . Secrets are passed by name. ForgeQE's own keys are never passed. Has secret values removed from its output , as on this machine. This needs a Linux or macOS machine, because the repository is mounted at its own path.

The workspace yaml Copy containers: workspace: image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright/dotnet:v1.63.0-noble # an exact version; the project's toolchain services: [db] # started first; reached by name env: { NEXUS_ENVIRONMENT: CI, DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD: Major } secrets: [TEST_DB_PASSWORD] # by name; values from the environment or .env With containers.workspace set: Scribe's shell runs in the container. The agent runtime runs each command as $SHELL -c <command> . ForgeQE sets SHELL to a script that runs the same command with docker exec … sh -c <command> , in the same folder, in the workspace container. A folder outside the repository is refused, since the container has only the repository. The agent is told its commands run in a Linux container of that image. Every test ForgeQE runs goes to the same image: the coding loop's runs, heal , suite 's existing tests and run_tests . Each run gets its own container ( docker run --rm ), so stopping a run removes it. Browsers the test starts are found with docker top , as ForgeQE finds them on this machine. What stays on this machine: the agent runtime, the model key, ForgeQE's other secrets, the file tools (read, edit, write; the repository is the same folder in both places), and ForgeQE's own agent, which works with you on this machine and keeps its shell here. FORGEQE_HOST_RUN=1 runs everything on this machine for a session. The container: one per ForgeQE process and project, forgeqe-<project>-workspace-<id> , removed when ForgeQE ends; the repository mounted read-write at its own path; credential files in it ( .env , .env.* except templates, .npmrc , .netrc , *.pem , *.key , id_* keys) covered with an empty read-only file, and .ssh , .aws , .azure , .docker , .kube and .forgeqe/sessions with an empty folder; HOME on the project's volume forgeqe-<project>-home , so NuGet, npm and pip caches outlive the session. Docker creates the volume for root, so ForgeQE runs chown in it once, with a fixed command; this machine's user ( --user uid:gid ), no-new-privileges , --pids-limit 4096 , the project network; only CI=1 , HOME , the env and secrets listed, and, in each command, the environment's FORGEQE_APP_* and FORGEQE_VAR_* and the saved logins' variables, by name. containers.tests still names the image run_tests uses when it is set. Without it, run_tests uses the workspace's image. This needs a Linux or macOS machine, as tests in a container do.

The browser in a container yaml Copy browser: provider: docker # or per run: --browser-provider docker containers: browser: # optional image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.63.0-noble # default; needs Node.js and /ms-playwright headless: false # default: browser.headless; a visible browser runs on a virtual display (Xvfb) One container per use: each browser run (a suite runs suite.parallel at once) gets its own, and a coding job gets one that its replay and live browser share. Each is removed when its run or job ends. Connection: Chromium listens on 127.0.0.1 inside the container. CDP has no authentication of its own, so a small gateway in front of it ( BROWSER_SERVER in src/containers/browser.ts , run with the image's Node.js) accepts a connection only with a random 48-character token in its path, compared in constant time, and refuses a browser Origin that is not local. The port is published on 127.0.0.1 only. The token reaches the engine, the replay and the live browser's MCP server through the environment, never a file or a command line. Visible or headless: a visible browser runs on Xvfb inside the container. Sites that turn headless browsers away see an ordinary one, but you do not see it on your screen. Runs keep screenshots and traces as usual. Reaching the app: the container joins the project network, so a declared service is reached by its name ( http://order-api:8080 ). An app this machine serves is http://host.docker.internal:<port> ; localhost is the container itself, and ForgeQE warns when a run starts there. Replay: one pass, in a new browser context. The second pass (without Playwright's automation switches) needs a launch, which a running browser does not have. A run explored in a container is replayed in one even when the provider is changed back later ( run.json ).

Testcontainers (Scribe) When a test needs a real service, or the repository already uses Testcontainers (Java, .NET, Node, Python, Go), Scribe loads the testcontainers skill. It reuses the repository's containers and fixtures, pins images, waits for readiness, uses the mapped port, and sets the app's own configuration from it. It never uses privileged mode, the host network, the Docker socket, or a docker command from a test. These containers belong to the tests in the repository: the tests start and stop them, wherever they run.

Mocks mock_service builds WireMock stubs and runs WireMock on a free port of 127.0.0.1: From a run (the default: the latest run, or run_dir ): One stub per method, path and query of the app's own API calls, answering with the last status, content type and body the app got. Other sites' calls are left out unless third_party is set. Failed calls are left out. Answers that were cut when recorded are listed under skipped . From a description ( spec : OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2, a link or a file): One stub per REST operation. Each stub answers with the operation's first success status and a body from the schema's examples, or values made from its types. A path parameter ( /orders/{id} ) matches any one path segment. Instead of a description, you can give a contract set from api_contracts ( set_id ). GraphQL, SOAP and gRPC are listed under skipped , not mocked. A spec given as a link is fetched by ForgeQE itself, with no credentials, as api_contracts does. The stubs are written to .forgeqe/mocks/<name>/mappings/ . You can read and edit them there. The folder is mounted read-only at /home/wiremock/mappings . WireMock runs with --enable-stub-cors , so a web app on another local port can call it. With for_app: <api app> , the active environment's API app points at the mock for the rest of the session. That covers the API tools, and the tests ForgeQE runs, which read FORGEQE_APP_<APP>_URL . env.yaml itself is not changed.

Lifetime Services and mocks the agent starts are removed when the shell, forgeqe run , or forgeqe mcp ends, as are the workspace and browser containers ( forgeqe.kind workspace and browser ). The home volume stays. forgeqe services up keeps its services running after the command ends, until forgeqe services down . Container names are forgeqe-<project>-<service> . <project> is a hash of the project folder, so two projects never share a container. Starting a service replaces its earlier container. Removing a container also removes the anonymous volumes its image declares (a database's data folder), so nothing is left on the machine. A container is never reused with old settings. Labels: each container carries forgeqe=1 , forgeqe.project , forgeqe.service and forgeqe.kind . down and status look only at this project's containers.

Security ForgeQE's agent reads text other people control: tickets, web pages, repositories. A container command built from that text could mount the whole disk or run privileged, so: No commands from the model. The agent names services that forgeqe.yaml declares, and ForgeQE builds the argument array ( docker run … ). It never uses a shell. Images, flags and mounts never come from a request. The same restrictions for every container: --security-opt no-new-privileges , --pids-limit 1024 , ports on 127.0.0.1, and read-only mounts. There is no setting to turn these off. Mounts are checked like uploads (except a mock's stubs folder, which ForgeQE writes itself and mounts read-only). The path is resolved with realpath and must be inside the project. A mount that is or holds a hidden file or folder ( .env , .git , .npmrc ), a file named like a key ( *.pem , id_rsa , llms.json ) or a link is refused. A container can send what it reads anywhere. Environment: The docker and podman programs see only the system settings and the variables they need to find their daemon ( DOCKER_HOST , DOCKER_CONTEXT , CONTAINER_HOST , …), plus the service's listed secrets. A container gets only its env and secrets . Logs and errors have secret values replaced with *** . Not in the agents' shell: docker , podman , nerdctl , docker-compose and podman-compose are denied in the shell of ForgeQE's agent and of Scribe. So the only way to start a container is these tools. Asked first: services up and mock_service ask the user before starting, as run_tests does.

Operations Scheduled monitoring with alerts Runs checks on a schedule and alerts Teams or email when one keeps failing, and again when it recovers. Ask it Check the login flow every 15 minutes and alert Teams What it needs Required A live model profile in llms.json (an API key or Microsoft Entra ID sign-in) Optional Alert channels: monitor.alerts.teams or monitor.alerts.email in forgeqe.yaml Tools monitor In detail

Monitoring forgeqe monitor runs a set of checks on a schedule and alerts Microsoft Teams and email when one breaks. A check is any test case forgeqe suite takes (section 7): a YAML or Gherkin file, a folder, Jira keys or JQL, an Azure DevOps plan, TestRail, and so on. yaml Copy monitor: checks: [checks/smoke.yaml] every: 15m # 30s, 15m, 1h, 1h30m; at least 10s replay: verify # verify | trust | off parallel: 1 fail_after: 1 # failing rounds in a row before the first alert remind_every: 2h # repeat while it keeps failing; default: never keep: 100 # round folders kept write_back: false # post each round's results to the source system # out_dir: ./.forgeqe/reports/monitor # report_url: https://reports.example.com/monitor alerts: teams: webhook_env: TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL email: host: smtp.office365.com # or SMTP_HOST port: 587 # STARTTLS; 465 is TLS from the start (secure: true) username_env: SMTP_USERNAME password_env: SMTP_PASSWORD # from: ForgeQE <qa-bot@example.com> to: [qa-team@example.com, oncall@example.com] bash Copy forgeqe monitor --test-alerts # send a sample alert through every channel forgeqe monitor # monitor.checks every monitor.every, until Ctrl+C forgeqe monitor checks/checkout.yaml --every 5m forgeqe monitor --once # one round, then exit (cron, scheduled pipelines) Each round runs the checks like a suite, without writing tests, and replays the flows from page memory (section 5). A flow that passed before costs one model call to confirm the expected results ( replay: verify ), or none ( replay: trust , which trusts the replay without checking). A new or changed flow falls back to the full agent. Rounds start every apart; a round that overruns is followed by the next one straight away. Alerts go out when something changes, not every round: A check that fails fail_after rounds in a row gets an alert. With fail_after: 2 a single flaky failure is never reported. While it keeps failing, nothing more is sent, unless remind_every is set. When it passes again, a recovery alert says how long it was down. A round that cannot run at all (a test system is down, a source is empty, the engine will not start) alerts as the check "ForgeQE monitor", and the other checks keep their state. All changes in one round go out as one message. Teams gets an Adaptive Card with each check, why it failed and at which step, a link to the test case, and an "Open report" button. Email gets the same as text and HTML, with the failing checks' last screenshots attached (up to five). For Teams, create an incoming webhook on the channel, or a Workflows flow with the trigger "When a Teams webhook request is received" and the action "Post card in a chat or channel"; both take the card as it is. Put the URL in TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL . For email, any SMTP server works: Office 365 ( smtp.office365.com:587 , with SMTP AUTH allowed for the mailbox), Gmail with an app password, SendGrid, or a relay on your network (no username needed). The webhook URL and the SMTP password stay in the environment; if a send fails, the error never contains them. The terminal shows one block per round: text Copy Monitoring checks/smoke.yaml every 15m · replay verify · alerts: Teams, email to qa-team@example.com · Ctrl+C stops [14:15] ✗ 4/5 passing · 38s · 6.2K tokens ✗ SHOP-12 Checkout: failing since 14:15 The Pay button is missing on the payment page ↑ Alert sent: Teams, email Report .forgeqe/reports/monitor/20260929-141500/report.html Next round at 14:30 [14:30] ✗ 4/5 passing · 35s · 5.9K tokens ✗ SHOP-12 Checkout: failing since 14:15 (2 rounds, already alerted) Report .forgeqe/reports/monitor/20260929-143000/report.html Next round at 14:45 Files. Each round is a suite folder in .forgeqe/reports/monitor/<time>/ ( report.html , junit.xml , suite.json , the runs, and alerts.json when it alerted), so the report's trends and flaky tests cover the rounds. Folders beyond keep are deleted. state.json in .forgeqe/reports/monitor/ remembers which checks are failing, since when, and when they were last alerted; delete it to start fresh. Set report_url to where you publish .forgeqe/reports/monitor/ and alerts link <report_url>/<round>/report.html ; without it they name the local file. Scheduling. Run forgeqe monitor in a long-lived session (tmux, a service, a container), or forgeqe monitor --once from cron or a scheduled pipeline. --once exits 0 when every check passed, 1 when any failed, and 2 when stopped. In a pipeline, cache .forgeqe/reports/monitor/state.json between runs; without it every run starts fresh, and a failure alerts every time. Only one monitor can use an out_dir at a time, so an overlapping cron run exits instead of racing. You can also ask ForgeQE's agent. In the shell, "check the smoke cases once" runs one round and shows it as a card, and "monitor the smoke cases every 10 minutes" starts a monitor in the background: you keep working, each round appears as a card, "is anything failing?" shows the state, and "stop monitoring" ends it. A background monitor lives as long as the shell (or forgeqe mcp ) and stops when it closes; forgeqe run refuses to start one, because it would stop when the command exits. While one is running, a one-off round on the same out_dir is refused rather than run twice. For monitoring that keeps going after you close the shell, "monitor the smoke cases every 10 minutes and alert the QA channel in Teams, always on" makes the agent set up monitor: in forgeqe.yaml , send a test alert, and tell you how to keep forgeqe monitor running (or add a scheduled pipeline).

Operations Background jobs on a schedule Runs ForgeQE commands (suites, monitor rounds, regression packs, healing, pull-request tests, browser goals) on a schedule or once in the jobs service, apart from the conversation and after it closes, and watches an existing GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps pipeline (read-only). A failed pipeline run or pack run is investigated: the healing agent works on each failure on a local branch of its own (a fix for review, or an app bug), never pushing. Says how each job goes when asked, shows runs as they end, and sends failures, recoveries and findings to Teams or email. Ask it Run the release-2.3 pack every weekday at 2am in the background Watch the pipeline in the background and investigate failures How are my jobs doing? What it needs Optional A notification channel: notify.channels in forgeqe.yaml, each a Teams Workflows webhook (in an environment variable) or email Tools jobs In detail

t: The jobs service: scheduled and long jobs apart from the shell
x: The jobs service: scheduled and long jobs apart from the shell forgeqe jobs runs ForgeQE commands on a schedule, or once, in a service of their own, so they keep going while you work on something else in the shell, or with the shell closed. Each run is its own forgeqe process with its own output and session log; you ask how a job is going at any time, and its failures and recoveries go to Teams. bash Copy forgeqe jobs add nightly-pack --cron "0 2 * * 1-5" -- pack run release-2.3 # weekdays at 02:00, this machine's time forgeqe jobs add smoke --every 30m -- suite checks/smoke.yaml forgeqe jobs add heal-login --now -- heal --focus login # once, now forgeqe jobs # every job: running or how its last run ended, and when it runs next forgeqe jobs status nightly-pack # its last runs, and the last lines of the latest forgeqe jobs logs nightly-pack --tail 100 forgeqe jobs run nightly-pack # run it now as well forgeqe jobs stop nightly-pack # stop the run that is going forgeqe jobs disable|enable|remove nightly-pack forgeqe jobs shutdown # stop the service; scheduled jobs wait until it starts again What a job runs. One ForgeQE command: suite , monitor , run , heal , pr-tests , pack run , pack triage or pipeline watch , with its arguments after -- . Nobody is there to answer a question while a job runs, so a run job is a browser run of the goal ( --direct ), and a pack run job carries --yes : adding the job is your approval, and the command you agree to shows it. It runs with the project's own forgeqe.yaml , model profile and approvals: a job cannot set --config , --profile or --yes , and nothing else is started (no shell, no other program). A monitor job runs one round each time it is due ( --once ), on the job's schedule; it sends its own monitor.alerts , so its job is quiet unless you add it with notices on. When. --every 15m (at least 1m), --cron "0 2 * * 1-5" (minute hour day month weekday, local time), or neither: it runs when asked, and add starts it at once. --now also runs a scheduled job straight away. A run missed while the service was down starts once when it is back. When several are due, the one that has waited longest goes first. How many. jobs.parallel in forgeqe.yaml (default 2) runs at once over all jobs, and never two runs of one job. A run past --timeout (default 6h, at most 24h) is stopped and marked timed out. The service. forgeqe jobs add and forgeqe jobs run start it when it is not running, as a process of its own that outlives the command and the shell; forgeqe jobs serve runs it in the foreground (for a container or a system service). It is one per project, on this machine, until you stop it or the machine restarts. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, with a random token kept in your own ForgeQE folder ( ~/.forgeqe/jobs/ , readable by your user only, never in the project, which others may read), and refuses requests from web pages. A second service for the same project is refused. .forgeqe/jobs/ and .forgeqe/pipelines/ get their own .gitignore , so runs and logs are never committed. Files. .forgeqe/jobs/<job>/job.json and, for each of its last 50 runs, runs/<run>/run.json and output.log ; .forgeqe/jobs/events.jsonl lists what happened; .forgeqe/jobs/service.log is the service's own output. A run that was going when the service stopped is marked interrupted. Watching a CI pipeline. forgeqe jobs add ci --every 10m -- pipeline watch --github org/app --workflow ci.yml --branch main (or --ado-project Shop --pipeline 12 ) looks at the pipeline's latest completed run each time, read-only: it starts, re-runs and changes nothing. A new failed run is triaged like a pack's (the JUnit or TRX files in its artifacts on GitHub, the Test Runs API on Azure DevOps; without results, the job and step that failed), in .forgeqe/reports/pipelines/ . The job fails while the latest run is failed, so the team hears once when the pipeline breaks and once when it is green again; a cancelled run changes nothing. forgeqe pipeline watch … on its own does one look. GitHub needs the gh CLI signed in; Azure DevOps the same sign-in as the rest of ForgeQE. Investigating failures. When a pipeline watch or pack run job fails, the failures that healing can decide (an element not found, an expected value that does not hold; not the environment, flaky tests or broken test code, and nothing while the environment is down) are investigated, at most 3 a run, jobs.parallel at once. Each goes to the healing agent in a git worktree of its own, on a new local branch forgeqe/investigate/<test>-<time>-<n> , from the commit the failing run tested when this clone has it (fetched when it can be, else HEAD , which the finding says). The agent re-runs the flow in the browser: when the flow works it heals the test, and the fix is committed on that branch for you to review; when the browser fails at the same step it is an app bug, and no branch is kept. Your checkout, its branch and its files are never touched; nothing is pushed or merged; the worktree is removed at the end. node_modules , .venv and venv from your checkout are linked into the worktree so the tests can run, and never committed. The failure is told at once ( job_failed ), the findings when they are in ( job_investigated ); forgeqe jobs status lists them, .forgeqe/jobs/<job>/runs/<run>/investigations.json and investigate.log have the detail, and forgeqe investigate <run folder> runs an investigation by hand. --no-investigate turns it off for a job. From the shell. Ask ForgeQE's agent: "run the release-2.3 pack every weekday at 2am in the background" makes it propose the job, and ForgeQE asks you to agree to its exact command and schedule before adding it ( Add the job / Don't add it ). You keep working; when a job's run ends, a line says so in the conversation ("Job nightly-pack failed: …"), and "how are my jobs?" or "show the end of the nightly-pack log" get answers from the service. The agent adds a job only when you ask for one, and never one that runs anything but the

Operations Teams and email notifications Tells the team in Microsoft Teams channels or by email when a suite fails or passes, when a release readiness verdict is in, and when the domain evaluation falls below its gate, with the failing cases, their bugs, and links to the report and the CI build. Each channel picks its events; the agent also posts a summary to a channel when asked. Ask it Post the results to the QA channel Tell the release channel the verdict is NO-GO What it needs Required A notification channel: notify.channels in forgeqe.yaml, each a Teams Workflows webhook (in an environment variable) or email Limits Automatic notifications come from runs nobody is watching (forgeqe suite, forgeqe run, pipelines, the MCP server), not from the interactive shell, where the agent posts only when asked. Tools notify In detail

Notifications ForgeQE tells the team in Microsoft Teams channels, or by email, when something they should know happens. Each channel picks its events: yaml Copy notify: report_url: https://reports.example.com/forgeqe # where .forgeqe/reports is published, so cards link to each report channels: qa: teams: { webhook_env: TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL } on: [suite_failed, eval_failed] release: teams: { webhook_env: TEAMS_RELEASE_WEBHOOK } on: [release] leads: email: { host: smtp.office365.com, port: 587, username_env: SMTP_USERNAME, password_env: SMTP_PASSWORD, to: [qa-leads@example.com] } on: [suite_failed, release] Event When The card shows suite_failed A suite ends with a case that did not pass, or a test that did not Each failing case (up to 10) with its kind of failure, the test case and bug links, tests written, and the report and build suite_passed Every case passed The count, how long it took, where it ran release A release readiness verdict GO, GO WITH RISKS, or NO-GO, the counts, every blocker and risk, and the wiki page when published eval_failed forgeqe eval domain --min falls below its gate Coverage for each variant and invented ids job_failed A job of the jobs service fails or runs out of time, after passing or for the first time (not again while it keeps failing) The job, its command and schedule, how long it ran, its last lines of output, and where its output is job_recovered A job passes again after failing The same, for the run that passed job_done A job that runs only when asked ends The same, whether it passed or failed job_investigated The investigation of a job's failed run is done Each failure: a test out of date with its fix on a branch, an app bug, or not decided, with the agent's reasons A channel without on gets suite_failed , release , eval_failed , job_failed , job_recovered , and job_investigated . Email adds the failure screenshots. A stopped suite is not announced. Monitoring keeps its own monitor.alerts , with the same cards. Events are sent from runs nobody is watching: forgeqe suite in a pipeline or on a schedule, forgeqe run , and the MCP server. In the shell, where people try things out, nothing is sent on its own; ask instead ("post the results to the QA channel", "tell the release channel the verdict"), and ForgeQE's agent posts a card with notify . Links: with report_url , cards open the report where the reports folder is published. In Azure Pipelines and GitHub Actions they also open the build, where the report is an artifact. Without either, the card names the report's path. Setting up a Teams channel: In the channel, open Workflows and choose Post to a channel when a webhook request is received , then copy the URL it gives you. Microsoft is retiring the older Office 365 "Incoming Webhook" connectors; Workflows webhooks take the same cards. The URL is the secret (anyone with it can post): keep it in the environment, the system's credential store ( forgeqe auth login TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL ), or a pipeline secret, never in forgeqe.yaml . Create the workflow with a shared or service account: a workflow belongs to whoever made it and stops when they leave. Your tenant must allow the Workflows app. forgeqe notify test [channel] sends a test card to check it arrives.

Ask it Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs tests/cases.yaml on every PR, and make it green What it needs Required git on PATH Required gh on PATH, for GitHub Actions; or az on PATH, for Azure Pipelines Tools push_branch set_ci_secret In detail

Pipelines ForgeQE's agent writes, runs, and fixes GitHub Actions and Azure Pipelines. Run it in the repo (or pass --repo ) and ask: bash Copy forgeqe run "Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the smoke cases in cases.yaml on every pull request" forgeqe run "Set up an Azure DevOps pipeline that runs test plan 12 every night and posts results back" forgeqe run "The ForgeQE workflow is failing, fix it" What it does: Works out the platform from the git remote (github.com, or dev.azure.com / visualstudio.com) and reads the repo's existing CI, so it can add a job to it or write a new file. Writes the pipeline so it installs Bun and uv, runs npm install -g @capagents/forgeqe and forgeqe setup , then forgeqe suite <source...> --no-code --plain --out <dir> , and publishes junit.xml and the report folder. On GitHub the suite adds a results table to the job summary. Validates it (actionlint when installed, otherwise by parsing the YAML) and commits it. Pushes to a new branch named forgeqe/ci-<topic> with ForgeQE's push_branch tool. That tool refuses the default branch, main , and master , and never forces; git push itself is blocked for the agent. Merging stays with you. Stores the keys the pipeline needs (the model's key from llms.json , and ADO_PAT , JIRA_EMAIL and JIRA_API_TOKEN , or XRAY_CLIENT_ID and XRAY_CLIENT_SECRET ) with ForgeQE's set_ci_secret tool. The agent only names the variable; ForgeQE passes the value from its own environment to gh secret set (on stdin) or az pipelines variable (through the environment), and never shows it. A variable that is not set in ForgeQE's environment is reported, not guessed. Triggers the run with gh workflow run or az pipelines run , watches it, reads the logs of failed steps, fixes the pipeline (or the code), pushes again, and repeats until the run passes or code.max_attempts runs have failed. It reports the run link and the result. It needs gh logged in for GitHub, or az with the azure-devops extension logged in for Azure DevOps. Without them it still writes, validates, and commits the pipeline, then tells you the commands to run. Set llm.active to a live profile in the committed forgeqe.yaml . With a github_copilot profile the pipeline needs a GitHub token for Copilot in COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN (see In pipelines ).

Ask the orders database Show me the tables in the shop database Write the SQL for revenue per country last month and run it Check the connection to the reporting database What it needs Required A database under databases: in forgeqe.yaml or env.yaml: a connection string in an environment variable (url_env), or host, database, user and password_env; auth: azure or aws_iam for token sign-in Limits One statement at a time: SELECT (with CTEs and set operations), SHOW, DESCRIBE and EXPLAIN SELECT anywhere; INSERT, and UPDATE or DELETE with a WHERE clause, only on databases marked writable and after you confirm Never DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE), procedures, or functions that read files, sleep or reach other servers MongoDB is queried with find, aggregate, count and distinct (JSON operations); its test data is not made yet; other non-SQL stores are not supported Tools databases database_schema run_sql In detail

Databases ForgeQE's agent can read your databases and answer questions from them in plain language: "which customers in India have paid orders?", "show me the tables in the shop database", "write the SQL for revenue per country and run it". It reads the schema first (through DB-GPT 's connectors), writes SQL in the database's own dialect, runs it, and shows you the rows and the SQL. Supported: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server and Azure SQL, Oracle, Snowflake, Redshift, CockroachDB, SQLite, DuckDB, and MongoDB. The first use sets up the data engine (its own Python, in ~/.forgeqe/data ) and that database's driver. MongoDB ( engine: mongodb , or url_env with a mongodb:// or mongodb+srv:// string): the agent lists the collections with the fields of a sample of documents, and queries with find, aggregate, count and distinct, written as JSON. Operators that run code on the server or write elsewhere ( $where , $function , $accumulator , $out , $merge ) and system.* collections are refused; inserts, updates and deletes need writable: true and your confirmation, and an update or delete needs a filter. MongoDB has no read-only session, so connect as a read-only user. Test data is made for the SQL databases only. Add the databases under databases: in forgeqe.yaml, or under an environment in env.yaml (the active environment's entries win by name). No secret goes in either file: name the environment variables that hold them. yaml Copy databases: orders: # a whole connection string in a variable: URI, JDBC, or ADO.NET as Azure shows it url_env: ORDERS_DB_URL description: Orders written by the checkout app reporting: # or the parts engine: postgres # postgres, mysql, mariadb, mssql, oracle, snowflake, redshift, cockroachdb, sqlite, duckdb host: reporting.postgres.database.azure.com database: reporting user: qa_reader auth: azure # a Microsoft Entra ID token (az login, managed identity, service principal) billing: engine: mysql host: billing.abc123.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com database: billing user: qa_iam auth: aws_iam # an RDS IAM token from your AWS profile; the region is read from the host fixtures: engine: postgres host: localhost port: 5432 database: test user: qa password_env: FIXTURES_DB_PASSWORD writable: true # allows confirmed INSERT, and UPDATE or DELETE with a WHERE clause Save a secret once with /auth ORDERS_DB_URL in the shell (or set it in the environment). In the shell, /db lists the databases, /db test <name> connects, /db tables <name> [words] shows the tables (or those whose names, comments or columns hold the words), /db refresh <name> reads the schema again, /db batches shows test data batches, and /db examples <name> the remembered queries. /db add sets one up with the agent: it asks how to connect, writes the entry, and has you save the secret with /auth , so no password goes through the chat. The same commands work outside the shell ( forgeqe db test orders ), and for scripts: bash Copy forgeqe db query orders "SELECT status, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY status" --json # one checked read forgeqe db query orders "SELECT ..." --dry-run # the database checks every name; no rows are read forgeqe db query orders "SELECT * FROM orders" --max-rows 1000 # rows to read (default 200, at most 5000) forgeqe db ask "paid revenue per country last month" --db orders --save queries/revenue.sql # the agent writes and validates it; stdout is only the SQL Drafts, files and examples. Ask for a query without running it ("write the SQL for ...") and the agent validates it with a dry run: the database resolves every table and column (and shows its plan where it can) without reading or writing anything. Ask it to keep a query and it saves a .sql file in the project with the question as a comment. When you confirm a result is right, the agent remembers the question and its SQL for that database ( .forgeqe/data/<name>/examples.jsonl ) and follows it for similar questions: your names for things and your filters. Other settings: schema (default: the user's), port , path (sqlite, duckdb), timeout_seconds (default 30), ssl ( verify , the default for Azure, AWS and GCP hosts; require ; disable ), ssl_ca (a CA file), region (aws_iam), sample_rows (0 to 5 sample rows per table shown to the model; default 0), mask (more column name patterns to hide), and options ( warehouse and role for Snowflake; odbc_driver for SQL Server with auth: azure , which needs Microsoft's ODBC Driver 18). What ForgeQE does with them: Reads run in a read-only session where the database has one (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQLite, DuckDB), with a statement timeout and a row cap (200 by default), and are rolled back. Use a read-only login all the same; SQL Server and Snowflake have no read-only session, so there the login is the limit. Every statement is checked first. One statement only: SELECT (with CTEs, joins and set operations), SHOW, DESCRIBE, or EXPLAIN of a SELECT. Refused: DDL, procedures, SELECT INTO, FOR UPDATE, MySQL's executable comments, and functions that read files, sleep, or reach other sessions or servers ( pg_read_file , LOAD_FILE , xp_cmdshell , OPENROWSET , UTL_HTTP , ...). Writes run only on a database marked writable: true , and only after you confirm the exact statement: one INSERT, or one UPDATE or DELETE with a WHERE clause. Masked values: columns named like passwords, tokens, hashes, card numbers, IBANs and tax ids show as ••• . What the model sees: table and column names, types, keys and comments, and the rows of the queries it runs. Passwords and tokens never reach it, its shell, or the tests. ForgeQE's agent cannot run database clients ( psql , mysql , sqlcmd , sqlplus , ...) in its shell. The schema is read once and kept in .forgeqe/data/<name>/catalog.json . ForgeQE checks a cheap fingerprint of the schema (its tables, columns and types) every few minutes and reads it again when a migration changed it, or after a week; /db refresh <name> reads it at once. For a large database the agent gets the table

Data Test data on demand Makes realistic test data from a spec that fits the database's schema (types, sizes, NOT NULL, unique keys, CHECK lists, enums), parents before children, the same rows for the same seed. Or takes a masked subset of a real database: the rows you pick and every row they need, with names, emails, phones, addresses and other personal columns replaced the same way every time. Shows a preview, writes CSV, JSON or SQL files for automation, or inserts the rows into a database marked writable after you confirm, as a batch that can be removed again. Specs live in the project, so tests and pipelines make the same data with forgeqe data gen. Ask it Generate test data: 20 customers with 1 to 3 orders each in the shop database Make test data for the orders tables as CSV files for our automation Insert 50 test users into the fixtures database Copy 100 paid orders from prod into fixtures as a masked subset Remove the test data batch we inserted yesterday What it needs Required A database under databases: in forgeqe.yaml or env.yaml: a connection string in an environment variable (url_env), or host, database, user and password_env; auth: azure or aws_iam for token sign-in Limits Inserts only into databases marked writable, after you confirm; removes only rows of a batch it inserted A subset reads its source in read-only sessions; its start condition is a filter of one table, and personal columns are found by name (mask: adds others) Simple CHECK constraints (a list of values, bounds) are read; other rules the database enforces may refuse rows, and then nothing is kept Tools generate_test_data test_data_batches In detail

Test data ForgeQE makes test data that fits your schema: ask "generate 20 customers with 1 to 3 orders each in the shop database", "make the orders tables as CSV for our automation", or "insert 50 test users into fixtures". The agent reads the schema, writes a spec, shows you a preview, and then writes files or inserts the rows. A spec is YAML you can keep in the project, so tests and pipelines make the same data again: yaml Copy database: fixtures # optional: else --db, or the only database seed: 42 # the same seed makes the same rows locale: en_IN # Faker's locale for names, addresses, phone numbers edge_cases: true # a few rows per table at the limits: longest text, unicode, nulls where allowed tables: customers: rows: 20 columns: email: {faker: email, unique: true} country: {one_of: [IN, UK, US], weights: [5, 3, 2]} orders: per: {customers: [1, 3]} # each customer gets 1 to 3 orders columns: status: {one_of: [NEW, PAID, SHIPPED]} total: {range: [5, 500], decimals: 2} placed_at: {date_between: ["-90d", "today"]} reference: {sequence: "ORD-{n:05d}"} order_items: per: {orders: [1, 4]} columns: product_id: {ref: products.id} # rows already in the database Rules: a plain value, faker (a Faker method, with args ), one_of (with weights ), range (with decimals ), date_between (dates, today , or -30d , -6m , +1y ), sequence ( {n} counts from 1), bothify ( # a digit, ? a letter), ref ( table.column ), null_ratio , and unique . Two rules keep a row consistent: {ref: products.price, via: product_id} takes the price of the very product the row points at, and {template: "{first_name}.{last_name}@shop.test"} builds a value from the row's other columns. Columns without a rule are filled from the schema: their type and size, NOT NULL, unique keys, a CHECK constraint's list of values or bounds, enum types, and their name ( email , phone , city , created_at , ...). Keys the database makes (serial, identity, auto-increment) are left to it, and foreign keys point at rows the spec makes or rows already in the database. A schema without declared foreign keys is matched by name ( orders.customer_id to customers ). From the command line, for automation and pipelines (no model): bash Copy forgeqe data gen test-data/shop.yaml # what it makes forgeqe data gen test-data/shop.yaml --format csv --out test-data/shop # csv, json or sql (INSERTs in the database's dialect) forgeqe data gen test-data/shop.yaml --insert --yes --json # into a writable database; prints the batch id forgeqe data batches --db fixtures forgeqe data clean 20261019-173810-9f5b5f --db fixtures --yes # removes exactly that batch, children first Inserts go only into a database marked writable: true , in one transaction: if the database refuses a row, none are kept. In the shell, ForgeQE asks first; on the command line, --yes is needed. Batches: every insert records the keys it made in .forgeqe/data/<database>/batches/ , so clean removes those rows and nothing else. Files are written inside the project only, never to a hidden folder. Test data in test cases and suites. A test case in a YAML or JSON case file can bring its own data: the rows go in before the case runs and come out after it (and after the test ForgeQE writes for it), and the case's text uses their values: yaml Copy - id: CHECKOUT-7 title: A returning customer pays by card data: test-data/checkout.yaml # or {spec: ..., database: fixtures, keep: true} steps: - action: Log in as {{data.customers.0.email}} - action: Open order {{data.orders.0.reference}} and pay it expected: The order page shows Paid for {{data.customers.0.name}} {{data.<table>.<row>.<column>}} takes a value of the rows as inserted, keys the database made included ( {{data.customers.email}} is row 0). A whole suite can have data too: forgeqe suite cases.yaml --data test-data/shop.yaml ( --data-db NAME , --keep-data to leave it for a look), or data_spec when the agent runs cases. The data goes only into a database marked writable ; these hooks do not ask first, because the team wrote them. In automation scripts. The tests ForgeQE runs, and the tests it writes, read the inserted rows from the JSON file FORGEQE_DATA_FILE names. In a pipeline, make that file with the same spec: bash Copy forgeqe data gen test-data/checkout.yaml --insert --yes --json --export test-data/.run/checkout.json > batch.json FORGEQE_DATA_FILE=test-data/.run/checkout.json npx playwright test forgeqe data clean "$(jq -r .batch batch.json)" --db fixtures --yes # in an always() step Scribe, ForgeQE's coding agent, writes tests that read their data from that file (its test-data skill), and can look at the databases and preview test data through ForgeQE's data tools; it never changes a database itself. A masked subset of real data. Instead of tables: , a spec can take real rows from another database: the rows you pick, every row they point at (and the rows those point at), and the child tables you name, with personal data replaced: yaml Copy database: fixtures # where the rows go (or --db); leave it out for files seed: 7 # the same seed masks the same way subset: from: prod_copy # a databases: entry, read in read-only sessions start: {table: orders, where: "status = 'PAID' AND created_at >= '2026-01-01'", limit: 100} children: [order_items, payments] mask: # more columns to mask: a Faker method, or null to empty them customers.notes: paragraph keep: [customers.country] # columns whose names look personal but are not Masked by name: names (in tables of people: customers, users, employees, contacts, ...), emails, phones, addresses, post codes, cities, birth dates, national and tax ids, card numbers, IBANs, IP addresses, and passwords, hashes and tokens. Keys are never masked. The same everywhere: a value always becomes the same fake value, in every table and every run, so joins on a masked column still match; a masked value in a unique column stays unique. The start condition is a filter of the start table only: one condition, no UNION, and only tables of t

Data Data flows between systems Checks the data that passes between your systems' databases (the digital channel, CRM, billing, a warehouse), by batch ETL or in real time: each hop's rows arrived, complete, with every mapped column right after its rule, on time for its SLA, without duplicates. Follows one record end to end, says what a change to a table or column reaches downstream, and writes the flows from your mapping documents wherever they are, or suggests them from the schemas. Ask it Check that customers from the digital database reach the CRM correctly Trace customer 42 from digital through CRM to billing What does a change to digital.customers.email affect downstream? Write the data flows from mapping.xlsx Reconcile yesterday's orders between the ERP and the warehouse What it needs Required A database under databases: in forgeqe.yaml or env.yaml: a connection string in an environment variable (url_env), or host, database, user and password_env; auth: azure or aws_iam for token sign-in Limits Hops between SQL tables, Kafka topics, and APIs (a target by key, a source by its list; GET or POST only); MongoDB is not checked At most 200,000 source rows a flow per check, compared by key Reads only; flows are written into flows.yaml, and nothing in the databases changes Tools data_flows check_flows trace_record read_mapping_file In detail

Data flows When your systems pass data to each other (a customer signs up in the digital channel's database, the CRM gets a contact, billing gets an account), ForgeQE checks each hop: ask "check that customers reach the CRM correctly", "trace customer 42 from digital to billing", or "what does a change to digital.customers.email affect downstream?". The hops are in flows.yaml , beside forgeqe.yaml. ForgeQE writes it from your mapping documents, wherever they are (a spreadsheet in the project, a Confluence page, a Jira or Azure DevOps item, a text file), or suggests flows from the schemas and a sample of keys when there are none; it shows you each flow and saves the ones you confirm. You can write it by hand too: yaml Copy flows: signup_to_crm: from: {db: digital, table: customers, key: id, changed: updated_at} to: {db: crm, table: contacts, key: source_customer_id} # the target column that holds the source key mode: realtime # it moves as it changes (API, queue, CDC) sla: 15m # a source row changed longer ago than this must have arrived extra: true # also report target rows with no source row columns: email: {to: email_address, rule: lower} full_name: {to: full_name, template: "{first_name} {last_name}"} country: {to: country_code, map: {India: IN, United Kingdom: GB}} orders_to_crm: from: {db: digital, table: orders, key: id} to: {db: crm, table: crm_orders, key: source_order_id} mode: batch # an ETL job copies it ready: {sql: "SELECT MAX(finished_at) FROM etl_runs WHERE job = 'orders'", wait: 10m} # wait for a run to finish since: 7d # only rows changed in the last week (needs from.changed) columns: total: {to: amount, rule: "round(2)"} status: {to: status_code, map: {PAID: P, NEW: N}} Rules: same (the default), lower , upper , trim , round(n) (half up, as databases round), date , number , string , map , template (from the source row's columns), and default (for a null). Kafka and APIs. A hop's side can also be a Kafka topic or an API: yaml Copy databases: events: engine: kafka host: broker1:9092,broker2:9092 user: qa-reader # SASL; leave out for a broker without sign-in password_env: KAFKA_PASSWORD options: {security_protocol: SASL_SSL, sasl_mechanism: SCRAM-SHA-512} yaml Copy flows: signup_events: from: {db: digital, table: customers, key: id, changed: updated_at} to: {db: events, topic: customer-created, key: customerId} # a field of the message; $key for the message key mode: realtime sla: 5m columns: email: {to: email, rule: lower} country: {to: address.country, map: {India: IN}} # nested fields by their dotted names contacts_api: from: {db: crm, table: contacts, key: contact_id} to: {api: crm_api, path: "/contacts/{key}", key: id} # an API app of the environment (kind: api) columns: email_address: email web_signups: from: {api: web_api, path: "/signups?status=new", key: id, items: data.items, next: links.next, changed: createdAt} to: {db: crm, table: contacts, key: contact_id} columns: email: email_address contacts_graphql: from: {db: digital, table: customers, key: id} to: api: crm_api path: /graphql method: POST # a lookup or a search: GET or POST only body: {query: "query($id: ID!) { contact(id: $id) { id email } }", variables: {id: "{key}"}} items: data.contact key: id columns: email: email Topics are read without a consumer group, so no offset is committed and no other consumer is affected; a read stops at the end of the topic as it was when the check began. A topic can be a source (its message time is when a record changed) or a target. /db test events checks the brokers, and /db tables events lists the topics with the fields of their latest messages. APIs are called at the base URL of the environment's API app, with the headers api.headers gives in forgeqe.yaml ( Authorization: Bearer ${CRM_API_TOKEN} ). As a target , an API answers for one key: {key} goes in its path ( /contacts/{key} ) or its body, one call a key; a 404 counts as missing; at most 500 keys a check, so narrow a large source with since: . As a source , it is a list endpoint (no {key} ), read page by page through the response's next link; changed names the field that says when a record changed, for since: and SLAs. A record can be followed ( flows trace , trace: ) from an API list too. items says where the records are in a response ( data.items ); without it, ForgeQE takes the response itself, or its first list among items , data , results , value , records and content . Calls are GET or POST (a lookup, a search, a GraphQL query): a check never changes data, so PUT, PATCH and DELETE are refused. Redirects are not followed, and a next link that leaves the API's host is refused, so the headers never reach another server. What a check reports for each flow: Missing: source rows whose key is not in the target. For a realtime flow, a row is late once its change is older than the SLA, and still in flight before that (not a failure). Wrong: rows where a mapped column does not hold the expected value, with the key, the source value, the value expected after the rule, and the value found. Numbers compare as numbers (12.5 and 12.50), date-times to the second, and trailing spaces of fixed-width text do not count. Duplicated: target keys that appear more than once; with extra: true , target rows with no source row. Batch: with ready , the check waits for a run of the job that finished after it began (up to wait ), and says so when it had to check the last run's rows. Following what a test case created. A case in a case file can follow the record its steps made through the flows; the case passes only when the record arrived, right, at every hop: yaml Copy - id: SIGNUP-3 title: A new customer reaches the CRM and billing steps: - action: Sign up with the email qa+{{unique}}@shop.test expected: The welcome page shows trace: from: digital.customers # or flows: [signup_to_crm, crm_to_billing] where: {email: "qa+{{unique}}@shop.test"} wait: 120 # seconds each hop may take {{unique}} is a token made for each run of the case, so

Tests After a run passes, Scribe , ForgeQE's coding agent, turns it into a test in your repo. In the shell and forgeqe run , every passed run then becomes a test, and so does each test case that passes when you ask the shell to run test cases: in the current folder, or in the repo you give per run or in forgeqe.yaml . --no-code turns it off; you can still ask for a test ("write a Playwright test for that run"). bash Copy forgeqe run "Log in and open the invoices page on staging.app.test" --repo ../app yaml Copy code: repo: ../app # relative to forgeqe.yaml max_attempts: 5 # test runs before giving up test_timeout_seconds: 600 # per test run stall_after: 5 # stop the agent's turn when one command it runs has failed this many times replay: true # before the agent starts, run the steps as a Playwright script and hand over what worked live_browser: true # once a step fails, the agent looks at that page in a Playwright browser graph: true # the code graph: find page objects without reading files, and reuse what already locates an element # model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 # runtime: /path/to/agent-runtime # default: the runtime ForgeQE downloads What happens after the run passes: ForgeQE writes handoff.md into the run directory: the goal and result, how ForgeQE's browser was set up (browser and version, headless or headed, user agent, navigator.webdriver , launch switches, extra headers, language, time zone, viewport), every step in order with the value typed (secrets as process.env.NAME ) and the JavaScript the browser agent ran, the browser agent's own note before each group of steps (what it saw and why it acted, so a sign-in pop-up it closed or steps it redid after a banner covered the page read as such), each element's best locator and the others with their confidence %, and a short table of each visited page's other elements for assertions (weak locators under 30% are left out, and elements the steps already use are listed with the steps, so the handoff stays small; the full lists are in the page-memory files it points to). The agent's result and the final URL are marked as coming from one run on live data, to be checked as rules (the results load, the order holds, the fields have the right format), not copied as expected values. Pop-ups and banners the run met are handled wherever they appear (Playwright's locator handlers or the repository's helper), since the next run can show them at another moment or not at all; the agent's retries are not copied. A site can also serve different versions of a page to different visits (A/B tests, such as a classic search box or a free-text one), so the test handles every version the run or the agent saw, or waits for one control from either version. The handoff also lists the browser agent's checks : before it finishes, the browser agent records each result the goal asks to verify with the exact text the page showed ( record_check ; a text the page does not show is refused). They are saved in workflow.yaml under checks: . The test asserts these and nothing else. ForgeQE replays the run's steps as a Playwright script ( <run>/replay/flow.mjs ), in the run's browser setup (channel, headless or headed, user agent, language, time zone, viewport), with 10 seconds per step. Text is typed key by key, as the browser agent typed it, so search suggestions and other typing handlers fire. If the replay does not reach the run's final page, it runs again without Playwright's automation switches ( navigator.webdriver false, as in ForgeQE's browser). The handoff gets the result: which steps worked, and for each failed step, Playwright's reason (for example a dialog that intercepts the click), the page, the dialogs open on it, how many elements each of the element's other locators matched, and a screenshot and page snapshot. It also saves Playwright's page snapshot of each page the replay visited (roles, accessible names, and text, as the replay left the page; the last page once it stops changing), so Scribe takes locators for its steps and assertions from real pages instead of guessing them. On the last page it looks up each of the browser agent's checks and puts the Playwright locator that matched its text into the handoff (a heading or text match, the container it sits in when there are several, or the form field that holds it), so assertions come with a locator that worked. For a heading it also gives the part of the page the heading names (an element labelled by it, the section it heads, or the element right after it), with its locator and how many links and list items it holds, so a check such as "an In the news section with at least one item" is asserted inside that part, not on the heading alone. A step that fails while every step after it still works and the replay reaches the final page (a click that did nothing on the run, or a control this version of the page doesn't have) doesn't count as a failed replay: Scribe decides from the step whether the goal needs it and ports the rest as it is. When only the second launch got through, the handoff says the browser setup is the difference and which launch settings fix it. The first time, Playwright (about 13 MB) is downloaded into ~/.forgeqe/tools ; it drives the installed Chrome. A run that only opened a page still replays when it recorded checks, to look them up; with neither it skips this, and replay: false turns it off. Scribe first reads the repo (as a read-only agent: it cannot change files or use the live browser yet), while the replay runs when there is one, so the two overlap. What it learns (the framework, the command that runs one test, where page objects and config live, the conventions) is saved with page memory in scribe-notes.json , with the tests each job writes there. The next job in the same repo starts from those notes and that list instead of reading the repo again, and extends those tests' page objects when its flow overlaps; notes older than 30 days are read again.
