How Scribe writes a test Reuse before rebuild, extend before duplicate. Before Scribe writes anything, write_test measures what the repository's tests already cover of the run, from evidence rather than guesswork: each step and check the browser agent made on an element is matched, through page memory, to the page-object member that locates it, and the code graph says which tests reach that member (through the page methods they call, or a property they assert, such as Expect(practicePage.AjaxStatus) ). Steps on elements no page object locates yet are listed as not measured, since a test may do them its own way. Then: What it finds What happens One test covers every measured step and check Reuse : Scribe only finds the command that runs it, and changes nothing. If it fails, nothing is changed: you are asked whether to update it or write a new test. One test covers most (40% or more) Extend : Scribe adds only the missing steps and checks to that test, keeping every step and assertion it has; the reviewer rejects a removed or weakened assertion, or the steps copied into a new file Two or more tests cover most of it You choose : the evidence and the options (reuse, extend with how many steps it adds, a new test, cancel) Nothing covers much New : a new test, reusing the page objects and helpers as before A card says which it did and why ( Extending PracticeTests.Flow · covers 12 of 15; only 3 are missing ). Say how when you know ("extend the login test", "write a separate test", "update it") and ForgeQE's agent passes that on without asking. In every mode Scribe adds page-object members rather than changing what an existing member does for the other tests that use it. The same flow asked again. When a session writes tests and you ask for a flow an earlier job already wrote a test for, ForgeQE runs that test first, before any browser run. If it passes in a real browser, that is the answer: no browser run, no Scribe, and no new test file, in the seconds the test takes ( ✓ Existing test passed · 19s · no browser run or new test needed ). If it fails, the flow runs in the browser and Scribe updates that test instead of writing another. ForgeQE's agent rewords a goal a little each time, so goals count as the same flow when they share their content words (endings, case, and phrasing aside) and the new goal keeps everything the earlier one checked; the same steps with a different final check, a shorter flow, or another site are a new flow. The agent also compares the earlier goal with your request and runs fresh when you ask for a check the earlier test does not have. Ask for "a fresh run" or "a new test" to skip the reuse. When the flow cannot be reproduced. If ForgeQE's own replay of the run could not reach the run's final page and Scribe's first test fails too, the job stops there and says which replayed step failed and why, instead of spending its remaining attempts on a flow no script can repeat as recorded. Why a test failed. When ForgeQE's run of Scribe's test fails, the ✗ line and the next attempt say why in the test's own words: dotnet test's Error Message, pytest's E lines, or the error with its Expected and Received values (Playwright, Jest, JUnit), not the runner's summary line. Keeping Scribe's cost down. ForgeQE reads the repository's test setup itself before Scribe starts (stack, settings files and their browser values, the test id attribute, base classes, page objects and their methods, one test command) and hands it over, so Scribe does not discover it with dozens of file reads. Each attempt after the first starts a fresh session from a summary of the job (handoff, files changed, what each attempt did, the latest failure), so later attempts cost about what the first did. code.max_attempts (default 3) and code.max_tokens (default 1,500,000; 0 turns it off) cap a job, and the token budget is checked during an attempt too, so one long attempt is stopped when the total passes it. The reviewer sorts its issues into correctness (the test does not test what the goal says, or not reliably) and coding standards (test data or credentials in a page object, naming, hard waits, leftovers). Coding standards never fail a test that works: it is accepted, and the coding agent gets one more round (not counted in max_attempts ) to fix them; if that round breaks the test, ForgeQE puts back the version that passed and lists the standards issues in the notes ( code.tidy: false skips the round). A test the reviewer rejects twice for correctness stops the job with its issues, since that usually means the test case and the page disagree. Under each step, the handoff shows that step's part of the page (its section and neighbours, from the replay's page snapshot) instead of whole snapshots. When a test fails, ForgeQE shows the failing element on the test's page at the failure and on the replay's page, so most failures are fixed without opening a browser. Scribe's live browser is switched on only when the same failure repeats, and it does not send a page snapshot after every click or keystroke. code.max_steps (default 50) caps the tool calls in one of Scribe's turns. code.review_profile runs the reviewer on a cheaper llms.json profile. Scribe's rulebook: the same mistake once. When a job passes after a failed test run or a reviewer's change, Scribe's report gives up to three one-line rules that would have avoided the mistake ("Wait for the cart badge with toHaveText before clicking Checkout; it updates after a request"). ForgeQE keeps them in .forgeqe/scribe-rules.json in the repository, and every attempt of later jobs, and every healing session, starts with them. A lesson from a job that did not pass, or that passed at once, is not kept: only a fix that worked becomes a rule. The book stays small, since it is sent with each model call: at most 15 rules of one line each; a lesson learned again is merged into its rule (shown as "learned 3 times") instead of added; when it is full, the rule confirmed least and l

If it passes, there is nothing to heal and no model is called. Scribe starts in the repo as a healing agent, with the failing output. For each failing test it reads the test and the page objects it uses, then re-runs the test's flow in the real browser with ForgeQE's browser_run (the goal in plain words, not the old selectors). If the browser run passes, the test is out of date. The agent reads that run's steps and locators with run_details , updates the test (in the page object when the locators live there), and runs it with run_test . If the browser run fails at the step where the test fails, the app is broken there. The test is left as it is and the failure is reported as an app bug. It never deletes or skips a test, loosens an assertion, or raises a timeout to make a test pass. ForgeQE runs each healed test's own command, then the whole command. A healed test that still fails goes back to the agent with the output, and so does any other failure left in the whole run, until everything passes or code.max_attempts rounds are used. text Copy ▸ ForgeQE runs the tests: npx playwright test ✗ Tests failed, exit 1 (41s) ▸ Scribe (azure/gpt-5.4) is healing the failing tests in app ⚙ read tests/pages/LoginPage.ts ▸ Browser: Sign in to staging.app.test and open the invoices page ✓ Task complete · 9 steps ⚙ edit tests/pages/LoginPage.ts ▸ ForgeQE runs: npx playwright test tests/login.spec.ts ✓ login › signs in passed in 6s ▸ ForgeQE runs the tests: npx playwright test ✗ Tests still fail, exit 1 (39s) ┃ ┃ ✗ Tests still failing 2/5 attempts · 2m 40s · 61.2K tokens · azure/gpt-5.4 ┃ ┃ ✓ login › signs in healed ┃ The Sign in button is now "Log in"; LoginPage uses the new label ┃ ! invoices › totals app bug ┃ The total column is empty; the browser run failed at the same step ┃ ┃ 1 failure is in the app, not the tests; the tests were left as they are. ┃ Command npx playwright test (exit 1 after 39s) ┃ Changed tests/pages/LoginPage.ts ┃ Report .forgeqe/reports/heal/20260929-101500/heal.md The report is heal.md and heal.json in .forgeqe/reports/heal/<time>/ : each test's verdict and reason, the files changed, the browser runs (their folders sit next to the report), and the test output before and after. Ask in your own words: text Copy Build a regression pack for sprint 12 and run it on TestMu Which tests should we run for the PRs merged this week? Any mix of: an Azure DevOps sprint, area, epic or feature, or work item ids: their stories and bugs, the test cases each is tested by, and the files their linked pull requests changed; the commits between two refs of a repository ( from and to ): the product's repository, or the test repository's own; work items the commit messages name ( AB#123 , #123 , PAY-12 ) are read too; pull requests by number or URL, or the ones merged in the last N days (Azure DevOps or GitHub); anything ForgeQE's agent can read through its connected tools (a Jira release, GitHub issues, a Confluence release note): it reads the items and passes them in with their text and links. Why each test is in. A test can be in for more than one reason, and the card and <name>.md say each one: Reason Meaning linked it automates a test case that tests a changed work item ( .forgeqe/test-cases.json , or a case id in the test's attributes) test code changed the change is in the test repository, in code the test uses matches a change the work item's or pull request's words name what the test does: the elements it uses, its page, its name risk area the release touches an area with defects or failures before, and the test works there smoke the test is tagged smoke, so it is in every pack Gaps. ForgeQE asks before it runs anything. Flaky tests Every run_tests and pr-tests run keeps each test's result in .forgeqe/test-history.json in the repository (commit it to share the history, or keep it between CI runs as a cache). A test that fails runs once more in the same run, with the framework's own option (Playwright --last-failed , pytest --lf , Jest --onlyFailures ; otherwise the whole command again when the selection is small): when it then passes it is flaky , not failed, and the run does not fail because of it. "Which tests are flaky?" ( flaky_tests ) reads the history: each test's last results ( ✓✗✓↻✓ , where ↻ means it passed only when run again), its pass rate, a flakiness score (passes on retry plus pairs of flip-flops in the last 20 runs), and the likely cause from its failure messages, with an example: Cause From messages like Timing timeouts, waiting for an element, detached or stale elements An overlay another element intercepts the click, the element is covered or not visible Data expected one value, received another Network net::ERR_… , resets, 5xx responses Environment the browser closed or crashed, the server was not ready A test that only fails is broken, not flaky. Quarantine keeps a flaky test running, so its history goes on, but its failures stop failing the run and CI ( pr-tests --run exits 0 when only quarantined tests fail); no test code changes. A quarantined test that passes 5 runs in a row is offered for release. The agent offers quarantine_tests (it asks you first) and heal_tests to fix the cause. yaml Copy flaky: retries: 1 # runs of a failed test in the same run (0 to 3) quarantine: suggest # suggest (the agent asks), auto (ForgeQE quarantines), or off (history only) flaky_after: 2 # flakiness score from which a test counts as flaky

13 API Contracts and end-to-end scenarios, without a browser

API API and contract testing Builds API contracts (status, schema, key fields) from the calls a browser run saw or from an API description (OpenAPI, Swagger, WSDL, GraphQL, .proto, gRPC reflection), and end-to-end API scenarios from runs, descriptions, test cases, or plain English. Runs them straight against the API without a browser, or writes them as tests in the repository. REST, GraphQL, SOAP, and gRPC. Ask it Turn the last run's API calls into tests Test the API in openapi.yaml Write API scenario tests for the order lifecycle What it needs Optional The coding agent, Scribe: a live model profile (or code.model) and the agent runtime, which forgeqe setup installs Limits Functional API testing, not load or stress testing. Tools api_contracts run_api_contracts api_scenarios run_api_scenarios write_api_tests In detail

API and contract tests ForgeQE tests APIs directly too: REST, GraphQL, SOAP, and gRPC. API tests check the same logic as UI tests in a fraction of the time, and they do not break when the page changes. Contracts come from two places: A browser run. Every browser run records the application's own API calls (XHR, fetch, event streams) in network.json in the run folder: method, URL, status, timing, and the request and response bodies when they are JSON, XML, or text. Secrets never reach the file: Authorization , cookies, and API key headers are dropped (only the kind of auth is kept, e.g. bearer), and fields named like a password, token, key, session, or card number are redacted in bodies and query strings. Analytics and monitoring calls are left out. "Turn the last run's API calls into tests" ( api_contracts from run ) groups the calls into operations: one per method and path, with ids in paths turned into {id} ( GET /api/orders/{id} ), GraphQL by operation name, SOAP by action, gRPC-web by method. Several calls to one operation make a better contract: a field in every answer is required, a value that differs between calls is not pinned. No model is used. An API description, by link or file: OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2 (JSON or YAML, or the Swagger UI page, which ForgeQE looks behind for the document), WSDL for SOAP, a GraphQL endpoint (read by introspection) or an SDL or introspection file, .proto files, or grpc://host:port for a gRPC server with reflection (through grpcurl ). Each operation gets an example call from the description's examples; values it gives no example for are made up and the contract is marked as needing real values. Each contract has one example call and what its answer must have: the status , the content type , the body's schema , and key fields (ids, statuses, names, totals: present, with their type; a value only where it does not change between calls, like a status). GraphQL answers must have no errors ; SOAP answers no Fault and the expected elements; gRPC calls the OK status. Contract sets are saved in .forgeqe/reports/api/<id>/ : contracts.json (edit the examples freely, e.g. to give real ids) and api.md . Then: Run them now ( run_api_contracts , or forgeqe api run ): ForgeQE makes each call and checks the answer, without a browser or a model. Calls that change data (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, mutations, SOAP and gRPC calls not named like reads) are left out unless you allow them, on a test environment; the agent asks first. Calls with made-up values are skipped until you give real ones. Results go to results.json and junit.xml , with report.html (each contract a case, its checks the steps, with what the API answered) and suite.json beside them; a 401 or 403 says which header the call needs. Write them as tests ( write_api_tests , or forgeqe api tests ): Scribe writes them in the repository's own framework and HTTP client (Playwright's request fixture, pytest with requests, REST Assured, RestSharp or HttpClient, supertest...) with the base URL from configuration and credentials from environment variables, and ForgeQE runs them until they pass. Credentials for API calls go in forgeqe.yaml , as references to environment variables; the values are sent, never stored or shown to a model: yaml Copy api: capture: true # record the application's API calls in every browser run (default) base_url: https://staging.shop.example # where contracts run when not where they were recorded or described headers: Authorization: Bearer ${API_TOKEN} X-Tenant: ${API_TENANT} third_party: false # keep calls to other sites than the page's (sign-in providers, CDNs) timeout_seconds: 30 bash Copy forgeqe api contracts --spec https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.json forgeqe api contracts --run # the latest browser run's API calls forgeqe api run --base-url https://qa.shop.example # exit 1 when a contract fails: a CI gate forgeqe api tests --repo ../app # Scribe writes them as tests

End-to-end API scenarios A scenario is API calls in order, where later calls use values earlier answers gave: create a cart, add an item to {{cartId}} , place the order, read {{orderId}} . Each step has its own checks (status, schema, key fields). {{$unique}} is new on every run, for emails, usernames, and references that must not clash; {{$uuid}} , {{$now}} , and {{$randomInt}} are there too. Scenarios are saved in the contract set's contracts.json (edit them freely) and listed in api.md . There are four ways to make them ( api_scenarios ): From How Model A browser run ( --run ) The calls the application made, in order. A value an answer gave (an order id) that a later request sends, in its path, query, or body, becomes a variable: saved from that answer, used in that request. A GET made again (polling) is kept once. Emails and usernames sent to sign-up endpoints get {{$unique}} . The UI flow becomes the same flow at the API level. no An API description ( --spec , or a saved set) For each resource with an item path ( /pets and /pets/{petId} ): its lifecycle (create, read, update, read, delete, then read gives 404), browsing (the list, then its first item), the description's OpenAPI links , and negative cases : an id that does not exist gives 404, no credentials give 401 or 403, an empty body gives 400 or 422. The id comes from the links, else the field named like the path parameter, else id . no Test cases ( --cases ado:2238,jira:SHOP-12 ) One scenario per test case, planned by the model against the set's operations: the calls, the data, the values to carry, and the case's expected results as checks. Cases with nothing to test are left out with the reason (the same rules as the test case check). The scenario keeps its test case. yes Plain English ( --text "..." ) or a story "Create a user, log in, add two items, check out, verify the order total." Planned the same way. yes The planner only uses operations the set has: a step no operation does is listed as unmatched, never invented. Give it the API's operations with --spec (an OpenAPI or Swagger link or file) or a saved set; without a description, make contracts from a browser run first. Every plan is checked before it is saved (each operation exists, each variable is saved before it is used) and shown step by step; nothing runs until you run it. run_api_scenarios (or forgeqe api run-scenarios ) runs them against the API, without a browser or a model: each step in order, the values passed on, every step's checks. A failed step stops its scenario, and the scenario's cleanup steps (deleting what it created) run, those whose values exist. Scenarios that change data run only after you agree (in CI: --allow-writes ), on a test environment. Results go to scenario-results.json and scenarios-junit.xml , with report.html (each scenario a case, its calls the steps) and suite.json beside them. API runs count in the team report . On your existing API automation. write_api_tests with scenarios (or forgeqe api tests --scenarios ) has Scribe write each scenario as an end-to-end test in the repository, built on what is already there: It maps the repository's API layer first: clients, request helpers, auth and base URL fixtures, data builders, schemas. Each step calls the helper that already calls that operation; only operations without one get a new helper, in the same style. It reuses helpers, never tests: a scenario never runs another test as a step, and sets up its own data. A shared helper is only added to, never changed in a way its tests rely on. When Scribe changes one, ForgeQE also runs the tests that use it, and sends any failure back until both pass. A scenario test for a test case is named after it and recorded in .forgeqe/test-cases.json , and set as the Azure DevOps test case's Associated Automation when write-back is on. bash Copy forgeqe api scenarios --run # the latest browser run's flow, chained forgeqe api scenarios --spec https://shop.test/openapi.json # lifecycles, browsing, links, negative cases forgeqe api scenarios --cases ado:2238,ado:2239 --spec openapi.yaml forgeqe api scenarios --text "create a user, add two items, check out, the total is the sum" --spec openapi.yaml forgeqe api run-scenarios --allow-writes --base-url https://qa.shop.test # exit 1 when one fails forgeqe api tests --scenarios --repo ../api-tests # on the repo's existing helpers
14 Quality Accessibility, page performance, and visual changes

Quality Accessibility and page performance Checks every page a run visits against WCAG rules (axe-core) and measures its Core Web Vitals, against budgets, with trends over time per page. Ask it Is the checkout page accessible? Did page performance get worse this week? What it needs You give a browser run (from browser_run or run_test_cases); new runs need a live model Limits Per-page Core Web Vitals, not load testing under many users. Tools quality_report quality_trends In detail

Accessibility and performance budgets Every browser run checks each page it visits and times it, with no extra step: Accessibility: axe-core (installed with ForgeQE) runs the rules of the standard you choose on each page as the agent finds it. The report lists the rules that passed and each rule that failed , with its WCAG success criterion and level, its impact (critical, serious, moderate, minor), the elements, and how to fix it. Automated checks find a part of the WCAG problems (often 30–50%): they are a pre-check, not conformance, and a manual review still matters. quality.accessibility.engine: basic uses ForgeQE's own smaller set of checks instead. Performance: each page's Core Web Vitals, measured in the browser the agent drives: LCP (largest contentful paint), CLS (layout shift), INP (the slowest interaction the agent made), FCP , TTFB , load time, requests and transfer size. These are lab values from one visit, not field data from real users. A run fails on them only when a budget is exceeded . Without budgets they are reported and tracked, never failed. When a budget is exceeded, the run's steps still passed: forgeqe run exits 1, the browser run says budget_exceeded , a suite case counts as failed (a bug is filed when bugs are set up), and a test is still written for the flow. yaml Copy quality: accessibility: standard: wcag21aa # wcag2a, wcag21aa (default), wcag22aa, wcag21aaa, section508, en301549, best-practice best_practice: false # also axe-core's best-practice rules budgets: accessibility: # most violations per page by impact; unset impacts have no limit (or: accessibility: true for 0 critical, 0 serious) critical: 0 serious: 0 rules: [color-contrast, label] # must pass everywhere ignore: [region] # not counted performance: # or: performance: web-vitals (LCP 2.5s, CLS 0.1, INP 200ms, FCP 1.8s, TTFB 800ms) preset: web-vitals lcp_ms: 3000 load_ms: 5000 pages: # by path prefix; the longest match wins /search: { lcp_ms: 4000 } Over time: every run adds each page's violations and timings to .forgeqe/reports/quality-history.json (keep it between CI runs as a cache). "Did accessibility regress?" or "is checkout getting slower?" ( quality_trends , or forgeqe quality trends [page] ) shows each page's violations over the last runs, the rules that newly fail or were fixed since the previous run, and each timing against its usual value (the median of the last 10 runs; slower or faster only beyond noise). forgeqe quality [run] ( quality_report ) shows one run's WCAG results, timings and budgets. bash Copy forgeqe quality # the latest run: WCAG rules passed and failed, Core Web Vitals, budgets forgeqe quality trends shop.test # per page over time; exits 1 when a page got worse

Quality Visual comparison with baselines Compares each page a run captures with its approved baseline and shows what changed; intended changes become the new baseline once the user agrees. Ask it What changed visually since the last run? Approve the new header What it needs You give a browser run (from browser_run or run_test_cases); new runs need a live model Tools visual_compare visual_approve In detail

Visual comparison Every browser run also captures each page it visits and compares it, pixel by pixel, with that page's approved baseline : Capture: the state the flow leaves each page in, with animations and transitions frozen, the text caret hidden, and the regions you mask hidden (their space kept), so a page compares on what changed, not on what moves. ForgeQE's own overlay is never in the picture. The viewport by default; full_page: true captures the whole page (up to 8000 px tall). Baselines: in .forgeqe/visual-baselines/ next to forgeqe.yaml (commit them to share), one per page, screen size and operating system, since fonts render differently. A page's first capture becomes its baseline ( auto_baseline: false turns that off), and baselines.json records which run each baseline came from and why. Compare: each page is same , changed (the share of pixels that differ, and a diff image with the changed pixels in red), or new . Anti-aliasing is ignored; threshold sets how different two colours must be to count. A taller or wider page counts its new area as changed. Budget: a run fails only when quality.budgets.visual is set and a page changes by more than that share of its pixels (a page can have its own limit). Without it, changes are reported, never failed. Approve: when a change is intended, "approve the new home page" ( visual_approve , or forgeqe visual approve [run] --page /home ) makes the run's capture the new baseline, after you agree. An unintended change is a visual defect. The report's Visual page shows the baseline, this run, and the difference side by side for every page, changed pages first; click any image to see it full size. yaml Copy quality: visual: mask: [".clock", "#ad-slot", "[data-testid=carousel]"] # hidden on every page pages: /news: { mask: [".ticker"], max_diff_percent: 5 } # by path prefix full_page: false threshold: 0.1 # colour difference that counts (0–1) auto_baseline: true budgets: visual: 0.5 # most a page may change, in percent of its pixels (or: visual: true for 0.1%) bash Copy forgeqe visual # the latest run's pages against their baselines forgeqe visual approve --page /home # make this run's /home the baseline (asks first; --yes to skip)

Quality Defect intelligence: trends and prediction Groups failures into defects, keeps their history across suites (new, known, gone, back again), and gives defect trends and where a change is likely to cause defects, with the cases to run first. Ask it Which defects keep coming back? What can the changes since main break? What it needs You give suites run into one folder (suite.out_dir) Optional git on PATH, for predictions from the product's repository Limits Prediction is a heuristic from the saved suites and the change, not a trained model; its accuracy shows once suites have scored it. Tools defect_trends predict_defects In detail See Bugs for failures .

Defect trends and prediction forgeqe defects (or "which defects keep coming back?") reads the suites saved in suite.out_dir and their defect-history.json , and writes defect-trends.md next to them: how many defects are still there, gone, or came back after a fix; the time they took to go away; the most seen ones with their bugs; defects by area (a page or an API route, by its path without ids); defects per suite; and how often predictions were right. The report's Defects page shows the same under Across runs . forgeqe defects predict [--repo DIR] [--base REF] [--head REF] (or "what can the changes since main break?") says where a change is likely to cause defects. It reads the change between the merge base of base (default: the remote's default branch, else main or master ) and head in defects.product_repo (else the working directory). A change touches an area when it changes a file named after it ( server/cart.ts for /api/cart/:id ) or its diff mentions the route. Each touched area gets a score from what the saved suites know: Signal Score The diff mentions the area's route +3 A changed file is named after it +2 Each earlier defect there (three at most) +2 Defects there came back after a fix +2 A defect there is still open +1 Its cases failed in 20% (50%) of recent runs +1 (+2) 6 or more is high, 3 or more medium. It lists the cases that ended on the high and medium areas as the ones to run first, and the changed product code that no case reaches. It is a heuristic, not a trained model: each prediction is saved in defect-predictions.json , and the first suite after it scores it (did its defects fall in the areas rated medium or high; did the high areas get one), so forgeqe defects gives its accuracy. Release readiness uses the defects too: a regression on a case in scope blocks the release (NO-GO), and a new defect with no bug is a risk.
15 Release Requirement coverage and a release verdict

Release Requirement coverage and release readiness Gives requirement coverage and a GO / GO WITH RISKS / NO-GO verdict for a sprint, area, epic, or stories, from test cases, results, bugs, and flaky tests; can publish it to the wiki. Ask it Are we ready to release? Coverage of sprint 12 What it needs Required Azure DevOps or Jira: set up under sources: in forgeqe.yaml, or sign in with /auth Tools release_readiness In detail

Requirement coverage and release readiness "Are we ready to release sprint 12?", "coverage of epic 300" (or release_readiness ) builds the coverage matrix for an Azure DevOps scope: a sprint ( current or a name), an area path, an epic or feature and every story under it, or story ids. Each story with the test cases that test it ("Tested By"), whether each is automated (Automation status, or .forgeqe/test-cases.json ), and its last result: the newest test point outcome in Azure DevOps, or, where no plan has run it, ForgeQE's own runs (suite reports, then the automated test's history). Gaps: stories with no test case, test cases nobody automated, cases that have not run. Open bugs in the scope and linked to its stories, by severity. Flaky and quarantined tests from the test history. The verdict: NO-GO when something blocks (open critical or high bugs past the limit, a story with a failing test case, the pass rate below the minimum), GO WITH RISKS when something is missing (stories without test cases, cases not run or blocked, flaky or quarantined tests, other open bugs), else GO; each with its reasons. The report is saved as readiness.md (and readiness.json ) under .forgeqe/reports/readiness/ , shown as a card, and published to the project wiki with publish: "/Release readiness/Sprint 12" after you agree. The agent can also build an Azure DevOps dashboard for it with create_ado_dashboard . yaml Copy release: max_critical: 0 # open severity-1 bugs allowed max_high: 0 # open severity-2 bugs allowed min_pass_rate: 95 # percent of executed test cases that must pass require_tests: true # a story without a test case is a risk

Release Reports you can share Writes up what the Orchestrator found, such as open defects across projects, release status, or pipeline health, as a page with filters (project, state, priority, assignee, …), charts, and a sortable table, plus Markdown and CSV. Every table is built from evidence: the results of the tool calls the agent made, or a read-only query ForgeQE runs itself, listed on the page's Sources with each raw result kept beside the report. Ask it Create a release report for all projects Write up the open defects as a report I can share What it needs Required A live model profile in llms.json (an API key or Microsoft Entra ID sign-in) Limits Rows come only from tool results in the session or a query ForgeQE runs; the agent writes only the summary, which is not checked figure by figure. A WIQL query reads up to 1000 work items; the page says when a query matched more. The page is not published anywhere unless the reports folder is served (notify.report_url). Tools write_report In detail

Reports from the agent Ask for a report and ForgeQE's agent writes one you can share: "generate a defect report for all open defects", "create a release report for all projects", "summarise this sprint's test results as a report". Every table in it is built from evidence , not typed by the model: ForgeQE keeps the result of every tool call in the session (its own tools, and the Azure DevOps and Jira MCP servers). A dataset of the report names the calls it comes from, and ForgeQE takes the rows from their results. Or the dataset is a read-only query that ForgeQE runs itself when it writes the report: a WIQL query reads up to 1000 work items with their project, type, state, priority, severity, assignee, area, iteration, dates, and a link. The agent uses this for "all" of something. Or the dataset is ForgeQE's own past results ( history: ): suites (one row per run, with its run type in suite_scope ), case_results , step_results , writebacks , readiness , readiness_stories , or readiness_cases , from every run on this machine and the bundles teammates shared with forgeqe bi export (see Team report ). Every row has user and machine . The agent writes only the summary paragraph. The report goes to the reports folder ( export.out_dir , .forgeqe/reports/ by default): text Copy .forgeqe/reports/open-defects-all-projects-20261013-101512/ report.html # one file: summary, filters, charts, sortable table, Sources report.md # the same, to edit, paste into a wiki, or attach open-defects.csv # each dataset's rows evidence/E1.json # the raw result of each tool call the report used The page adds filters for the columns that are in the data (Project, State, Type, Priority, Severity, Assigned To, Area, Iteration, …, and other columns with a short list of values). The counts, the charts (click a bar to filter by it), and the table follow the filters, and Export CSV saves the rows you filtered. Sources lists each tool call, when it ran, and how many rows it gave, with a link to its raw result. The chat gets a short summary and a card with the paths as links, and Open the report appears as a next step. To post it, ask for it ("post the report to the release channel") once notify.channels is set up; the reports folder is linked when it is served ( notify.report_url ).

Team report forgeqe bi builds one report from every run in the reports folder: browser suites, monitor rounds, release readiness, single browser runs, desktop and mobile runs, exploratory testing, and API runs, each tagged with its run type. It builds an Evidence site (needs Node.js); without Node.js, or when Evidence fails, it writes ForgeQE's own page, which opens straight from disk ( bi: in forgeqe.yaml ; see README.md ). bash Copy forgeqe bi init # scaffold the Evidence project and install its packages forgeqe bi build # refresh the data and build (ForgeQE's own page if Evidence cannot build) forgeqe bi build --static # ForgeQE's own page only, no Node.js needed forgeqe bi sync # refresh the datasets and pages, without building forgeqe bi export [--out FILE|DIR] # your runs, in one file to share forgeqe bi build --from //share/qa-reports # this machine's runs plus every bundle there (repeatable) For one report across the team, each person runs forgeqe bi export , which writes their runs and readiness reports to one file in .forgeqe/reports/shared/ . Whoever builds puts the files in <out_dir>/collected/ ( .forgeqe/reports/collected/ by default), or lists shared folders under bi.collect , or passes --from , and runs forgeqe bi build . Every table gets user and machine columns; the report adds Results by run type and Case results by person tables. A run that arrives twice (in two bundles, or a bundle and this machine) counts once. A bundle is read as data only: a file that is not one, or is larger than 64 MB, is skipped with a note. In the shell, /report builds ForgeQE's own page from the same data, /report export writes your bundle, and /report <what> asks the agent for a report (see Reports from the agent ).

Static BI forgeqe bi adds an offline BI layer on top of those reports. It exports curated CSV datasets from ForgeQE's own suite history and release-readiness reports, plus optional Azure DevOps WIQL and Jira JQL datasets from bi.datasets in forgeqe.yaml , into an Evidence project that reads them through its CSV source, then runs evidence sources and evidence build to produce a static site in the configured build directory. ForgeQE uses the open-source Evidence line ( @evidence-dev/evidence 40.x, pinned in the generated package.json ), because the newer Evidence Studio CLI has no local build and keeps data in its cloud. Building it needs Node.js 18 or later; serve the folder to view it ( npx serve ), since it cannot load its data when opened from disk. When Node.js is missing or the Evidence build fails, forgeqe bi build writes ForgeQE's own self-contained page from the same data instead, which opens straight from disk, and says why; --static always does that, and --evidence fails instead of falling back. Dataset ids become table names ( forgeqe.<id> ), so they use letters, digits, and _ . Pages ForgeQE generates carry a "Managed by forgeqe bi" comment in their front matter; a page without it is yours and is never overwritten. Tables with no rows yet stay out of the Evidence project (Evidence cannot build over an empty table), and their sections read "None yet." No backend service stays up between runs. yaml Copy bi: title: ForgeQE BI datasets: ado_current_sprint: kind: ado_wiql project: Shop wiql: | SELECT [System.Id] FROM WorkItems WHERE [System.TeamProject] = @project AND [System.WorkItemType] IN GROUP 'Microsoft.RequirementCategory' jira_open_bugs: kind: jira_jql jql: project = SHOP AND issuetype = Bug AND statusCategory != Done bash Copy forgeqe bi init # scaffold the Evidence project and install its packages forgeqe bi build # refresh the data and build the site (ForgeQE's own page if Evidence cannot build) forgeqe bi build --static # ForgeQE's own page only, no Node.js needed

t: One report for the whole team
x: One report for the whole team Each person runs forgeqe bi export , which writes every kind of run they have (suites, monitor rounds, single browser runs, desktop, mobile, exploratory and API runs, and release-readiness reports) to one JSON file in .forgeqe/reports/shared/ , each run tagged with its run type. Whoever builds the report puts the files they receive in .forgeqe/reports/collected/ (or lists shared folders under bi.collect in forgeqe.yaml , or passes --from FILE|DIR , repeatable) and runs forgeqe bi build . Every table gets user and machine columns, the home page and ForgeQE's own page gain "Results by run type" and "Case results by person" tables, and a run that arrives twice (from two bundles, or a bundle and this machine) counts once. A bundle is read as data only: anything that is not one, or is larger than 64 MB, is skipped with a note, and a malformed run inside one is skipped whole. In the shell, /report builds ForgeQE's own page from the same data, /report export writes your bundle, and /report <what you want> asks the agent, which can now build write_report datasets from these past results ( history: case_results , suites , readiness , …) as well as from live Azure DevOps or Jira queries. bash Copy forgeqe bi export # your runs, in one file to share forgeqe bi build --from //share/qa-reports # this machine's runs plus every bundle in that folder

Model prices and usage Prices. ForgeQE prices every model call at the model's list price , from two public price lists: models.dev (the list the agent runtime uses) and LiteLLM's model price list, which also has Azure's Data Zone prices. It keeps the few fields it needs in ~/.forgeqe/prices.json , waits a few seconds for it the first time, refreshes it once a day in the background, and uses the last copy offline; only the public lists are downloaded, nothing about your runs is sent ( FORGEQE_PRICES=off stops the downloads). Costs at list price say so: $1.73 (list price of gpt-5.4 (Azure Global) from models.dev, 2026-10-06) . For an Azure Data Zone deployment, which costs about 10% more, set "deployment_type": "data_zone" on the profile. Model parameters. Models differ in what a request may carry: reasoning models (o1, o3, o4, gpt-5) take max_completion_tokens instead of max_tokens and only the default temperature, and some OpenAI-compatible servers refuse max_completion_tokens , reasoning_effort or response_format . ForgeQE works this out by itself. A profile is a reasoning model when its model or deployment name says so (an Azure deployment called chat-prod with "model": "gpt-5.4" counts), or when it sets "reasoning": true ; "reasoning": false says it is not. When the API still refuses a parameter, the browser, desktop and mobile agents send the call again without it and leave it out of later calls to that model. Nothing needs setting for a new model. A profile's own "price": { "input": 2.5, "output": 15, "cached_input": 0.25 } (per million tokens) wins, for a negotiated or enterprise rate. Leave currency out and reports use this machine's currency, or set "currency": "USD" . Without cached_input , cached input gets the model's cache discount from its list price, and the cost is marked as an estimate ( ≈$1.52 ); with no list price for the model either, cached input is charged at the full rate and the cost is an upper bound ( up to $6.11 ). When your price differs from the list price, ForgeQE says so ( forgeqe models , the shell, and the start of each command), since that is usually a typo or an old price. Anthropic's cache writes are priced at their own rate. A provisioned (PTU) deployment is billed per hour, not per token, so its costs are what the tokens would cost at list price. Requests over a model's long-context threshold (272K tokens for GPT-5.4) cost more and are priced at the normal rate. Usage after every job. Every browser run, Scribe job, heal, suite, and monitor round ends with a Usage line: tokens in (and how many of them were cached), tokens out, and the cost at the profile's price. A request to ForgeQE's agent in the shell, and every forgeqe run , code , suite , and heal command, ends with the total for everything it started, by role: text Copy This request used 1.1M tokens (1.1M in, 30.0K of it cached · 34.7K out) · $3.07 — ForgeQE's agent 42.0K · $0.12, browser agent 52.7K · $0.15, Scribe 1.0M · $2.80

Spending budgets A budget warns you before model spend gets out of hand. Set it under budget: in forgeqe.yaml , in the currency of your prices (see Model prices and usage ): yaml Copy budget: run: 2 # one browser run day: 25 month: 400 # currency: USD # default: the currency of the model's price Set any of the three. A budget only warns; it never stops a run . Each budget warns once at 80%, once at 90%, and once at 100%. When spend jumps past more than one of these at once, you get one warning, for the highest: text Copy Budget: this month's model spend is at $245.10, 82% of the $300.00 month budget (budget.month in forgeqe.yaml). Nothing is stopped. Where you see it. In the shell, the warning is a line in the conversation. Every other forgeqe command writes it to the terminal's error output. What counts. run is the spend of one browser run. day and month add up every ForgeQE process on this machine (days and months are in UTC). Runs that the agent starts through the MCP server count too, because every process writes its model calls to the usage ledger in ~/.forgeqe/usage/ ( FORGEQE_USAGE_DIR moves it). The ledger holds counts, times, and names, never prompt or response text. With FORGEQE_USAGE=off , nothing is kept on disk, and a budget counts only the calls of the process that warns. What does not count. A call with no price, such as a github_copilot profile without a price , and a call priced in a different currency than the budget. Spend from before. If you start ForgeQE when the day or month is already past 80%, it does not repeat that warning. It warns only for a threshold that spend passes from then on. In reports. The Trends and forecast page of a report's Tokenomics shows spend on this machine and the next days at the recent pace, against the budget.

Servers ForgeQE's agent connects to When ForgeQE's agent starts, it connects to an MCP server for each system set up under sources: . The server settings come from the same place as everything else: the organization and project, the site URL, and the names of the environment variables that hold the tokens. You don't write MCP config for these. Azure DevOps. Microsoft's Azure DevOps MCP server , run as npx -y @azure-devops/mcp <org> -a pat -d core work work-items pipelines : projects and teams, iterations and boards, work items, and pipelines. Every tool's definition goes to the model with each request, so ForgeQE loads only these groups (about 19 tools, roughly 9.5K tokens, against about 18K for all of them); its own tools cover test plans, wiki pages, dashboards, and pull request reviews, and query_api reads anything else, such as classic releases. The organization comes from org_url ( https://dev.azure.com/acme or https://acme.visualstudio.com ). ForgeQE passes the PAT from token_env (default ADO_PAT ) the way the server wants it; without a PAT it uses your az login session. Its tools are azure_devops_* . mcp_domains adds groups: test-plans , repositories (repos, branches, pull requests), wiki , search (code, wikis, and work items), advanced-security , or [all] . It needs Node.js. Azure DevOps Server (on-premises) isn't supported by Microsoft's server, so it uses ForgeQE's API. yaml Copy sources: azure_devops: org_url: https://dev.azure.com/acme # the MCP server takes the organization, not a project # project: Shop # optional: limit ForgeQE's own API calls to one project token_env: ADO_PAT mcp: true # false: API only mcp_domains: [core, work, work-items, pipelines, repositories] # optional: the default four, plus repos Microsoft's server has no dashboard tools and can't save queries. The PAT needs Work Items (read and write) and permission to edit dashboards. Chart widgets are not made through the API; for those the agent uses the browser, which has to be signed in to dev.azure.com ( forgeqe login <name> with a login for it under logins: ). Logs for debugging Every session ( forgeqe start , run , suite , heal , monitor , code , mcp , login , setup ) writes a log to .forgeqe/logs/ next to forgeqe.yaml (the newest 30 are kept). It has the versions and settings in use, what you asked, ForgeQE's agent's answers and every tool call with its result, every browser step and result, the browser engine's own log lines, and errors. Secrets are replaced before anything is written: API keys, tokens and passwords from the environment, keys in llms.json , and credentials you gave in a message. To share a session, type /logs in the shell ( /logs shots adds screenshots), or run forgeqe logs bundle afterwards. Either writes one .tar.gz with the session log, the run folders it mentions ( run.json , steps.json , trace.md , resume.json , workflow.yaml , the failure screenshot), your forgeqe.yaml , your profiles without keys, and the versions. forgeqe logs lists recent logs. Start with --debug (or set FORGEQE_DEBUG=1 ) for more: the browser engine logs at debug level, and long values such as tool results are kept whole instead of cut at 8,000 characters.

Which tools ForgeQE's agent gets Every model call carries the definitions of the tools the agent has, so it does not get all of them. Each turn gets: the core: help, setup, use_capabilities , and the test environments and their apps; the capabilities the request is about , picked without a model call from its words (each capability's keywords in src/capabilities/registry.ts ), the apps of the environment it names (a mobile app means the mobile tools), and links (the browser); capabilities used in the last few turns , so a conversation keeps its tools. A capability this project cannot use yet (no mobile apps, no Jira) is not picked from words alone. When a request needs a capability the turn did not get, the agent calls use_capabilities , and ForgeQE continues the same request with its tools. With fewer tools in view, the agent also cannot mix up similar ones ( browser_run , desktop_explore , mobile_explore ). forgeqe context shows what a turn carries, and what each capability adds. The session log ( /logs ) records which capabilities each turn got and why ( agent.scope ). Pin capabilities on, or switch them off for a project, in forgeqe.yaml (ids from forgeqe features ): yaml Copy agent: capabilities: always: [regression-packs] off: [desktop-apps] FORGEQE_TOOL_SCOPE=off gives every tool on every turn. MCP clients of forgeqe mcp (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Claude Code) list tools once rather than per turn, so they get the core and every capability this project can use (no desktop tools without desktop apps, no tracker tools without a tracker). use_capabilities adds others and sends notifications/tools/list_changed , which tells the client to read the list again. For a client that ignores it, forgeqe mcp --all-tools lists every tool.

How a run flows One model config: llms.json → UFO UFO picks its model client by API TYPE through ufo.llm.base.BaseService.get service , which every model call goes through ufo/llm/llm call.py . The adapter adds the type forgeqe : write ufo config writes UFO's config/ufo/agents.yaml from its template, with API TYPE: forgeqe , the model's name, and no endpoint and no key, for HOST AGENT , APP AGENT , BACKUP AGENT and EVALUATION AGENT . ufo bridge.install makes get service "forgeqe", … return ForgeQEService , which calls the profile through the openai SDK models.py : azure key or auth: entra , openai , openai compatible key or Entra , and ollama through its OpenAI compatible /v1 . Keys, Azure endpoints and Entra use the browser engine's own helpers forgeqe engine.llm , so a profile means the same thing in both. Keys stay in environment variables. Each call's time and tokens go to ForgeQE's usage ledger as the "desktop agent" counts only, never the prompt . Explore sends screenshots, so its profile must take images: "vision": true or false on the profile says so; without it, ollama profiles are refused and others accepted. Healing sends a screenshot only to a profile that takes images. The request parameters suit the model by themselves: a reasoning model o1, o3, o4, gpt 5, by the profile's model or deployment name, or "reasoning": true on the profile gets max completion tokens and no temperature from the first call, and when the API refuses a parameter max tokens , temperature , frequency penalty , response format , … the call is sent again without it, and later calls to that model leave it out py/forgeqe engine/model params.py . The browser agent does the same. Workflow YAML forgeqe desktop v1 Ops: launch , click , double click , type , select , keys , expect , expect image , wait at most 60 s , wait for , close . Locators use UIA properties, never screen coordinates: automation id , name , control type , class name , index when several match , and path the ancestors' control type and name . A target needs an automation id or a name . Replay looks in the launched app's own windows only. Variables: {{name}} from the workflow's variables or name=value on the command line; {{secret:NAME}} from the environment, only for names in desktop.secrets . A secret ForgeQE itself uses a model key, a tracker token is refused there. Values are substituted once and never expanded again. Targets take {{name}} too a CSV row's {{customer}} as the control to click , never a secret. Keys: ctrl , shift and alt with one named key or character ctrl+s , alt+f4 , enter , f5 . The Windows and context menu keys are refused: Win+R followed by typing runs any command. Typing is literal: pywinauto's key syntax ^ , % , + , ~ , {ENTER} in the text is escaped. Recording by hand When you know the steps, do them yourself instead of describing a goal: no model and no UFO are involved, so it costs nothing and does exactly what you did. ForgeQE starts the app and watches the mouse and keyboard low level Windows hooks , asking UI Automation which control each click and key went to. Do the steps, then: Ctrl+Shift+F11 with the mouse over a control adds a check: an expect step with the text it shows now a status message, a saved total . Add one at the end, so the replay tests the outcome, not only the steps. Ctrl+Shift+F12 , or closing the app, finishes. The console shows each step as it is recorded. What becomes a step: You do Step Click a control two quick clicks: double click click with its AutomationId, name and control type Pick an item in a drop down select on the drop down, with the item's name Type into a field corrections and pastes included one type with the field's text when you move on, read from the field A key chord outside a text field ctrl+s , enter , f5 keys Ctrl+Shift+F11 over a control expect with its text Passwords: a password field is never read; its step types {{secret:NAME}} the one name in desktop.secrets , or <APP PASSWORD , which the result tells you to set . Text equal to a desktop.secrets value is written as its placeholder. The typed characters themselves are never kept, only the field's text when you move on. Only the app: clicks and keys outside the app's own process are not recorded; nor are the Windows and menu keys, or controls with neither an AutomationId nor a name. The result lists what was left out. The run folder has workflow.yaml , run.json and report.html , like explore. Replay it with forgeqe desktop replay . Fixing a workflow from chat When a replayed step fails because the app was slow or a dialog was in the way, ForgeQE's agent fixes the workflow with desktop edit workflow : it proposes the change a longer timeout or retries on the step, a wait for before it, a dialog button in dismiss , a healed locator, a corrected text , shows you the diff, and writes the file only when you agree. For example, after "step 4 timed out while the invoice list loaded": Each change has a fixed shape set , unset , set step , add dismiss , insert step , remove step , set variable ; step numbers are the replay report's. Anything else is refused. The changed workflow is checked by the engine's own validator before it is shown; one that would not run is not offered. Comments and layout are kept. The old text is kept in the reports folder desktop edits/ , and a file that changed since the edit was proposed is not overwritten. The workflow must be a .yaml inside the working folder or the reports folder. Waits, retries and dialogs Real apps are slow in places: a splash screen, a form that loads its data, a "Tip of the day" or "Save changes?" dialog. A workflow says how to wait for them, without fixed wait steps: Each step waits for its control up to its timeout . click , type and select also wait until the control is enabled and visible a form that is still loading greys its buttons out . wait for waits until a control is there, shows a text , or with gone: true has gone. retries applies to click , double click , type , select , keys , expect and expect image . Between tries, replay pauses 1 s, 2 s, … up to 5 s and closes any dismiss dialog. An error in the workflow itself a missing variable is not retried. dismiss lists at most 10 targets, checked like any target. When a control is not found, or something waits to go away, replay clicks the dismiss controls that are on screen and looks again, up to 3 times per lookup. The report and the console name every dialog closed, and how many tries a step took. Visual checks expect image expect compares text. When what matters is drawn a chart, a signature, a colour, a layout , expect image compares pixels with a baseline image: The first run with no baseline saves what it captured and passes; the report says so. Commit the baselines folder with the workflow. update baselines replaces them after an intended change. A pixel counts as different when a colour channel differs by more than 32 of 255, so anti aliasing and ClearType do not fail a check. A different size another screen scale or window size fails with both sizes named. The report shows the baseline, what was captured, and the differences in red, with the share of pixels that differ images/NNN baseline actual diff.png in the run folder . Image names are file names only letters, digits, , , ending .png . A path, .. , or a link that leads out of the baselines folder is refused. Run visual checks on one machine with a fixed resolution and scale see DESKTOP CI.md DESKTOP CI.md . Unattended runs Replay needs a signed in, unlocked Windows session. Before it starts the app, it checks the session and fails at once with the reason if it is a Windows service session 0 , a locked screen, or a disconnected Remote Desktop session. forgeqe desktop doctor runs the same check. To run the suite every night on a machine of your own, see DESKTOP CI.md DESKTOP CI.md : a runner set up in the user's session ci/desktop runner/prepare runner.ps1 , a nightly workflow ci/desktop runner/desktop nightly.example.yml , and junit results. Updating UFO² UFO² is pinned to one commit. Moving it is checked before it is pinned: 1. .github/workflows/forgeqe desktop ufo update.yml runs weekly, or by hand with a commit. It sets up that UFO on Windows FORGEQE UFO COMMIT , which takes a full 40 character commit id only , runs the adapter tests against its real code and a scripted explore of Notepad, and says in the job summary whether it passed. 2. When it passed: bun scripts/ufo bump.ts <commit writes the new pin into src/desktop/setup.ts , py/forgeqe desktop/ufo runner.py and this page. Run the tests and push; the Windows CI job tests the pin again. When it fails, the failing step names what changed in UFO usually the action executor or the config layout that the adapter wraps . Keep the pin until the adapter is updated for it. Checks of the outcome A recording of actions only proves the steps run. When UFO has finished, and before the app closes, explore shows the model the goal and the app's controls with the text each shows now, and the model picks up to three whose text proves the goal a status message, a saved value , by number, with the part of the text to expect. A check is kept only when that text really is in that control, so the model can choose among what is on screen but never invent it; text holding a desktop.secrets value is never offered. The checks are saved as expect steps at the end of the workflow, and the report says how many there are. With none, the report and the agent say so: add expect steps by hand. Recording UFO's own step log names the control and a per step id, not its AutomationId, so the adapter wraps UFO's ActionExecutor.execute and records each action with the UIA properties of the control it acted on. record.py turns that trace into steps: click input → click / double click , set edit text → type , keyboard input → keys one allowed chord or type , select → select . Coordinate clicks, scrolls and anything else are listed as not recorded in the report. A typed value equal to a desktop.secrets value is written as its placeholder; typed text that only looks like {{…}} is kept literal, so a model told to type {{secret:X}} cannot make replay type the secret. Security The YAML, the trace, the app's screen text and the model's replies can all be written by someone else. The rules in the repository's CLAUDE.md apply; for this engine: No command in the workflow. app: names a desktop.apps entry: an absolute .exe a .bat or .cmd would run through cmd.exe , which reparses its arguments and an argument list, started with subprocess.Popen path, args . UFO gets UI tools only. Each explore writes UFO's mcp.yaml with UICollector , HostUIExecutor and AppUIExecutor . UFO's default CommandLineExecutor , which runs shell commands, and its Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF executors are left out. The adapter starts the app, so UFO never launches a program. Keys: during explore the adapter refuses UFO's Windows and menu keys too, and the report lists what it refused. No one at the console: UFO's safe guard asks before sensitive actions; explore answers no, since nobody is there. Environment: the engine process gets system settings, the profile's key variable or Entra's and desktop.secrets , nothing else desktopEnvNames . Explore controls the real mouse and keyboard. It asks before starting yes to skip; required with no terminal . Use a test machine or VM and a test account. Agent tools: a workflow path the agent gives must be a .yaml inside the working folder or the reports folder real path, so a link out is refused ; variables are names and text only; heals are reported, never written. Healing: the model picks one of the window's real controls by number; control text is passed as data, and any other answer heals nothing. Heals are written into the workflow only when accepted. Report: every value is escaped; images are only the engine's own steps/NNN.png and images/NNN baseline actual diff.png . Baselines: expect image names are file names, and their real path must be inside the workflow's baselines folder, so a workflow cannot read or overwrite another file. Unattended machines: prepare runner.ps1 never handles a password; automatic sign in uses Sysinternals Autologon, which stores it encrypted. Install: UFO is cloned and checked out at the pinned commit or FORGEQE UFO COMMIT , a full commit id only , and the checkout's HEAD is verified; replay's packages are pinned to exact versions. h: What breaks a desktop run, and how ForgeQE tells you
Leaving Remote Desktop without locking the session
x: Desktop replay clicks and types into real windows. It needs what a person at the machine would have: a signed in Windows session, unlocked, with a screen. GitHub's hosted windows 2022 runners have that, and ForgeQE's own CI runs Notepad there. Your own apps usually need a machine of your own, with the app installed, its test database, and a network route to its servers. This page sets one up as a GitHub Actions self hosted runner. The same rules apply to Azure DevOps agents and Jenkins nodes. What breaks a desktop run, and how ForgeQE tells you Situation Effect Fix The runner is a Windows service Session 0 has no desktop; every control lookup times out Run the runner in the user's session below The screen is locked Windows sends no input to apps No inactivity lock, no screen saver lock A Remote Desktop session was disconnected The session is locked Leave Remote Desktop with tscon below , or don't use it on the test machine The machine slept or the screen turned off Input and screenshots stop Power plan: never sleep, never turn off the screen After a restart nobody signs in No session at all Sysinternals Autologon Before each replay or explore, the engine checks the session py/forgeqe desktop/session.py . On a session it cannot drive, the run fails at once with the reason, instead of timing out step by step. forgeqe desktop doctor runs the same check from a shell or a job: It exits with 1 when the desktop cannot be driven, so a job stops before the suite runs. Set up the test machine Use a test machine or VM, and a test account: the runner's jobs control its mouse and keyboard. 1. Sign in as the account the tests will run as. 2. Install the runner GitHub: Settings → Actions → Runners → New self hosted runner . Give it the label forgeqe desktop . When config.cmd asks whether to run as a service, answer no . 3. Run ci/desktop runner/prepare runner.ps1 in an elevated PowerShell WhatIf first to see the changes : It stops sleep, screen off and the screen saver lock. It turns the inactivity lock off and registers a logon task that starts run.cmd in this account's session. It warns you if the runner is also installed as a service. It never handles a password. 4. Sign in automatically after a restart with Sysinternals Autologon https://learn.microsoft.com/sysinternals/downloads/autologon , run as the test account. It stores the password encrypted by Windows. Never put the password in a script, a registry value you write yourself, or the repository. 5. Fix the screen size. A visual check expect image compares pixels, so the resolution and scale 100%, 125% must match the machine where its baselines were saved. Set them once and leave them. 6. Restart and check that the runner shows as idle on GitHub. Then run forgeqe desktop doctor from a job. Leaving Remote Desktop without locking the session Closing a Remote Desktop window disconnects the session, and Windows locks it. To leave it running instead, hand the session back to the machine's console. In an elevated prompt inside the Remote Desktop session: On a VM, the hypervisor's console Hyper V, VMware, VirtualBox needs no such step. The nightly job ci/desktop runner/desktop nightly.example.yml is a ready workflow. Copy it into .github/workflows/ in the repository that holds your desktop workflows. It: runs at night on self hosted, windows, forgeqe desktop , one run at a time; installs a pinned ForgeQE and runs forgeqe desktop setup and forgeqe desktop doctor ; replays every workflow in a folder: forgeqe desktop replay desktop tests/ junit results/desktop.xml ; keeps the reports, screenshots and image diffs as an artifact. junit writes one test case per workflow and per CSV row with data , which CI servers show as test results. runs.json in the output folder has the same, with the path of each report. Secrets the workflows type {{secret:NAME}} come from the CI's secret store as environment variables, and must be listed in desktop.secrets or the environment's secrets in env.yaml . Pick the environment with FORGEQE ENV or env . Healing calls the model. In a nightly run, either give the job the model's key so moved controls are healed and reported in heals.json never written into the workflow without accept heals , or pass no heal so a moved control fails the run.

Status: the engine and its tests run on any OS, against a fake Appium server and a stand in for Maestro. The CI job .github/workflows/forgeqe mobile android.yml runs it on an Android emulator: Appium explores and replays the emulator's Settings app, and Maestro replays the same workflow. iOS runs the same code with the XCUITest driver, but no CI job tests it yet it needs a macOS runner with a simulator . ForgeQE drives mobile apps two ways, and one workflow format runs on both: Appium Maestro Runs step by step, through an Appium server yours or a device cloud's the whole workflow as one Maestro flow Explore a goal with the model yes no Heal a control that moved yes, one model call, reported for review no Visual checks expect image yes no Your team's own flows n/a forgeqe mobile maestro , checked against an allowlist Needs appium with UiAutomator2 Android or XCUITest iOS , a device or emulator maestro and a device or emulator Use Or ask ForgeQE's agent in the shell or forgeqe run : "sign in to the courier app and save it as a test", "replay the courier login on Maestro", "run our Maestro flows". Its tools are mobile explore , mobile replay and mobile maestro . It asks before each one starts, and desktop edit workflow fixes a mobile workflow after a failed replay, the same way as a desktop one. Apps and settings Mobile apps come from the active environment in env.yaml, or from mobile.apps in forgeqe.yaml: Each run writes a folder under the reports folder mobile explore … , mobile replay … , mobile maestro … with run.json , report.html , step screenshots, and for Maestro runs the flow, maestro.log and Maestro's JUnit report. Workflow YAML forgeqe mobile v1 Ops: launch , tap , double tap , long press , type , expect , expect image , swipe direction up, down, left or right, optionally on a target , scroll to scrolls until the target is on screen , back , hide keyboard , keys enter , back , tab , delete , search , wait , wait for , close . Timeouts, retries and dismiss work as in desktop workflows. Explore saves a tap on a system dialog another package's control, such as Android's notification prompt under dismiss , not as a step, so the workflow still runs where the dialog never shows; on Maestro, each dismiss target is tapped after a launch if it is there. Targets use the desktop keys, mapped per platform: automation id is the Android resource id with or without the package:id/ prefix or the iOS accessibility identifier; name is the Android text or content desc, or the iOS label; control type is the Android class android.widget.Button or the iOS type XCUIElementTypeButton ; index picks one of several matches. Explore The model sees the goal, its steps so far, the numbered controls on screen with the text each shows, and a screenshot when the profile takes images. It answers with one action on a control by its number tap, long press, type , a swipe or scroll, back, or done. So it can only act on a control that is on screen. When it says done, it picks checks of the outcome from the controls' current text, kept only when that text is really there, as on the desktop. The app's text is passed as data. Maestro ForgeQE workflows on Maestro. driver maestro writes the workflow as a Maestro flow flow.yaml in the run folder and runs maestro test . Maestro's debug output gives each workflow step its result. Variables are filled in first. Values are matched literally, so Maestro's regular expressions never see them as patterns. A secret becomes ${MAESTRO NAME} , which Maestro reads from the environment ForgeQE gives it, so a secret's value never lands in the flow file or on a command line. A value holding ${…} is refused, because Maestro would run it as JavaScript. Your team's flows. forgeqe mobile maestro <files or folders checks each flow, and every flow it runs, before Maestro gets it: Only UI commands pass: launchApp , tapOn , inputText , assertVisible , scrollUntilVisible , swipe , extendedWaitUntil , runFlow , repeat , retry and the like. These are refused: runScript , evalScript and assertTrue , which run JavaScript. Maestro's AI commands, which send screenshots to a service. takeScreenshot , recordings and addMedia , which read or write files. ${…} may only name a variable ${USERNAME} , never an expression. when: {true: …} is refused, because it is JavaScript. openLink takes http s or the app's own deep links, never javascript: , file: or intent: . runFlow files must be .yaml inside the working folder; links out of it are refused too. Nesting stops at 5 levels. A refused flow does not run, and the error names the command. TestMu AI formerly LambdaTest Both drivers run on TestMu's devices. Upload the app once, then use the lt:// id it returns as the app's app : From the shell, ask in words "upload builds/courier.apk to TestMu for courier" : mobile upload asks first, uploads the build it must be inside the working folder , and saves the lt:// id as that app's app: in forgeqe.yaml. The user and key come from LT USERNAME and LT ACCESS KEY or the variables the config names , for example in a .env file in the project folder. samples/mobile testmu/ is a ready project with TestMu's Wikipedia sample app. Appium needs nothing else: the Appium driver talks to the hub with the user and key from the two variables. Maestro runs through HyperExecute. ForgeQE writes a HyperExecute project in the run folder and starts the CLI. The project holds the flows in their folder layout so runFlow still works , the app an lt:// id is passed as the device's appId ; a build file is uploaded with the project , a fixed setup script Android platform tools 35.0.2 and Maestro 2.6.1 from its release, both checked against their SHA 256 and a fixed run script, and hyperexecute.yaml . Team flows are checked against the allowlist first, as always. Flow file names may only use letters, digits and . / and one leading dot, for .maestro/ , because HyperExecute's shell reads them. After the job, ForgeQE downloads its artifacts Maestro's command results and JUnit reports , so each step gets its own result in the report. Secrets on Maestro on TestMu: a workflow that types a secret is refused there for now HyperExecute would need the value in its own vault . Replay it on TestMu with driver appium . The access key is passed to the CLI as an argument. It is removed from the CLI's output and from every file in the run folder. Neither the user name nor the key is passed to the flows' environment. .github/workflows/forgeqe mobile testmu.yml runs all three on TestMu Appium, Maestro with a workflow, a team flow with TestMu's Wikipedia sample app, once the repository has the secrets LT USERNAME and LT ACCESS KEY . Security No commands from the workflow or the model. app: names a configured app a platform and an id . Appium is spoken to over HTTP, and maestro is started with an argument list, never a shell. Locators go into XPath as quoted literals, so a target cannot change the query. Secrets: {{secret:NAME}} reads only mobile.secrets and the environment's secrets, and ForgeQE's own keys are refused there. Explore types a secret from its placeholder, so the model never sees the value. The engine's environment holds system settings, the profile's key, the listed secrets, the cloud's user and key, and JAVA HOME / ANDROID HOME , nothing else. Cloud credentials come from the variables mobile.appium.username env and access key env name; a user or key in the URL is refused. TLS is verified as usual. App builds are absolute paths to an app file, https URLs, or a device cloud's own upload ids bs:// , lt:// , storage:filename= ; file:// and other schemes are refused. Status: the tests run against a fake runtime on any OS. They check the commands ForgeQE builds, the checks on config, compose files, mounts and secrets, the mock stubs, and tests in a container. tests/containers.live.test.ts runs on real Docker and is skipped without it : Postgres from forgeqe.yaml and from a compose file. A WireMock mock that answers a recorded run's calls. A tests container that reaches the database by name and writes its results into the repository as this machine's user. .github/workflows/forgeqe containers.yml runs both on GitHub's Docker. There, a skipped live test fails the job. ForgeQE uses Docker or Podman, when one is installed, for five jobs: Services a test run needs: a database, a queue, a cache, or the API under test. The project declares them in forgeqe.yaml, or in a docker compose file that forgeqe.yaml names. Mocks of an API: WireMock stubs made from the calls a browser run recorded, or from an OpenAPI description, so the tests can run without the real service. The repository's tests in a container: run tests runs the command the user confirmed in an image, instead of on this machine, after starting the services the tests need. A workspace for the coding agents: with containers.workspace , Scribe's shell commands build, restore, run, git and every test ForgeQE runs for it go to a container of the project's image. The agents stay on this machine. A browser in a container: with browser.provider: docker , the browser agent, the replay and Scribe's live browser drive Chromium in a container of Microsoft's Playwright image. Scribe also has a testcontainers skill, for tests that start their own services from code below . ForgeQE's agent uses them through two tools, services and mock service . The CLI has forgeqe services . When neither Docker nor Podman is on PATH, the agent isn't offered these tools. Use In the shell or forgeqe run , you can ask, for example: "start the database" "is the queue up?" "mock the payments API from the last run" "make a mock service from openapi.yaml and point order api at it" "stop the services" The agent asks before it starts anything. Declaring services Setting Rule Service name Lower case letters, digits and , starting with a letter. Names starting with mock are kept for mocks. image Must have an exact tag or a digest. Lifetime Services and mocks the agent starts are removed when the shell, forgeqe run , or forgeqe mcp ends, as are the workspace and browser containers forgeqe.kind workspace and browser . The home volume stays. forgeqe services up keeps its services running after the command ends, until forgeqe services down . Container names are forgeqe <project <service . <project is a hash of the project folder, so two projects never share a container. Starting a service replaces its earlier container. Removing a container also removes the anonymous volumes its image declares a database's data folder , so nothing is left on the machine. A container is never reused with old settings. Labels: each container carries forgeqe=1 , forgeqe.project , forgeqe.service and forgeqe.kind . down and status look only at this project's containers. Security ForgeQE's agent reads text other people control: tickets, web pages, repositories. A container command built from that text could mount the whole disk or run privileged, so: No commands from the model. The agent names services that forgeqe.yaml declares, and ForgeQE builds the argument array docker run … . It never uses a shell. Images, flags and mounts never come from a request. The same restrictions for every container: security opt no new privileges , pids limit 1024 , ports on 127.0.0.1, and read only mounts. There is no setting to turn these off. Mounts are checked like uploads except a mock's stubs folder, which ForgeQE writes itself and mounts read only . The path is resolved with realpath and must be inside the project. A mount that is or holds a hidden file or folder .env , .git , .npmrc , a file named like a key .pem , id rsa , llms.json or a link is refused. A container can send what it reads anywhere. Environment: The docker and podman programs see only the system settings and the variables they need to find their daemon DOCKER HOST , DOCKER CONTEXT , CONTAINER HOST , … , plus the service's listed secrets. A container gets only its env and secrets . Logs and errors have secret values replaced with . Not in the agents' shell: docker , podman , nerdctl , docker compose and podman compose are denied in the shell of ForgeQE's agent and of Scribe. So the only way to start a container is these tools. Asked first: services up and mock service ask the user before starting, as run tests does. The team's own rules for every agent ForgeQE runs, to keep them grounded. Each bullet line " rule" in a .md or .txt file in this folder is one guardrail; headings, other lines and HTML comments are ignored. guardrails.md is the file ForgeQE's agent adds to when you ask it for a new rule.
