h: 6. Learning: how the registry fills itself
x: Status: proposal · 2026 10 15 ForgeQE pays the model for work it has already done. This document sets out how ForgeQE decides when the model is needed at all, and how much of it. The approach is built from published, measured techniques. The goal for known work: a rerun of an existing test costs 0–5% of its first run , and the model is paid only for what is new or broken. 1. What a request costs today measured From the session logs in a live project .forgeqe/logs , Azure OpenAI gpt 5.4 : Request Agent calls Input tokens Output tokens Cached "Are we ready to release?" one release readiness tool call 12 577K 2.6K 518K Test authoring session many 1.9M 8.9K 1.65M These numbers show three things: 1. Fixed overhead per call. Every chat agent call resends about 45K tokens of system prompt, tool definitions and history. Output is under 0.5% of tokens, so the cost is the context, not the work. 2. Calls multiply. The deterministic release check took 12 calls, because the agent asked questions, searched for files, read config and summarised. 3. Known work is not recognised: Every request goes through the chat agent, including the rerun link. Page memory finds a saved flow only by the exact goal text plus the URL memory.py: goal key , so a reworded goal misses it. replay: verify replays every step, then starts the browser agent to check the result. Prompt caching already works about 90% of input is cached . It lowers the price per token, but not the number of tokens or calls, so on its own it cannot reach the target. 2. The approaches this design uses Technique Evidence Where it applies here Workflows before agents. Use fixed code paths for predictable tasks; keep agents for open ended ones. Anthropic, Building effective agents https://www.anthropic.com/research/building effective agents 2024 Tier 0: rerun, run case, run suite, release check Plan caching. Extract a plan template from a finished run, match new requests by key, and adapt the template with a small model. Zhang et al., Agentic Plan Caching https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14852 , NeurIPS 2025: 50.3% lower cost and 27.3% lower latency on average, performance maintained Tier 1: known flow, new wording or new data Workflow memory. Turn successful trajectories into reusable routines. Wang et al., Agent Workflow Memory https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429 , ICML 2025: +51.1% relative success on WebArena, fewer steps Flows saved from passing runs, shared across cases Model cascade and routing. Try the cheapest model or step that can answer, and escalate only when a check fails. Chen et al., FrugalGPT https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176 up to 98% savings, task dependent ; Ong et al., RouteLLM https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18665 , ICLR 2025 over 2x savings at about 95% quality The router MODEL ROUTING.md ; result checks on the reviewer model Content addressed memoization. Key cached work by a fingerprint of its inputs; any change to the inputs invalidates it. Standard in build systems Bazel, Gradle remote cache and in test impact analysis Registry fingerprints, the tool result cache Record–replay with self healing locators. Already in ForgeQE replay.py , ranked locators Tier 0 and Tier 2 execution The published figures come from the authors' own benchmarks. ForgeQE has to measure its own section 7 . 3. The execution ladder Every request is resolved to the lowest tier that can do it . A tier escalates only on a concrete failure signal, never on a guess. Tier When Model use Target cost vs. first run 0: Deterministic The request resolves to a known entity, and replay and end state checks pass None. The reply is filled in from the result. 0% 1: Adapt A known flow, but with new wording, new test data, or an end state check that is unsure One call to the small reviewer model with a short prompt about 2K tokens ≤5% 2: Heal Replay stopped at step k , or a check failed The agent starts at step k with the steps so far as context, not from the beginning Proportional to what broke 3: Explore No match in the registry: a new goal or new kind of task Full agent, as today 100% Resolver no model . Matches IDs TC 123 , SHOP 12 , plan/suite numbers, run folders, last , file and test names, and aliases from the registry. The rerun link and /rerun call it directly. Plain requests try it before any model is called. Router small model . Runs only when the resolver is unsure. It sees the request and the top registry candidates ranked by alias and keyword match , not the full tool catalogue. It returns {entity, tier} or novel . Safety rules non negotiable : A Tier 0 pass needs evidence: replay complete and every recorded end state check passing. Anything else escalates. Freshness. A flow is marked stale when the app changes: a new deploy or build id when configured , a changed page fingerprint seen during replay, or the age limit registry.maxAgeDays . A stale flow runs at Tier 1 once to re confirm it. Canary. Every N th Tier 0 run of an entity default 10 runs at Tier 1, so a check that silently passes is caught. The user can always force a tier: /rerun verify , /rerun fresh . 4. The registry: one indexed catalogue The registry is one SQLite file per project: .forgeqe/registry/registry.db . Bun ships bun:sqlite and Python ships sqlite3 , so there are no new dependencies. It is local, and git ignored by default its folder carries its own .gitignore . Existing JSON stores page memory, code graph, quality history stay where they are. The registry indexes and links them, it does not replace them. 4.1 Taxonomy Every row has a kind , and every kind has a single source of truth: Kind Source of truth Example test case ADO / Jira / Xray / TestRail / cases file ado:QI Claims:TC 4812 code test Repo test code code graph PlaywrightPom.Web.Tests.LoginTests.ValidLogin flow Page memory flows/ recorded steps for a goal page , element Page memory pages/ /login , username suite , plan ADO / cases file plan 12 / suite 34 work item ADO / Jira story, bug, feature pipeline , environment , login Config, ADO, saved sessions QI Claims nightly , staging , saucedemo standard run , report .forgeqe/reports run folders 4.2 Tables 4.3 Fingerprints and invalidation A cached item is valid only while its fingerprint matches its source: test case: hash of the normalised steps plus expected results, together with the ADO rev . This replaces matching on goal text, so rewording a request no longer misses the flow. code test: git blob sha of the test file and of the page objects it reaches from the code graph . flow: hash of its steps, together with the page fingerprints seen on its last pass. tool cache: the source's own version work item rev , sprint id, ETag where one exists; otherwise a short TTL. Writes always bypass it. 5. Building context for Tiers 1–3 The agent's fixed 45K token context is the main cost driver. Context is built from the registry instead of being discovered by the agent: Context packs. For each entity, a brief of a few hundred tokens: what it is, its linked case, code test, flow, pages and last results. The agent gets the brief rather than spending calls on read , grep and code outline . Tool listing by tier: Tier 1 gets one tool. Tier 2 gets the tools of the capability that broke. Tier 3 gets today's progressive listing routing.ts . Stable prefix first, variable last , so prompt caching keeps hitting. History compaction. After a request finishes, only its outcome and ids are carried forward, not its tool results. 6. Learning: how the registry fills itself Indexing. On forgeqe init , and incrementally on file change, the code graph and cases sources are indexed into entities , aliases and links . ADO and Jira items are indexed when they are first fetched. Promotion. A Tier 2 or Tier 3 run that passes, and passes the judge when it is on, writes or updates its plan and checks . A plan needs two passes, or one pass plus user confirmation, before it is allowed to run at Tier 0. Demotion. Failures increment failures . Two failures in a row mark the plan stale , and the next run goes to Tier 1 or 2. 7. Measurement and acceptance The ledger runs makes cost measurable per tier and per entity. forgeqe cost reports the following metrics. Each must meet its target before a phase counts as done. Metric Target Cost of a rerun of a known passing test, vs. its first run ≤5% Tier 0: 0 tokens Share of reruns served at Tier 0 or Tier 1 ≥90% Tier escalation rate on unchanged apps ≤5% False pass rate Tier 0 pass that a Tier 1 canary then fails 0 known; every one investigated Release check "are we ready", scope known 0–1 agent calls The evaluation is an offline replay suite under src/evals . It holds recorded requests rerun, reworded rerun, changed app, new goal , each with an expected tier and outcome. It runs on every change to the resolver, router or registry, and live against the real model before release. 8. Compatibility and rollout safety Nothing here may change what ForgeQE does today until it has been shown to give the same results. Built alongside, never in place of registry.mode: off shadow on in forgeqe.yaml . It defaulted to off through phases 1 and 2, and to on from 2026 10 15, after the live results in sections 9–10. With off , every request takes the agent's path, unchanged. The new code lives in src/registry/ . Existing modules gain only small hooks at their entry points: the chat request handler, the command parser and config. The chat agent, page memory, replay modes and tools keep their behaviour. Any registry error missing, locked or corrupt database, an exception in the resolver falls back to today's path. The registry is a cache: deleting it loses savings, never behaviour. Existing stores page memory, code graph, quality history, run folders keep their formats. The registry reads and indexes them and never writes to them. Tier 0 runs through the same browser run tool the agent calls. Existing test reuse, page memory replay, the configured replay mode, reports and quality checks all apply as they do today. Proven before it is switched on Tests that lock in today's behaviour. Written before the hooks, they pin down today's results: a request with the registry off goes to the agent, and the rerun link goes to the agent. They have to pass unchanged afterwards. Shadow mode. The resolver decides and records what it would do runs with mode = shadow , while the request still takes today's path. The decisions are compared with real outcomes before on . False pass check. During rollout, every Tier 0 pass is re checked at Tier 1. Any disagreement blocks the next phase. The full suite. Every existing test passes unchanged in every phase, with no existing test edited to make it pass. Switched on gradually One phase per release. Each one can be turned off on its own. A live check against the real model, Azure DevOps and Teams before each phase is called done. Every reply says which tier answered it. /rerun is an explicit command, and the agent remains one sentence away: anything the resolver is unsure of goes to it. 9. Phase 1 live result 2026 10 15 Live run against Azure OpenAI gpt 5.4 and a real headless Chrome: a /rerun of a 27 step practice form run whose first run used 242K tokens. Result Resolver Matched the run; no chat agent calls Page memory Replayed 26 of 27 steps without the model Step 27 A read only evaluate reading the fields to check them is not replayable, so the browser agent took over for 14 model steps Cost 178K tokens: 74% of the first run. The target is not met The remaining cost is the browser agent's check after replay. Phase 2 is the step that reaches the target. Read only steps evaluate , extract and the final check must be answered from recorded end state checks run.json already records checks with expected values . The agent comes in only when a check fails. 10. Phase 2 live result 2026 10 15 What phase 2 adds, with registry.mode: on only: evaluate steps whose script only reads the page are left out of a replay. The test is on the script's source and conservative: any assignment, any page changing call, any request or deferred code counts as writing. Checked against every evaluate in a live project's flows: no write was classed as read only. A passing run's record check results are kept in its flow, each with the step it was recorded after. A replay finds each check on the page again after that step, with no model. If every check holds, the run passes with no model. The first check that does not hold stops the replay there, and the agent takes over on that page today's path . The agent still judges the run when: a check is dynamic, the flow has not passed for 30 days, or it is every 10th replay of the flow the canary . Live, Azure OpenAI gpt 5.4 and headless Chrome: Flow Run Tokens vs. first run Wikipedia search 3 steps, 1 check first run 50.3K 100% rerun: the search suggestion did not show in time, so the agent took 2 steps 25.1K 50% rerun: replay complete, the check held 0 0% 6 s rerun with the saved check changed to text the page does not show 25.1K the replay refused to pass it, and the agent judged the real page Practice form playground 27+ steps reruns 122K, 135K, 82K 50%, 56%, 34% The practice page is built to resist replay: double click targets, clipboard paste and per key typing that replay's direct input does not reproduce. Its checks correctly never passed a replay that ended in a different state. Flows like that stay with the agent until replay can repeat those inputs a later phase . 11. Rollout Phase Scope Done when 1 Registry entities, aliases, plans, runs . Resolver plus Tier 0 for /rerun , the rerun link, and case and run ids. Fingerprint matching for test cases. Reply filled in from the result. A rerun of a known passing case logs 0 tokens; a reworded request still finds its flow 2 Recorded end state checks replace the post replay agent check. Canary and freshness rules. verify default costs one small model call or none; the false pass suite stays green 3 Router small model plus Tier 1 adapt. Repo code tests run directly dotnet test / npx playwright test with filters, results files parsed . Reworded and new data reruns at ≤5% 4 Tool result cache, context packs, history compaction. Release check as a fixed workflow. The release check takes 0–1 agent calls; the agent's average context per call is down by half 5 forgeqe cost report and the evaluation suite in CI Metrics in section 7 reported per release 12. Per turn tool scope 2026 10 17 Tool definitions are part of the fixed overhead in section 1, and they grew with the desktop, mobile and TestMu tools. The forgeqe agent's fixed context went past its budget. ForgeQE's agent now gets the tools of the capabilities a turn needs, not all of them src/mcp/scope.ts ; see ARCHITECTURE.md ARCHITECTURE.md tool scope srcmcpscopets srccapabilities : Every turn: the core help and setup, use capabilities , the test environments and their apps . Picked without a model call: up to four capabilities matched from the request's words, the apps it names, its links and issue keys. A capability the project has no apps or tracker for is not picked from words alone. Sticky: capabilities whose tools ran in the last three turns. On request: use capabilities adds one when the request turns out to need it, and ForgeQE continues the same request. forgeqe context , measured on this repo: Tokens The forgeqe agent's fixed context prompt 6.2K + core tools 1.6K 7.8K of a 10K budget A turn with the four largest capabilities 14.7K Every tool on every turn FORGEQE TOOL SCOPE=off about 26.7K Largest single capability api testing , systems 1.8K of a 2.5K budget per capability A typical turn "replay the courier login on Maestro" adds one or two capabilities, around 1–3K. Beyond the cost, fewer tools in view keep the agent from mixing up similar ones browser run , desktop explore , mobile explore . The test tests/agents.test.ts fails when an agent or a capability passes its budget. That keeps new tools from bringing the fixed overhead back. Still to measure: live model evaluations of the tool picks against FORGEQE TOOL SCOPE=off : the success rate, the use capabilities calls per request, and tokens per request. 13. Page memory at every step 2026 10 21 A suite run in a live project three Toolshop cases, Azure OpenAI gpt 5.4 showed why a rerun of a known case still cost what its first run did: Run Model steps Input tokens Replayed ADO 3287, first run an expected result did not hold at step 7 11 88K 0 ADO 3287, the reproduce run straight after 29 243K 0 Each model step costs about 8K input tokens, 6.3K of it the cached system prefix: the live page is a small part. So page memory can only lower cost by taking steps away from the model, and two things kept it from doing that: 1. A failed case saved nothing to replay. resume steps were kept for errors only; a run that failed because an expected result did not hold assertion failed , which is what a reproduce run or a rerun of a failing case is about saved no steps, and the next run explored the whole case again. Now the steps up to the first check that did not hold are kept assertion resume , marked assertion: true , the next run replays them, and the handoff tells the agent to check that result again where it is, not to redo the steps or try to make it true. 2. Known controls were described, not addressable. The site memory hints in the system prompt named the controls earlier runs used, but an action needs the element's index in this step's list, which changes with every page load, so the agent read the whole list anyway. Now each page memory knows gets a note after the element list, before the model call, naming up to 10 controls earlier runs used with the index each has right now MemoryStore.known controls , through the library's per step context messages . The page is observed once per step and that snapshot also scores the step's actions. 3. A replay to a failed check handed the check to the agent. The page that failed often shows its message only briefly a toast , so it was gone by the agent's first step, and the agent spent six steps looking for it live: 49.5K tokens, more than the first run . Now, with registry.mode: on and replay: verify , the run looks for the text the page showed instead right after the replay, with no model reproduced by check . Finding it again fails the run the same way at 0 tokens; not finding it hands over to the agent as before. A failure text that a passing check of that run also found a heading, the product name is never kept for this, since it shows whatever the outcome. Live, Toolshop, headless Chrome, Azure OpenAI gpt 5.4, a clean memory folder: Run Model steps Tokens Result A: first run of a 3 step case whose last expected result does not hold 5 37.1K failed; kept the 3 steps up to the failed check B: the same case again a rerun or reproduce run 0 0 5 s replayed 3 steps, found the same failure text, failed the same way C: a new goal on the same pages 4 30.1K passed; the agent was told the known control on each page with its index Run C is a different task, so it explores; the per step note saves steps on pages the site's earlier runs used, but does not replace exploration of a new goal. 13.1 Every case, every area 2026 10 21 The same project's history showed the wider gap: of 20 recorded web runs only 4 replayed anything 2.7M tokens in all , almost every miss a goal worded differently from its flow. Mobile and desktop explores never read what an earlier one saved, desktop and mobile heals were found again on every replay, API plans were made again for the same cases, and only browser goals could be rerun without the agent. What now holds in every area: Area Before the model is called No model at all when Browser the goal's flow, its failed run steps, an edited case's unchanged steps, else the start it shares with another goal on the host flowmatch checks of a replayed flow hold section 10 ; a failed check shows the same failure text again Mobile, desktop the goal's workflow, its failed run steps, else the shared start in the app app memory ; known controls marked for the model the goal's workflow replays and its checks hold Replay heals the target an earlier heal found it is on screen API the plan made from the same cases or text and operations always, for a repeated plan; saved API calls replay in browser flows when the status matches Reruns the registry runs the plan's own tool browser, mobile, desktop, API from the shell or forgeqe run the tool needs none forgeqe memory stats reports it per area. On the live project before this change: browser 18 runs, 4 22% reused history, none without the model. The memory gate workflow keeps it from regressing.

h: Limit what an area may use
x: With more than one model in llms.json , ForgeQE can give each kind of work the model it needs. A small, fast, cheap model can plan and review. A strong model can write code and find root causes. A model that takes screenshots drives the browser, and a model with a large window reads a large pull request. You do not need to know what each model can do: ForgeQE finds out. Turn it on In forgeqe.yaml : forgeqe init writes routing: auto for new projects. With no routing line it is off. shadow decides and logs each pick in the session log model.route but changes nothing, so you can see what the router would do before you let it. Shadow still runs the live checks and the rating call described below. Whatever routing says, the model an area gets must work: its key or sign in is set and it passed a live call one per model, kept for a day in .forgeqe/model checks.json once it passes; a failed one is never kept, and a failed check in model profile.json is checked again . When it does not, the next model that works is used, a GitHub Copilot profile first, and ForgeQE says why and how to fix the first. When none works, the error lists each model with the fix. Only profile skips this. With auto , a GitHub Copilot seat counts as costing nothing more per call, so it is picked whenever it is rated good enough. See the picks, and every model's check with its fix: The areas of work Area What runs in it Needs agent ForgeQE's agent: the shell, forgeqe run , forgeqe mcp tool calls; rated 4+ browser Browser, desktop and mobile runs, from screenshots images; rated 4+ coding Scribe writing and healing tests, API tests tool calls; rated 5 review Test reviewer, pull request review, evaluation judge tool calls; rated 3+ analysis Root cause of defects tool calls; rated 5 planning Refine, finding tests, API scenarios, exploratory charters tool calls; rated 3+ How a model is picked 1. Your choices win. profile or WP LLM PROFILE and code.model keep the router out. A profile pinned in llm.routes is used for its area. code.review profile still sets the reviewer. 2. Facts rule models out. The router never picks a model that: has no key, or failed its live check; takes no images, for browser work; takes no tool calls, for agent work; has a window too small for the prompt a large pull request diff, for example . The facts come from llms.json , a live check, and the public model lists models.dev and LiteLLM that ForgeQE already downloads for prices. A fact that nobody knows never rules a model out. 3. Ratings pick among the rest. The cheapest model rated at the area's bar is picked. Writing code and finding root causes ask for 5, because a weaker model there costs more in failed attempts than it saves. If no model reaches the bar, the best rated one is picked. With no ratings yet, the active profile is kept unless a fact rules it out. 4. A failed answer escalates once. When a root cause analysis finds nothing, or finds a cause with low confidence although it could read the product's code, it runs again on a stronger model: one rated higher for the area, or rated the same and priced higher. Both runs are counted in its cost. The same configuration and task always give the same model. A pick changes only when the models, the ratings or the size of the prompt change. Each pick is shown once "Model for planning: mini … " and is written to the session log. How ForgeQE learns the models The first routed call in a project with two or more usable profiles does this once: 1. A live check of each model python m forgeqe engine probe : one short structured answer and one image. This finds a deployment that does not exist, a wrong key, and whether the model really takes images. It also measures how fast the model answers. 2. One rating call. The active profile's model receives the facts of every model, never a key, an endpoint or an account. It rates each model 1–5 for each area and gives it a tier fast, balanced or strong . The result is kept in .forgeqe/model profile.json next to forgeqe.yaml . ForgeQE uses it until the profiles in llms.json change provider, model, deployment or endpoint . You can edit the ratings. ForgeQE keeps your edits while the profiles stay the same. It checks the file every time it reads it: names that are not profiles and unknown areas are dropped, and ratings are rounded to whole numbers from 1 to 5. The live checks reach every profile in llms.json that has a key, whatever llm.routes pins. A pin keeps your runs' data on one deployment; the checks carry nothing from your runs. To send nothing to the other profiles at all, use routing: off , keep one profile with a key, or pass profile .
